references: Supplied Constitutional Law detailed module notes, Module 1
modules.scope: Based on supplied study notes, not independently authenticated copies of the assigned judicial opinions. Case summaries remain review drafts. Historical cases are discussed for the assigned course, not as a complete statement of present law.

sections.heading: Constitutional structure
sections.body: Begin with the Constitution as a source of delegated powers, institutional design, and limits. Identify the government actor and the source of that actor’s authority before discussing whether its policy is desirable. Separate federalism, which distributes authority between national and state governments, from separation of powers, which distributes responsibilities among national branches. A dispute can implicate both dimensions.

sections.heading: Powers and rights are different questions
sections.body: Federal actors require a constitutional basis for action; state governments generally exercise a broader police power subject to constitutional limits. A claim that Congress lacks an enumerated power differs from a claim that an otherwise authorized measure violates a protected right. Work through both questions where the facts support them. Do not assume a legitimate governmental purpose alone supplies the missing constitutional authority.

sections.heading: Judicial role and analysis
sections.body: Judicial review operates through actual cases and controversies, so identify the court’s jurisdiction and the claimant’s ability to obtain the requested remedy. Constitutional supremacy does not eliminate procedural limits on adjudication. When reading an opinion, separate the governing text, the dispute’s procedural posture, the legal rule, its application, and the disposition. A judicial statement outside the ground necessary to resolve the case may have a different status from the holding.

sections.heading: Reading method
sections.body: For each assignment, make an actor–power–limitation–remedy map. Record which constitutional provision supports the power, which provision or structural principle limits it, and what a court could actually order. Use a case’s material facts to explain the boundary of the rule. The optional guide listed in the outline was not supplied, and a citation in the syllabus is not itself the underlying opinion.

sections.heading: Supremacy, validity and preemption
sections.body: The Supremacy Clause gives priority to valid federal law when federal and state obligations conflict. The validity qualification matters: a federal label does not cure a constitutional defect. Preemption concerns the displacement of state law in a field or particular conflict, while supremacy supplies the federal-state priority framework. A valid regulation can matter against a conflicting state statute; the analysis is not a mechanical ranking in which every statute defeats every regulation. Judicial constitutional interpretation can invalidate legislative action, so a list of constitutions, statutes, regulations and cases is not a simple ranking that makes decisions the weakest source.

sections.heading: Dual sovereignty and reserved powers
sections.body: Federal and state governments coexist as distinct sovereign systems. Shared authority to tax or maintain courts does not mean a state controls federal institutions: each operates its own governmental system within constitutional constraints. The Tenth Amendment refers to powers not delegated to the United States and not prohibited to the states. It should be read with express limits on state action, including Article I, Section 10, rather than as a promise of unlimited state authority. Always identify the sovereign, constitutional source and relevant restriction before evaluating the particular act.

sections.heading: Institutional design and history
sections.body: The supplied notes connect the Constitution’s stronger national structure to weaknesses under the Articles of Confederation, including difficulties involving interstate and foreign trade. Separation of powers divides federal institutional roles; checks and balances address how branches constrain one another. Congress may legislate while the President can sign or veto legislation, and courts resolve constitutional issues within actual cases. These relationships do not eliminate the need to establish the power for a particular action. Individual-rights guarantees can impose an independent limitation even when the government otherwise possesses power.

sections.heading: Federalism and separation of powers
sections.body:
Federalism allocates power between federal and state governments; separation of powers divides authority among federal branches. The notes connect both structures with checks on concentrated governmental power. Treat supremacy as a rule about valid federal law, not an assertion that states have no sovereignty.

Exam checklist: Identify the level of government, branch and source of power.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Congress pursues a worthwhile policy. Does a desirable goal alone establish constitutional authority to act?

Governing principle — Constitutional structure
Begin with the Constitution as a source of delegated powers, institutional design, and limits. Identify the government actor and the source of that actor’s authority before discussing whether its policy is desirable. Separate federalism, which distributes authority between national and state governments, from separation of powers, which distributes responsibilities among national branches. A dispute can implicate both dimensions.

Application and answer
No. Identify the government actor, the source and scope of delegated power, and any separate constitutional limitation. Policy desirability does not supply missing authority.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A desirable governmental policy supplies constitutional authority even when no constitutional source supports the action.
Do not use this incorrect approach: State sovereignty means state law always prevails over valid conflicting federal law.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Separation of powers and federalism describe the same division between national and state institutions.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A challenge concerns both federal power over states and the allocation of power between Congress and the President. Which structural doctrines differ?

Governing principle — Powers and rights are different questions
Federal actors require a constitutional basis for action; state governments generally exercise a broader police power subject to constitutional limits. A claim that Congress lacks an enumerated power differs from a claim that an otherwise authorized measure violates a protected right. Work through both questions where the facts support them. Do not assume a legitimate governmental purpose alone supplies the missing constitutional authority.

Application and answer
Federalism concerns national-state allocation; separation of powers concerns allocation among national branches. Analyze each supported issue separately and then identify jurisdiction and the available remedy.

Common mistakes to avoid

Do not use this incorrect approach: State sovereignty means state law always prevails over valid conflicting federal law.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Separation of powers and federalism describe the same division between national and state institutions.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Federal Jurisdiction and Judicial Review
references: Supplied Constitutional Law detailed module notes, Module 2; assigned Marbury, McCardle, Martin and Cooper readings
modules.scope: Based on supplied study notes, not independently authenticated copies of the assigned judicial opinions. Case summaries remain review drafts. Historical cases are discussed for the assigned course, not as a complete statement of present law.

sections.heading: Two jurisdictional layers
sections.body: Federal judicial power must fit an Article III category and a statutory jurisdictional grant. A claim’s federal character does not answer every jurisdictional question. Distinguish the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction from its appellate jurisdiction, and distinguish the constitutionally created Supreme Court from lower federal courts that Congress establishes. Identify the court and posture before discussing the merits.

sections.heading: Marbury and McCardle
sections.body: Marbury separates a legal right, the availability of a remedy in principle, and the jurisdiction of the court asked to supply it. The Court did not issue the requested writ because the claimed original jurisdiction exceeded Article III. McCardle concerns Congress’s withdrawal of the particular statutory appellate route used in a pending habeas appeal. It did not hold the detention constitutional or decide that Congress can eliminate every conceivable avenue of review.

sections.heading: Martin and Cooper
sections.body: Martin confirms that Supreme Court review can reach state-court judgments involving federal law; the source of the federal issue matters more than the tribunal in which litigation began. Uniform federal meaning and supremacy support that authority. Cooper addresses state officials’ obligation to comply with constitutional rulings rather than treating federal rights as optional when compliance provokes hostility. Keep state-court appellate review separate from the duty of state actors to obey controlling constitutional law.

sections.heading: Exam synthesis
sections.body: Ask which court is being asked to act, whether original or appellate authority is invoked, what Article III permits, what statute grants, and whether justiciability requirements are met. Then identify the legal issue and remedy. Explain why jurisdiction and merits are separate: establishing that government acted unlawfully does not automatically establish that this court can grant this form of relief. Use each assigned case for the specific institutional problem it resolved rather than citing all four as interchangeable statements of judicial power.

sections.heading: Constitutional and statutory jurisdiction
sections.body:
Federal courts need authority within Article III and an applicable statutory grant. An important federal issue does not by itself supply jurisdiction. The notes distinguish original and appellate jurisdiction and connect judicial review to deciding actual disputes within these limits.

Exam checklist: Identify court, posture, Article III category, statutory authorization and case-or-controversy limits.

sections.heading: Case brief — Marbury v. Madison
sections.body:
5 U.S. 137 (1803)

Facts: Marbury’s judicial commission was signed and sealed but not delivered before the change of presidential administration. Madison withheld it at Jefferson’s direction.

Posture: Marbury sought an original writ of mandamus directly from the Supreme Court.

Issue: Could this Court compel delivery under its claimed statutory original jurisdiction?

Holding: The writ was denied for lack of original jurisdiction, despite Marbury’s legal entitlement.

Reasoning: The Court separated the right to the office, availability of a remedy, and the tribunal’s jurisdiction. A statute could not enlarge the original jurisdiction Article III fixed. In resolving conflicting laws, the Court applied the superior Constitution.

Rule: A court must possess jurisdiction, and legislation conflicting with the Constitution cannot supply a valid enlargement of it.

Significance: Keep judicial review separate from a successful remedy. Marbury did not receive the requested commission through the Court.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Ex parte McCardle
sections.body:
74 U.S. 506 (1869)

Facts: A military detainee challenging Reconstruction sought habeas relief through an appellate route created by the 1867 statute. Congress withdrew that route while his appeal was pending.

Posture: Appeal from denial of habeas relief, after argument but before judgment.

Issue: Did repeal remove the Court’s authority over this appeal?

Holding: The appeal was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

Reasoning: The Exceptions Clause allowed Congress to withdraw the particular appellate grant. The repeal preserved no pending-case exception. The Court distinguished that grant from other habeas authority and did not decide the constitutional merits of detention.

Rule: The Court cannot reach merits once the applicable appellate jurisdiction has been validly withdrawn.

Significance: Identify the exact route removed. Do not state that McCardle approved detention or eliminated all possible habeas review.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Martin v. Hunter’s Lessee
sections.body:
14 U.S. 304 (1816)

Facts: Competing claims to Virginia land implicated federal treaties. Virginia’s highest court resisted the Supreme Court’s earlier reversal.

Posture: Review following the state court’s refusal to follow the federal mandate.

Issue: May the Supreme Court review state judgments resolving federal questions?

Holding: The Court upheld its appellate authority over the federal issue.

Reasoning: Article III describes categories of cases rather than only proceedings begun in federal courts. Supreme Court review protects supremacy and national uniformity of federal law, even where state courts initially adjudicate the dispute.

Rule: Authorized Supreme Court appellate review extends to qualifying state-court federal-law decisions.

Significance: Distinguish federal-question review from general supervision of state-law issues.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Cooper v. Aaron
sections.body:
358 U.S. 1 (1958)

Facts: Arkansas resistance and unrest obstructed the school district’s desegregation plan. The district sought a lengthy postponement.

Posture: The Supreme Court reviewed the rejection of a district-court delay.

Issue: Could official resistance or hostility justify suspending desegregation obligations?

Holding: The requested delay was denied; constitutional obligations remained binding.

Reasoning: Constitutional supremacy and officials’ oaths prevented state actors from nullifying Brown. Allowing hostility to defeat rights would reward resistance and undermine the authority of federal law.

Rule: State officials must comply with controlling constitutional decisions and cannot sacrifice established rights to public hostility.

Significance: Use Cooper for compliance and supremacy, while recognizing that judicial enforcement also depends on institutional cooperation.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A plaintiff has a legal right and an appropriate remedy in principle. Must the Supreme Court grant that remedy in an original action?

Governing principle — Two jurisdictional layers
Federal judicial power must fit an Article III category and a statutory jurisdictional grant. A claim’s federal character does not answer every jurisdictional question. Distinguish the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction from its appellate jurisdiction, and distinguish the constitutionally created Supreme Court from lower federal courts that Congress establishes. Identify the court and posture before discussing the merits.

Application and answer
No. It still needs the constitutionally and statutorily required jurisdiction. Marbury separates entitlement, remedy and the power of this tribunal to supply it.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A legal right automatically gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to order any suitable remedy.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A jurisdictional dismissal necessarily resolves the constitutional merits in favor of the government.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Supreme Court review of a federal issue in a state judgment is constitutionally impossible.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Congress repeals a pending appeal’s statutory route. Does dismissal necessarily establish that the challenged detention was constitutional?

Governing principle — Marbury and McCardle
Marbury separates a legal right, the availability of a remedy in principle, and the jurisdiction of the court asked to supply it. The Court did not issue the requested writ because the claimed original jurisdiction exceeded Article III. McCardle concerns Congress’s withdrawal of the particular statutory appellate route used in a pending habeas appeal. It did not hold the detention constitutional or decide that Congress can eliminate every conceivable avenue of review.

Application and answer
No. McCardle separates jurisdiction from merits and identifies the particular route removed. Determine whether another review route remains instead of assuming every form of judicial review disappeared.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A legal right automatically gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to order any suitable remedy.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A jurisdictional dismissal necessarily resolves the constitutional merits in favor of the government.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Supreme Court review of a federal issue in a state judgment is constitutionally impossible.

cards.title:
Explain and qualify this statement: 137 (1803)

Facts: Marbury’s judicial commission was signed and sealed but not delivered before the change of presidential administration.
cards.answer:
5 U.S. 137 (1803)

Facts: Marbury’s judicial commission was signed and sealed but not delivered before the change of presidential administration. Madison withheld it at Jefferson’s direction.

Posture: Marbury sought an original writ of mandamus directly from the Supreme Court.

Issue: Could this Court compel delivery under its claimed statutory original jurisdiction?

Holding: The writ was denied for lack of original jurisdiction, despite Marbury’s legal entitlement.

Reasoning: The Court separated the right to the office, availability of a remedy, and the tribunal’s jurisdiction. A statute could not enlarge the original jurisdiction Article III fixed. In resolving conflicting laws, the Court applied the superior Constitution.

Rule: A court must possess jurisdiction, and legislation conflicting with the Constitution cannot supply a valid enlargement of it.

Significance: Keep judicial review separate from a successful remedy. Marbury did not receive the requested commission through the Court.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Justiciability: Standing
references: Supplied Constitutional Law detailed module notes, Module 3; assigned standing cases
Supplied Constitutional Law Module 3 detailed notes, optional case discussions
modules.scope: Based on supplied study notes, not independently authenticated copies of the assigned judicial opinions. Case summaries remain review drafts. Historical cases are discussed for the assigned course, not as a complete statement of present law.

sections.heading: Constitutional minimum
sections.body: Analyze injury in fact, traceability, and redressability separately for each plaintiff, claim, and requested remedy. A concrete, personal injury must be actual or sufficiently imminent rather than an abstract desire for government compliance. Traceability asks whether the challenged conduct materially explains the injury; redressability asks whether the requested judicial relief would likely alleviate it. Uncontrolled third-party decisions can create problems for either inquiry.

sections.heading: Lujan and Lyons
sections.body: Lujan’s members had an interest in observing wildlife, but vague future plans did not establish imminent personal injury. The requested relief also raised redressability problems. Lyons shows why past injury may support a damages claim while failing to establish the future threat needed for an injunction. Do not convert evidence of a completed unlawful act into proof that the same plaintiff will personally experience it again.

sections.heading: Organizations, taxpayers, and third parties
sections.body: Organizational representation of members requires identifying an affected member and the relationship between the claim, the organization’s purpose, and individual participation. United Food allows statutory modification of the prudential participation restriction, not abolition of Article III injury. Flast recognizes a narrow taxpayer exception tied to taxing-and-spending action and a specific constitutional limitation. Eisenstadt illustrates third-party-rights reasoning in a prosecuted distributor’s challenge, not a general permission to litigate anyone’s rights.

sections.heading: Statutory labels and answer structure
sections.body: The course’s discussion of Air Courier uses zone-of-interests terminology. Keep that statutory cause-of-action inquiry distinct from the constitutional minimum, and flag the terminology rather than merging it into injury in fact. Structure an answer plaintiff by plaintiff and remedy by remedy. Identify the personal stake, causal chain, practical effect of relief, and any additional representational or statutory issue. A strong merits argument does not cure a standing defect.

sections.heading: Three different threshold failures
sections.body: Newdow, Murthy and FDA v. Alliance concern access to adjudication, but their reasoning should not be collapsed into one slogan. In the supplied notes, Newdow concerns a parent’s disputed authority to assert the child’s interests amid unresolved family-law arrangements. Murthy concerns traceability and redressability through independently acting platforms. FDA v. Alliance concerns the challengers’ own legally sufficient injury and the asserted connections to regulation of other people. Identify the particular plaintiff, right, defendant and remedy in each example before discussing the threshold defect.

sections.heading: From comparison to application
sections.body: For a new problem, ask whose injury is asserted, how the challenged defendant caused it, and how the proposed order would relieve it. A third-party representative must establish the legally relevant relationship; a causal chain must identify concrete links through intermediaries. An organization does not establish an injury merely by choosing to spend resources opposing a policy. Distinguish injury to operations from disagreement and voluntary advocacy spending. Do not infer a decision about a policy’s constitutionality or legality from dismissal on a threshold ground. These comparisons describe the supplied secondary notes, not independently supplied full opinions.

sections.heading: Review checklist
sections.body: Identify the parties, procedural posture, question presented and actual disposition. State the legal rule in the form relevant to the assigned issue. Apply material facts and distinguish threshold analysis from the merits. Confirm the date and citation where similarly named decisions appear in separate assignments. Check the linked original material before verifying this draft.

sections.heading: Article III standing
sections.body:
Standing requires a personal injury that is concrete and particularized, actual or sufficiently imminent, traceable to the defendant, and likely to be redressed by the requested relief. The requested remedy matters: a past injury does not by itself demonstrate the future threat needed for an injunction.

Exam checklist: Analyze injury, traceability, redressability and each requested form of relief.

sections.heading: Case brief — Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife
sections.body:
504 U.S. 555 (1992)

Facts: Organizations attacked a rule limiting endangered-species consultation. Members described past foreign travel and undated plans to return.

Posture: Standing challenge to the organizations’ requested declaratory and injunctive relief.

Issue: Did the members establish imminent personal injury and redressability?

Holding: The organizations failed to establish Article III standing.

Reasoning: An interest in observing animals can be cognizable, but a vague someday intention did not establish actual or imminent personal harm. The effects of the requested order on third parties also created redressability problems.

Rule: Article III requires a concrete personal injury, traceability, and likely redress by the requested relief.

Significance: State the factual defect in each element; do not confuse an important environmental issue with a personal stake.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — City of Los Angeles v. Lyons
sections.body:
461 U.S. 95 (1983)

Facts: Lyons alleged injury from a police chokehold during a traffic stop and sought damages and prospective restrictions on chokeholds.

Posture: Challenge to standing for an injunction.

Issue: Did his past encounter establish a sufficient future threat for injunctive relief?

Holding: It did not establish the required real and immediate future threat.

Reasoning: The future injury depended on another police encounter and another decision to apply a chokehold to Lyons. Past injury supported a different remedial inquiry and did not establish the necessary personal risk of recurrence.

Rule: Standing must be established for each requested remedy; past injury alone does not necessarily support an injunction.

Significance: Analyze damages and prospective relief separately rather than granting or denying standing for the entire complaint.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — United Food and Commercial Workers Union Local 751 v. Brown Group
sections.body:
517 U.S. 544 (1996)

Facts: A union sought backpay and benefits for affected workers under a statute expressly allowing representative labor-organization suits.

Posture: Dispute about an association’s ability to seek member damages.

Issue: Could Congress displace the usual individual-participation restriction?

Holding: Yes; the participation restriction was prudential and could be altered by statute.

Reasoning: Member injury and a suitable organizational connection remain distinct from the convenience concerns behind individual participation. Congress’s authorization could change the prudential restriction without eliminating Article III requirements.

Rule: Statutory representative authority can modify prudential associational-standing restrictions, not constitutional injury requirements.

Significance: Do not conclude that Congress may authorize an organization to sue without any injured member or redressable controversy.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Air Courier Conference of America v. American Postal Workers Union
sections.body:
498 U.S. 517 (1991)

Facts: Postal employees and unions challenged relaxed restrictions on private international remailing, asserting threatened jobs and revenue.

Posture: Challenge to the statutory basis for pursuing the postal-law claim.

Issue: Were postal workers’ employment interests within the statute’s protected zone?

Holding: The employment interests were outside the relevant zone of interests.

Reasoning: The statutory scheme protected postal revenues and the postal system rather than employment security as such. An economic injury did not alone establish that the particular statute authorized this plaintiff’s challenge.

Rule: A statutory claim requires the plaintiff’s interests to fall within the relevant statutory protection.

Significance: The course’s historical standing terminology should be distinguished from the modern cause-of-action characterization.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Flast v. Cohen
sections.body:
392 U.S. 83 (1968)

Facts: Federal taxpayers challenged congressional expenditures supporting religious-school instruction and materials.

Posture: Taxpayer-standing challenge to an Establishment Clause claim.

Issue: Did the claim fit the narrow exception to the general bar on generalized taxpayer grievances?

Holding: The taxpayers met the exception’s requirements.

Reasoning: The challenge connected taxpayer status to a taxing-and-spending enactment and to a specific constitutional limit on that power. The Court did not create a general right to challenge any unconstitutional action involving federal money.

Rule: Flast requires both the enactment nexus and the specific-constitutional-limitation nexus.

Significance: State the general bar first and apply both nexuses narrowly.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Eisenstadt v. Baird
sections.body:
405 U.S. 438 (1972)

Facts: Baird distributed contraceptive foam to an unmarried woman after a lecture and was convicted under a Massachusetts distribution law.

Posture: Challenge to the conviction and the law’s distinction between married and unmarried recipients.

Issue: Could the prosecuted distributor assert the rights of unmarried recipients?

Holding: The Court permitted the third-party claim and invalidated the distinction.

Reasoning: Baird faced prosecution personally, his activity was linked to the recipients’ interests, and practical obstacles affected their ability to litigate the issue themselves. The supplied notes distinguish his role as lecturer from an inaccurate physician description.

Rule: A personally injured litigant may satisfy a recognized exception to the ordinary restriction on asserting another person’s rights.

Significance: Analyze the representative exception instead of treating third-party standing as an absolute prohibition.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Elk Grove Unified School District v. Newdow
sections.body:
542 U.S. 1 (2004)

Facts: Newdow challenged the school-led Pledge on behalf of himself and his daughter while the child’s mother disputed his litigation authority under the custody arrangement.

Posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.

Issue: Could he assert the child’s interests despite uncertain representative authority?

Holding: The Court declined to reach the constitutional merits on the standing-related ground described in the supplied notes.

Reasoning: The unsettled family-law relationship and competing parental authority made this an unsuitable vehicle for adjudicating the asserted rights.

Rule: A federal constitutional theory does not automatically resolve who may represent a child where domestic-relations authority is contested.

Significance: Distinguish the threshold ruling from a merits holding about the Pledge, and identify whose rights the claimant seeks to litigate.

Source scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

sections.heading: Case brief — Murthy v. Missouri
sections.body:
603 U.S. 43 (2024)

Facts: States and social-media users sought prospective restrictions on officials’ communications with platforms, alleging that government pressure caused moderation.

Posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.

Issue: Were the asserted future injuries sufficiently traceable to the named officials and redressable?

Holding: The Court found that the plaintiffs lacked standing on the record.

Reasoning: The claimed chain did not connect particular plaintiffs’ moderation injuries to particular official communications, and platforms retained independent incentives and choices.

Rule: An injunction claim involving independent intermediaries still requires concrete causal links and likely redress for the plaintiff.

Significance: Do not infer that the Court approved the challenged conduct; the threshold ruling left the constitutional merits unresolved.

Source scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

sections.heading: Case brief — FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine
sections.body:
602 U.S. 367 (2024)

Facts: Doctors and associations who neither prescribed nor used the drug challenged FDA actions affecting others’ access to mifepristone.

Posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.

Issue: Did the challengers show the required personal injury, causation and redressability?

Holding: The Court unanimously found no standing and did not decide the FDA actions’ legality under the APA.

Reasoning: Moral opposition was not a personal injury; the asserted workload and conscience chains were insufficient on the record. An organization could not manufacture standing merely by spending money opposing a policy.

Rule: A policy disagreement or self-selected advocacy expense does not replace a legally sufficient injury connected to the challenged conduct.

Significance: Analyze standing before the merits and separate organizational injury from an attempt to sue on behalf of members.

Source scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A previously injured plaintiff seeks damages and an injunction based only on the past event. How should standing be analyzed?

Governing principle — Constitutional minimum
Analyze injury in fact, traceability, and redressability separately for each plaintiff, claim, and requested remedy. A concrete, personal injury must be actual or sufficiently imminent rather than an abstract desire for government compliance. Traceability asks whether the challenged conduct materially explains the injury; redressability asks whether the requested judicial relief would likely alleviate it. Uncontrolled third-party decisions can create problems for either inquiry.

Application and answer
Separately for each remedy. A completed personal injury can support damages, while an injunction requires an adequate showing of a future personal threat, as Lyons illustrates.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: An earlier injury automatically establishes a sufficient future threat for every injunction requested.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A serious objection to public policy replaces the need for the plaintiff to show a personal injury.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Independent third-party choices can be ignored when analyzing the causal chain and likely effect of relief.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A plaintiff seeks to stop government communications with a private platform. Why must the causal chain be explained?

Governing principle — Lujan and Lyons
Lujan’s members had an interest in observing wildlife, but vague future plans did not establish imminent personal injury. The requested relief also raised redressability problems. Lyons shows why past injury may support a damages claim while failing to establish the future threat needed for an injunction. Do not convert evidence of a completed unlawful act into proof that the same plaintiff will personally experience it again.

Application and answer
Trace the plaintiff’s particular injury to the challenged officials and test whether relief would change the platform’s independent choices. Murthy illustrates why a broad narrative of influence is not enough to establish traceability and redressability.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: An earlier injury automatically establishes a sufficient future threat for every injunction requested.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A serious objection to public policy replaces the need for the plaintiff to show a personal injury.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Independent third-party choices can be ignored when analyzing the causal chain and likely effect of relief.

sections.heading: Timing is distinct from merits
sections.body: Justiciability asks whether this dispute is suitable for adjudication now. Ripeness concerns a controversy asserted too early; mootness concerns whether a previously live controversy has ceased. The doctrines must be analyzed using the requested remedy and actual facts. Poe is the supplied primary anchor for the pre-enforcement side of this module. Its refusal to adjudicate did not validate the challenged contraception restrictions on the merits. The newly retrieved source does not supply all other timing cases assigned in the outline.

sections.heading: Why Poe was dismissed
sections.body: Patients and a physician sought declarations concerning Connecticut restrictions before the prosecutions they feared had occurred. The opinion announcing the judgment emphasized a long enforcement history and the actual prospect of prosecution, not only the fact that legislation remained on the books. The Court’s members differed over the justiciability analysis. Distinguish the plurality’s reasoning, a concurrence in the judgment, and dissenting views rather than attributing every paragraph to a unanimous Court.

sections.heading: How to analyze a pre-enforcement problem
sections.body: Identify the exact conduct the plaintiff wishes to undertake, the prohibition alleged to cover it, actual enforcement actions or threats, and the practical harm of waiting. Compare those facts with the historical enforcement record discussed in Poe. A theoretical legal disagreement or the mere existence of a statute should not replace an explanation of the controversy. Equally, do not turn Poe into a universal requirement that a person first violate a law and accept punishment before any challenge is possible.

sections.heading: Connections and limits
sections.body: For an answer about timing, first separate standing, ripeness and mootness rather than using them as interchangeable labels. sections.heading: Case brief — Poe v. Ullman
sections.body:
367 U.S. 497 (1961)

Facts: Patients and a physician sought pre-enforcement declarations concerning Connecticut contraception restrictions in light of medical needs and the state’s enforcement history.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the controversy was suitable for constitutional adjudication in the form presented.

Holding: The Court dismissed the appeals without resolving the constitutional merits.

Reasoning: The opinion announcing the judgment emphasized the actual enforcement history and absence of the concrete controversy it considered necessary. Separate opinions differed over the justiciability analysis.

Rule: Assess the actual pre-enforcement controversy rather than equating the existence of a criminal statute with a resolved merits dispute.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. A CourtListener mirror copy, not an authenticated official-report scan. Treat the historical decision separately from later legal developments.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Hypothetical: a plaintiff cites an old criminal statute but identifies no recent enforcement or concrete threat. What does Poe require the analysis to examine?

Governing principle — Timing is distinct from merits
Justiciability asks whether this dispute is suitable for adjudication now. Ripeness concerns a controversy asserted too early; mootness concerns whether a previously live controversy has ceased. The doctrines must be analyzed using the requested remedy and actual facts. Poe is the supplied primary anchor for the pre-enforcement side of this module. Its refusal to adjudicate did not validate the challenged contraception restrictions on the merits. The newly retrieved source does not supply all other timing cases assigned in the outline.

Application and answer
Examine the actual controversy, intended conduct, enforcement history and realistic prospect of enforcement, and the reasons for deciding now. Distinguish the threshold question from whether the statute is constitutional; do not turn Poe into a universal rule requiring prosecution first.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A refusal to decide an unripe claim necessarily means the challenged law was upheld on its merits.
Do not use this incorrect approach: The presence of an old criminal prohibition alone conclusively settles every pre-enforcement controversy.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Ripeness and mootness mean exactly the same thing and require no separate temporal analysis.

sections.heading: Political question
sections.body: Start with the particular issue and Baker’s factors rather than declaring every politically important lawsuit nonjusticiable. Textual commitment to another branch and the absence of judicially manageable standards require explanation from the constitutional provision and requested decision. Baker allowed the equal-protection claim to proceed. United States v. Nixon concerned a concrete evidentiary dispute; Nixon v. United States concerned Senate impeachment procedures. sections.body: Supreme Court review cannot change a judgment independently sustained by adequate state law. Identify every ground, remove the challenged federal ground, and ask whether the result would remain. Michigan v. Long addresses an ambiguous decision appearing primarily federal or interwoven with federal law and the effect of a plain statement of independent state-law control. Do not confuse this limit on review with a federal court’s discretionary abstention despite jurisdiction.

sections.body: Analyze clear state consent separately from congressional abrogation. Abrogation requires clear statutory intent and a constitutionally sufficient source of power. Fitzpatrick recognizes the significance of Fourteenth Amendment Section 5; Kimel requires examining whether the particular statute validly enforces the underlying constitutional right. Alden concerns a private federal damages claim in state court and the asserted use of ordinary Article I power. Changing the forum did not by itself defeat the nonconsenting state’s immunity. Pennhurst concerns a federal order directing state officials to obey state law. Labeling the requested relief prospective did not bring that claim within the federal-law rationale for Ex parte Young. Identify defendant, forum, source of the duty and remedy before selecting a supposed exception.

sections.heading: Compare rather than generalize
sections.body: Read these decisions beside Edelman’s distinction between prospective compliance and retrospective treasury payments and Fitzpatrick’s recognition of valid Section 5 enforcement authority. No one factual label resolves the entire inquiry: a suit against an official still needs the relevant federal-law basis, and a federal statute still needs a legally sufficient basis for abrogation. Distinguish the 1984 Pennhurst immunity decision from the 1981 Pennhurst decision separately listed in the spending-power assignments. Similar party names do not make the decisions interchangeable. These are review notes drawn from the supplied study material, not a substitute for absent primary opinions or later-law research.

sections.heading: Review checklist
sections.body: Identify the parties, procedural posture, question presented and actual disposition. State the legal rule in the form relevant to the assigned issue. Apply material facts and distinguish threshold analysis from the merits. Confirm the date and citation where similarly named decisions appear in separate assignments. Check the linked original material before verifying this draft.

sections.heading: Separate threshold doctrines before the merits
sections.body:
Political question, adequate and independent state grounds, and state sovereign immunity ask different threshold questions. Identify the parties, forum, legal source and relief before choosing a doctrine. The notes caution against treating every politically sensitive dispute as nonjusticiable or every claim involving a state as identical.

Exam checklist: Identify who sues whom, where, under what law and for what relief.

sections.heading: Case brief — Baker v. Carr
sections.body:
369 U.S. 186 (1962)

Facts: Tennessee voters challenged longstanding legislative apportionment that failed to reflect population changes.

Posture: Threshold review of whether the equal-protection challenge was justiciable.

Issue: Was this apportionment challenge a political question?

Holding: The equal-protection claim was justiciable.

Reasoning: The pleaded constitutional theory supplied judicially manageable standards, and the issue was not automatically committed elsewhere simply because apportionment was politically sensitive. The decision supplies the framework of political-question factors.

Rule: Political significance alone does not establish a political question; the relevant constitutional assignment and standards matter.

Significance: Identify the theory and relevant Baker factors rather than dismissing every districting dispute categorically.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — United States v. Nixon
sections.body:
418 U.S. 683 (1974)

Facts: A criminal-trial subpoena sought presidential recordings and documents. The President asserted an absolute confidentiality privilege.

Posture: Review of the dispute over enforcement of the subpoena.

Issue: Was the dispute reviewable, and did generalized confidentiality defeat the need for criminal-trial evidence?

Holding: The dispute was reviewable; the qualified privilege did not defeat the demonstrated evidentiary need.

Reasoning: Courts routinely resolve legal privilege disputes. Separation of powers did not eliminate judicial review, and the generalized confidentiality claim yielded to the specific needs of criminal justice on the facts.

Rule: Executive privilege is not an absolute barrier to a concrete criminal evidentiary demand.

Significance: Do not confuse this President Nixon case with the impeachment-procedure decision involving Judge Walter Nixon.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Nixon v. United States
sections.body:
506 U.S. 224 (1993)

Facts: Impeached Judge Walter Nixon objected that a Senate committee, rather than all senators, received evidence.

Posture: Judicial challenge to the Senate’s impeachment-trial procedure.

Issue: Could courts review the Senate’s chosen trial procedures under the cited constitutional text?

Holding: The challenge presented a nonjusticiable political question.

Reasoning: The sole impeachment-trial power was textually committed to the Senate, and the word try did not supply a manageable judicial test for the contested procedure. Judicial involvement threatened the finality and constitutional checking function of impeachment.

Rule: A textual commitment and lack of judicially manageable standards can foreclose merits review.

Significance: Explain the constitutional text and procedural issue; do not describe the result as judicial approval of the procedure’s fairness.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Michigan v. Long
sections.body:
463 U.S. 1032 (1983)

Facts: A Michigan decision suppressing car-search evidence discussed both federal and state constitutional law without clearly establishing an independent state basis.

Posture: Supreme Court examination of its ability to review the state judgment.

Issue: How is an ambiguous, apparently federal or interwoven state decision treated?

Holding: The Court presumed a reviewable federal basis absent a sufficient plain statement.

Reasoning: An adequate independent state ground would preserve the judgment despite reversal on federal law. A clear statement protects a genuinely independent state disposition, while ambiguity in a primarily federal analysis supports review.

Rule: Adequate and independent state grounds bar review; Long addresses the specified ambiguous-opinion setting.

Significance: Ask whether changing federal law could change the judgment. Do not treat any mention of state law as dispositive.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Edelman v. Jordan
sections.body:
415 U.S. 651 (1974)

Facts: Illinois benefit applicants sought future compliance and payment of benefits withheld during earlier violations.

Posture: Review of relief directed at state officials.

Issue: Could nominally equitable relief require retrospective payments from the treasury?

Holding: The retroactive monetary portion was barred by sovereign immunity.

Reasoning: The practical effect was liability payable from state funds for past conduct, unlike prospective compliance relief. Calling the remedy restitution did not change its effect. Participation in the federal program did not alone establish waiver.

Rule: Prospective compliance and retrospective monetary relief require separate immunity analyses.

Significance: Classify the actual financial and temporal effect of each remedy rather than relying on its label.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer
sections.body:
427 U.S. 445 (1976)

Facts: State employees challenged discriminatory retirement benefits under Title VII as amended to cover state employers.

Posture: Question concerning congressional authorization of monetary relief against a state.

Issue: Could Section 5 enforcement legislation abrogate state immunity?

Holding: Yes, Congress could act under its Fourteenth Amendment enforcement authority.

Reasoning: The later Amendment directly limited state power and conferred enforcement authority. The source of congressional power therefore mattered to the immunity analysis.

Rule: Valid Fourteenth Amendment Section 5 legislation can support abrogation when the governing requirements are met.

Significance: Establish both the clear congressional intent and a valid constitutional basis; this case does not validate every statute labeled enforcement.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents
sections.body:
528 U.S. 62 (2000)

Facts: State employees sought damages under the federal age-discrimination statute.

Posture: Review of whether the statute validly displaced state immunity.

Issue: Were clear abrogation language and the invoked enforcement power sufficient here?

Holding: The intended abrogation was not valid Section 5 enforcement as applied to the states.

Reasoning: The substantive constitutional protection against age classifications was narrower than the statute’s broad restrictions. The legislative record and remedy did not establish the required congruence and proportionality.

Rule: Clear intent and valid constitutional power are independent abrogation requirements.

Significance: Compare the constitutional right, evidence of state violations, and statutory remedy rather than stopping at express coverage of states.

Source scope: Review draft based on supplied detailed study notes; the underlying assigned opinion was not independently supplied for verification.

sections.heading: Case brief — Alden v. Maine
sections.body:
527 U.S. 706 (1999)

Facts: Probation officers pursued federal wage claims against Maine in state court after encountering immunity problems in federal court.

Posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.

Issue: Could Congress’s ordinary Article I commerce power authorize the private damages suit against the nonconsenting state?

Holding: The Court held that the asserted suit was barred by state sovereign immunity.

Reasoning: The immunity principle was structural and not confined to the literal party combinations or forum in the Eleventh Amendment’s text. Supremacy did not itself remove immunity.

Rule: Moving an ordinary Article I private damages claim to state court does not necessarily bypass a state’s immunity.

Significance: Keep this source-of-power problem separate from valid Fourteenth Amendment enforcement and specialized exceptions.

Source scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

sections.heading: Case brief — Pennhurst State School and Hospital v. Halderman
sections.body:
465 U.S. 89 (1984)

Facts: Residents obtained federal-court relief directing state officials to comply with duties based on state law.

Posture: The supplied notes describe the Court’s disposition of the stated constitutional threshold issue.

Issue: Could Ex parte Young support that order merely because relief was prospective?

Holding: The Court rejected the federal order enforcing state law against state officials.

Reasoning: The federal-law supremacy rationale for Ex parte Young did not support judicial orders based only on state law; supplemental jurisdiction did not override the immunity problem.

Rule: For the asserted official-capacity relief, prospective form alone does not suffice: the source of the violated duty matters.

Significance: Distinguish this 1984 state-law immunity case from the different 1981 Pennhurst decision listed as optional in the spending-power module.

Source scope: Optional reading. Review draft from the supplied detailed study notes; the original assigned opinion has not been independently supplied or authenticated.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A state official is sued for future federal-law compliance and payment for past violations. Is a single immunity conclusion enough?

Governing principle — Political question
Start with the particular issue and Baker’s factors rather than declaring every politically important lawsuit nonjusticiable. Textual commitment to another branch and the absence of judicially manageable standards require explanation from the constitutional provision and requested decision. Baker allowed the equal-protection claim to proceed. United States v. Nixon concerned a concrete evidentiary dispute; Nixon v. United States concerned Senate impeachment procedures. Reversing the case names reverses the lesson.

Application and answer
No. Separate defendants, forum, legal source, capacity and remedy. Prospective federal-law relief and retrospective treasury payments raise different issues under the supplied immunity notes.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: An order requiring payment for completed violations becomes prospective merely because it is called an injunction.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every dispute involving the President is automatically a nonjusticiable political question.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Mentioning state law anywhere in a judgment always prevents federal review, regardless of dependence on federal law.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Necessary and Proper Clause
references: McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. 316 (1819)
City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)
modules.scope: Original notes based on the identified historical judicial opinions retrieved from a documented CourtListener mirror. This is partial coverage of the assigned reading list, not a current-law certification or proof every assigned decision was supplied. The McCulloch mirror has inconsistent reporter-page metadata; verify official pagination before citing a pinpoint.

sections.heading: Enumerated ends and implementing means
sections.body: McCulloch separates a legitimate constitutional end from the means Congress selects to accomplish it. The Constitution need not list every instrument Congress may use in executing an enumerated power. The opinion treats incorporation of a national bank as an implementing measure rather than requiring a freestanding express bank clause. Explain the relation between the asserted end and chosen means; the Necessary and Proper Clause is not a substitute for identifying a constitutional objective.

sections.heading: Appropriateness and constitutional limits
sections.body: The classic formulation permits appropriate means plainly adapted to a legitimate end when they are not prohibited and remain consistent with the Constitution’s letter and spirit. That is not an assertion that any useful policy is valid. Identify the power being implemented, how the measure advances it, and any independent prohibition. The case also concerns a state’s attempt to tax a federal instrument, which raises supremacy and the ability to frustrate federal operations rather than merely another question about Congress’s preferred policy.

sections.heading: Enforcement is not rewriting the right
sections.body: City of Boerne examined RFRA in a dispute over a church building permit. The Court distinguished enforcing Fourteenth Amendment protections from changing the underlying substantive constitutional standard. Its congruence-and-proportionality formulation asks about the injury to be prevented or remedied and the fit of the chosen legislation. Identify the constitutional right, relevant state conduct, evidentiary justification and reach of the remedy instead of assuming that Congress’s use of an enforcement label establishes authority.

sections.heading: Exam comparison and source caution
sections.body: Analyze the source of power before selecting a standard. A measure implementing an enumerated end and a statute asserted to enforce a constitutional right raise related but distinct questions. Do not apply a single unexplained reasonableness test to both. The McCulloch mirror’s reporter page is inconsistent with the assigned citation; its identifiable opinion text supports these doctrinal notes, but its apparent page markers should not be used as authenticated pinpoint citations. Other assigned cases remain separate readings.

sections.heading: Case brief — McCulloch v. Maryland
sections.body:
17 U.S. 316 (1819)

Facts: Maryland challenged the federal bank and sought to impose a state tax affecting its operations.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether Congress could incorporate the bank and the state could impose the challenged tax.

Holding: The Court sustained the federal implementing power and rejected the state tax as asserted against the federal instrument.

Reasoning: The Constitution need not enumerate every implementing means. Appropriate means tied to a legitimate constitutional end remain bounded by constitutional limits and supremacy.

Rule: Identify the enumerated end, appropriate means, independent prohibitions and any state interference with valid federal operations.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. Mirror metadata/header incorrectly label the reporter page as 159. The text identifies the 1819 McCulloch opinion; the assigned citation is 17 U.S. 316. Source pagination has not been independently authenticated.

sections.heading: Case brief — City of Boerne v. Flores
sections.body:
521 U.S. 507 (1997)

Facts: A church’s building-permit dispute led to a claim under RFRA against local authorities.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Why must an answer distinguish a legitimate congressional end from its chosen means?

Governing principle — Enumerated ends and implementing means
McCulloch separates a legitimate constitutional end from the means Congress selects to accomplish it. The Constitution need not list every instrument Congress may use in executing an enumerated power. The opinion treats incorporation of a national bank as an implementing measure rather than requiring a freestanding express bank clause. Explain the relation between the asserted end and chosen means; the Necessary and Proper Clause is not a substitute for identifying a constitutional objective.

Application and answer
The implementing-means analysis needs an identified constitutional objective and a sufficient relationship to it, with independent constitutional limits preserved. Merely describing a policy as useful or calling a measure necessary does not establish the whole inquiry.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Congress must find an express clause naming every implementing instrument before using it for an enumerated end.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A measure described as necessary is valid even if it violates an independent constitutional prohibition.
Do not use this incorrect approach: The label enforcement alone permits Congress to redefine the underlying substantive constitutional guarantee.

Complete this principle: 316 (1819)

Facts: Maryland challenged the federal bank and sought to impose a state ____ affecting its operations.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Commerce Clause
references: United States v. Lopez, 514 U.S. 549 (1995)
United States v. Morrison, 529 U.S. 598 (2000)
modules.scope: Original notes based on the identified historical judicial opinions retrieved from a documented CourtListener mirror. This is partial coverage of the assigned reading list, not a current-law certification or proof every assigned decision was supplied.

sections.heading: Classify the asserted commerce power
sections.body: Lopez identifies channels of interstate commerce, instrumentalities and persons or things in commerce, and activities substantially affecting interstate commerce. Choose the relevant category before applying its test. The Gun-Free School Zones Act at issue addressed possession in a school zone without the interstate-commerce connection the government needed under the challenged theory. Do not assume that a local act is unreachable simply because it occurs within one state; explain why the asserted category does or does not cover it.

sections.heading: Nature of the activity and the causal chain
sections.body: The opinion distinguishes the regulated conduct from a lengthy series of effects on education, economic productivity and the national economy. If every link rests on a very broad generalization, explain why the proposed theory would lack a meaningful stopping point. Evaluate the activity, statutory elements, relation to a broader scheme and the particular constitutional theory rather than substituting the conclusion that the issue is important.

sections.heading: Morrison’s two sources of power
sections.body: Morrison rejected the federal civil remedy for gender-motivated violence under the theories before the Court. Its commerce discussion addressed noneconomic violent conduct and the claimed aggregate economic consequences. Its Fourteenth Amendment analysis separately addressed the state-action boundary and the remedy directed at private conduct. Congressional findings did not themselves decide the constitutional limit. Identify the claim against the actor and the source of authority separately.

sections.heading: Comparisons and unreviewed assignments
sections.body: When comparing Lopez and Morrison, focus on the regulated conduct, jurisdictional connection, inference chain and legal basis rather than equating all intrastate activity with invalidity. Distinguish state regulation from federal enumerated-power analysis. Raich is also assigned but was not located in this retrieval; these notes do not claim to resolve its broader-regulatory-scheme analysis from a missing primary text. Use a separate verified source before treating that part of the reading as complete.

sections.heading: Case brief — United States v. Lopez
sections.body:
514 U.S. 549 (1995)

Facts: A student prosecuted under the 1990 federal school-zone firearm statute contested Congress’s commerce authority.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the challenged possession provision fell within the asserted commerce power.

Holding: The Court affirmed the reversal of the conviction and rejected the provision’s asserted commerce basis.

Reasoning: The law before the Court regulated possession without the commercial connection required under the theory advanced. An attenuated economic-effects chain did not establish unlimited national authority.

Rule: Classify channels, instrumentalities/persons/things in commerce, or substantial-effects regulation before applying the relevant analysis.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. A CourtListener mirror copy, not an authenticated official-report scan. Treat the historical decision separately from later legal developments.

sections.heading: Case brief — United States v. Morrison
sections.body:
529 U.S. 598 (2000)

Facts: A federal statute supplied a civil remedy for victims of gender-motivated violence by private actors.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the remedy was supported by the asserted Commerce Clause or Fourteenth Amendment enforcement theories.

Holding: The Court rejected the challenged remedy under those theories.

Reasoning: The regulated violence was noneconomic in the Court’s analysis, and findings did not remove the constitutional boundary. The separate Section 5 argument confronted the state-action limitation.

Rule: Analyze each power and target independently; important objectives and findings are not by themselves constitutional authority.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. A CourtListener mirror copy, not an authenticated official-report scan. Treat the historical decision separately from later legal developments.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Hypothetical: Congress supports a law regulating local noneconomic conduct with findings about its national economic effects. Does that alone answer the commerce issue?

Governing principle — Classify the asserted commerce power
Lopez identifies channels of interstate commerce, instrumentalities and persons or things in commerce, and activities substantially affecting interstate commerce. Choose the relevant category before applying its test. The Gun-Free School Zones Act at issue addressed possession in a school zone without the interstate-commerce connection the government needed under the challenged theory. Do not assume that a local act is unreachable simply because it occurs within one state; explain why the asserted category does or does not cover it.

Application and answer
No. Classify the asserted category, examine the conduct, statutory connection and inference chain, and apply the relevant limits. Morrison shows that findings do not themselves establish constitutional authority; additional theories such as Section 5 need separate analysis.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Congressional findings about economic effects conclusively validate every regulation of local noneconomic activity.
Do not use this incorrect approach: All activity occurring within one state is categorically outside every category of federal commerce authority.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A valid commerce analysis makes a separate Fourteenth Amendment source-of-power analysis unnecessary.

sections.heading: Taxing, spending and direct regulation
sections.body: A measure can involve more than one proposed source of congressional power. Do not assume that failure of one theory determines all others. Dole concerns conditions on federal funding rather than a direct national command to enact a particular drinking age. NFIB requires separating the commerce argument, constitutional tax construction and spending condition attached to Medicaid expansion. Identify the precise provision and theory before stating the result.

sections.heading: Conditional spending under Dole
sections.body: The decision discusses the general welfare, clarity of conditions, relation to the federal program and independent constitutional limits. It also addresses when financial inducement could become coercion. The small percentage of highway funding at issue and the actual freedom to reject the condition mattered to the result. The fact that a spending condition encourages policy Congress could not simply command directly is not itself the same as requiring unconstitutional conduct.

sections.heading: NFIB’s distinct inquiries
sections.body: The individual-mandate payment was sustained under a constitutional taxing-power construction, and the opinion distinguishes a statutory label from the functional constitutional analysis. The Medicaid issue involved a threat to existing funding, not merely the terms of a new incremental grant. Compare the scale, notice, change in program and practical ability to refuse. A rule that any funding condition is voluntary whenever a state can theoretically say no misses the coercion issue.

sections.heading: Read the divisions in the opinions
sections.body: NFIB contains multiple opinions and different joiners for different sections. Record which proposition belongs to the Court, the Chief Justice’s separate analysis or another opinion before claiming a single unanimous rationale. Keep the 2012 statutory arrangement separate from current program details or later litigation. In an exam, analyze each provision under each asserted constitutional power and limit the conclusion to the issue the source actually resolves.

sections.heading: Case brief — South Dakota v. Dole
sections.body:
483 U.S. 203 (1987)

Facts: Congress withheld a small percentage of specified highway funds from states permitting alcohol purchase below the chosen age.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the conditional grant exceeded the asserted constitutional limits.

Holding: The Court sustained the condition in the arrangement before it.

Reasoning: The funding condition was analyzed through the spending framework, including general welfare, clear notice, relatedness, independent constitutional limits and the coercion objection.

Rule: Distinguish conditional spending from direct regulation and examine the actual financial and legal choice.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

sections.heading: Case brief — National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius
sections.body:
567 U.S. 519 (2012)

Facts: Challenges to the Affordable Care Act addressed an individual-coverage payment and conditions on expanded Medicaid.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: How the challenged provisions fared under the distinct commerce, taxing and spending theories.

Holding: The mandate payment was sustained under a taxing construction; the threatened loss of existing Medicaid funds received the separate coercion analysis and limitation described in the opinions.

Reasoning: The statutory label did not decide the constitutional tax characterization. A threat to established program funding differed from a modest new funding condition. Different parts of the opinions had different joiners.

Rule: Analyze each provision and power separately; do not attribute all reasoning to one unanimous Court or treat a hypothetical ability to refuse as dispositive.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. A CourtListener mirror copy, not an authenticated official-report scan. Treat the historical decision separately from later legal developments.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Why should a funding-condition answer compare the actual financial choice rather than simply say the state may refuse?

Governing principle — Taxing, spending and direct regulation
A measure can involve more than one proposed source of congressional power. Do not assume that failure of one theory determines all others. Dole concerns conditions on federal funding rather than a direct national command to enact a particular drinking age. NFIB requires separating the commerce argument, constitutional tax construction and spending condition attached to Medicaid expansion. Identify the precise provision and theory before stating the result.

Application and answer
The coercion inquiry concerns the nature and scale of the inducement, including the relationship to existing funding and the practical choice. Dole’s modest withheld share and NFIB’s existing-Medicaid threat were not equivalent arrangements.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: The theoretical possibility of refusing funds conclusively defeats every spending-coercion challenge.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A statutory use of the word penalty conclusively prevents any constitutional taxing-power analysis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: All parts of NFIB express one unanimous rationale that can be applied without separating provisions or opinions.

sections.heading: Case brief — New York v. United States
sections.body:
505 U.S. 144 (1992)

Facts: A federal radioactive-waste scheme used several incentives, including a take-title mechanism directed at states.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the federal mechanisms permissibly encouraged state action or impermissibly compelled it.

Holding: The Court upheld two mechanisms but rejected the take-title arrangement.

Reasoning: Congress’s substantial regulatory authority did not itself authorize commanding state government to assume the challenged regulatory burden. Presenting a choice did not cure the problem where its substance remained impermissible.

Rule: Identify the actual target and required conduct, distinguish inducement from commandeering, and analyze each provision separately.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Hypothetical: a federal law offers a state two options, both requiring the state to assume the federal program’s regulatory burden. Is the word choice dispositive?

Governing principle — Regulation and commandeering
New York addressed three mechanisms in a federal radioactive-waste scheme, not an undifferentiated rejection of federal environmental legislation. Congress could encourage state action through constitutionally permissible mechanisms, but could not simply compel the states to administer the federal regulatory choice. Identify who must act and what the challenged provision demands.

Application and answer
No. Identify the substance of both alternatives and whether they supply a genuinely permissible option. New York’s take-title analysis rejects relying on the form of a choice without examining its constitutional content.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Calling a compulsory arrangement a choice conclusively cures any commandeering objection.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Any federal influence on state policy is identical to a direct command to the state legislature.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Invalidity of one mechanism necessarily proves every incentive in a federal scheme is invalid.
