sections.heading: Different kinds of interstate-commerce burdens
sections.body: Separate discrimination against interstate commerce from incidental effects of an evenhanded local measure. Pike states the historical formulation for evenhanded regulation serving a legitimate local interest whose incidental burden is alleged to be clearly excessive relative to its putative local benefits. Hunt shows why facially neutral language does not end an inquiry into discriminatory effects. Identify the actual economic mechanism rather than choosing a test from the statute’s title.

sections.heading: Pike’s packing requirement
sections.body: Arizona’s order prevented the company from sending uncrated cantaloupes to a nearby California facility. Explain the imposed operational burden, the local purpose advanced and the relationship between them. The case’s balancing language is tied to that regulatory setting. A bare statement that compliance is expensive is not the entire analysis; identify the interstate burden and the claimed benefit with concrete facts.

sections.heading: Hunt’s labeling effect
sections.body: North Carolina required apple containers to show only the applicable federal grade or no grade, excluding Washington’s distinctive grading labels. The opinion examined the removal of a competitive advantage and the resulting interstate burden, notwithstanding neutral phrasing. Distinguish the stated consumer-protection rationale from the regulation’s actual impact and any less discriminatory way to pursue the objective.

sections.heading: Keep adjacent doctrines separate
sections.body: An answer should identify discrimination, purpose and effect, the relevant justification, and the burden under the selected framework. The outline also assigns market-participant and privileges-and-immunities materials; those are not interchangeable with Pike or Hunt and are not supplied merely by a citation here. These are historical source-based notes, not a claim to have researched every later limitation or refinement of dormant-commerce analysis.

sections.heading: Case brief — Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc.
sections.body:
397 U.S. 137 (1970)

Facts: Arizona required local packing that prevented shipment of uncrated cantaloupes to a nearby California packing facility.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the order imposed an unconstitutional interstate-commerce burden.

Holding: The Court upheld relief against the challenged order.

Reasoning: The opinion compared the operational burden and local interest under the historical framework for evenhanded regulation with incidental interstate effects.

Rule: Identify the concrete interstate burden, putative local benefit and applicable framework rather than asserting that any expense invalidates local law.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

sections.heading: Case brief — Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission
sections.body:
432 U.S. 333 (1977)

Facts: North Carolina’s apple-container rule excluded Washington’s state-grade labels despite their market significance.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the facially neutral label rule imposed impermissible discrimination and interstate burdens.

Holding: The Court affirmed the judgment invalidating the challenged restriction.

Reasoning: The regulation’s effects removed a competitive grading advantage and imposed discriminatory burdens notwithstanding its neutral phrasing. The stated purpose did not eliminate scrutiny of actual operation.

Rule: Facial neutrality does not end the discrimination inquiry; explain economic effects and the asserted justification.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

sections.heading: Source of executive authority
sections.body: The steel-seizure dispute concerned whether the President could direct federal possession and operation of private mills to avert a strike during a wartime emergency. The majority’s starting point was that authority must come from an act of Congress or the Constitution. Neither the urgency of the policy problem nor the President’s description of the crisis supplied a free-standing lawmaking power.

sections.heading: Majority and concurrence
sections.body: Identify Justice Black’s majority reasoning separately from Justice Jackson’s concurrence. The majority rejected the asserted seizure authority on the legal sources before it. Jackson’s familiar three-category framework evaluates executive action in relation to Congress: authorization, absence of grant or denial, and incompatibility with expressed or implied congressional will. The categories organize analysis; they are not a substitute for reading the statute or identifying an exclusive executive power.

sections.heading: Apply the categories with facts
sections.body: For an authorization claim, identify the statutory text and scope of the power granted. For silence, explain why the matter remains open and the President’s independent authority is relevant. For conflict, identify Congress’s position and why the claimed exclusive presidential power could or could not prevail. Do not classify a case as congressional silence merely because no single sentence says the President shall not do precisely this act.

sections.heading: Bounded conclusions
sections.body: Distinguish the domestic seizure of private property from all other foreign-affairs or emergency powers. sections.heading: Case brief — Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
sections.body:
343 U.S. 579 (1952)

Facts: The President ordered possession and operation of steel mills to avert the consequences of a threatened strike.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether statutory or constitutional authority supported that domestic seizure.

Holding: The Court rejected the asserted executive seizure authority.

Reasoning: The majority required a statutory or constitutional source rather than necessity alone. Jackson’s separate concurrence organized executive authority by its relation to Congress’s authorization, silence or opposition.

Rule: Distinguish majority reasoning from a concurrence and determine Congress’s actual position before applying the familiar categories.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

What is missing from an argument that an emergency alone authorizes presidential seizure of private property?

Governing principle — Source of executive authority
The steel-seizure dispute concerned whether the President could direct federal possession and operation of private mills to avert a strike during a wartime emergency. The majority’s starting point was that authority must come from an act of Congress or the Constitution. Neither the urgency of the policy problem nor the President’s description of the crisis supplied a free-standing lawmaking power.

Identify statutory or constitutional authority and Congress’s relevant position. Youngstown rejects treating necessity alone as a source of lawmaking power. Separate the majority’s reasoning from Jackson’s concurrence and apply the actual facts to any category used.

Do not use this incorrect approach: Congressional opposition always places presidential power in the maximum-authority category.

sections.heading: Case brief — Whitman v. American Trucking Associations
sections.body:
531 U.S. 457 (2001)

Facts: The EPA’s air-quality standard-setting authority was challenged as an unconstitutional delegation, alongside statutory interpretation issues.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether Congress supplied sufficient guidance and whether an agency could cure a missing constitutional standard itself.

Holding: The Court rejected the delegation challenge to the statutory standard and rejected the agency-cure theory; other issues received separate dispositions.

Reasoning: The constitutional inquiry concerned the delegation Congress actually made. An agency’s self-restraint could not create a missing congressional standard.

Rule: Keep delegation, statutory cost questions, appointment and removal issues analytically separate.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. A CourtListener mirror copy, not an authenticated official-report scan. Treat the historical decision separately from later legal developments.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Can an agency’s promise to exercise discretion narrowly cure a constitutionally standardless delegation under Whitman’s analysis?

Governing principle — Delegation as a distinct institutional question
Whitman examines the statutory standard guiding EPA air-quality decisions and the objection that Congress had transferred legislative power without an adequate principle. Begin with the actual provision and what policy choices it leaves to the agency. Delegation, appointment, removal and review of an officer’s decision are different issues even if they arise in the same administrative setting.

Application and answer
No. The Court treats the adequacy of Congress’s delegation as a constitutional question. A discretionary agency limitation cannot itself supply the legislative standard Congress omitted; assess the statute’s actual guidance.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: An agency can supply a missing constitutional legislative standard merely by promising voluntary restraint.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Delegation, appointment and removal are identical legal inquiries with identical governing rules.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Whitman establishes that every broad agency delegation is constitutional without reading its statutory guidance.

sections.heading: Case brief — Schick v. Reed
sections.body:
419 U.S. 256 (1974)

Facts: A presidential commutation replaced a death sentence with life imprisonment subject to a no-parole condition.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether the condition was invalid because it was not specifically supplied by the sentencing statutes.

Reasoning: The constitutional clemency power included the recognized ability to impose conditions that did not themselves offend the Constitution, even without a matching statutory condition.

Rule: Identify the clemency act and asserted independent limit. Do not assume every possible condition is valid or confuse clemency with executive privilege.

Does Schick establish that any condition attached to a presidential commutation is valid?

Governing principle — Clemency and privilege must be separated

Nixon notes concern a claim of executive privilege against a criminal-trial subpoena. Do not use this incorrect approach: A condition not specifically listed by statute is necessarily forbidden under Schick.

references: Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982)
Clinton v. Jones, 520 U.S. 681 (1997)
modules.scope: Original notes based on the identified historical judicial opinions retrieved from a documented CourtListener mirror. This is partial coverage of the assigned reading list, not a current-law certification or proof every assigned decision was supplied. Newer assigned decisions not available in this collection remain unbriefed; do not extrapolate this historical treatment to those decisions.

sections.heading: Separate actor, conduct and proceeding
sections.body: An immunity analysis must identify who is sued, for what conduct, in what proceeding and for which remedy. Harlow concerns senior presidential aides and civil damages for official acts. Clinton v. Jones concerns civil litigation against a sitting President based on alleged unofficial conduct preceding the presidency. Neither can be used as a universal answer to every presidential criminal, civil or legislative-immunity problem.

sections.heading: Harlow’s objective formulation
sections.body: The decision articulates protection from civil damages tied to clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable official would have known. Identify the relevant right and the law at the time of the challenged conduct. The objective formulation serves the concern with avoiding unnecessary litigation burdens associated with inquiries into subjective good faith. Establishing that conduct was wrong is different from completing the qualified-immunity analysis.

sections.heading: Clinton and unofficial pre-office conduct
sections.body: The Court rejected the claim that the Constitution required general postponement of this civil suit until the President left office. The functional rationale protecting official decision-making did not automatically extend to the alleged earlier unofficial conduct. Distinguish categorical immunity or mandatory delay from ordinary case-management measures a court can consider in handling litigation responsibly.

sections.heading: Do not fill gaps with assumptions
sections.body: The outline separately assigns Trump v. United States and Hutchinson v. Proxmire, which concern other immunity settings. The retrieved historical collection does not supply the 2024 Trump opinion; this guide does not invent its criminal-immunity analysis. For an exam, first classify actor, function, timing, proceeding and remedy, then apply the correct source. An answer about presidential status alone misses the legally significant distinctions.

sections.heading: Case brief — Harlow v. Fitzgerald
sections.body:
457 U.S. 800 (1982)

Facts: Senior White House aides faced civil-damages allegations concerning official conduct in the Fitzgerald dispute.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: What standard governed the immunity asserted by these officials.

Holding: The Court articulated an objective qualified-immunity formulation tied to clearly established rights.

Reasoning: The standard addresses rights a reasonable official would have known at the relevant time and the burdens associated with subjective-good-faith litigation.

Rule: Analyze actor, function, time, right and civil remedy. Establishing a legal violation alone does not complete the qualified-immunity inquiry.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Source scope: Historical primary-opinion study draft. A CourtListener mirror copy, not an authenticated official-report scan. Treat the historical decision separately from later legal developments.

sections.heading: Case brief — Clinton v. Jones
sections.body:
520 U.S. 681 (1997)

Facts: A civil action sought damages from the sitting President based on alleged unofficial conduct before taking office.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the stated constitutional or institutional issue; see the linked source record for the full procedural history.

Issue: Whether presidential status constitutionally required general deferral of that action until the term ended.

Holding: The Court rejected the asserted categorical constitutional postponement.

Reasoning: The functional protection of official decision-making did not automatically cover the alleged pre-office unofficial conduct. Litigation management was distinct from immunity.

Rule: Classify official versus unofficial conduct and civil versus criminal proceedings; this historical civil decision does not substitute for the unreviewed 2024 criminal-immunity assignment.

Significance: Use the facts and posture to state the decision’s boundary; distinguish it from later legal developments and other assigned cases not reviewed here.

Neither can be used as a universal answer to every presidential criminal, civil or legislative-immunity problem.

Application and answer

How would you structure a fact-specific analysis of this module’s constitutional issue?

Governing principle — Harlow’s objective formulation
The decision articulates protection from civil damages tied to clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable official would have known. Identify the relevant right and the law at the time of the challenged conduct. The objective formulation serves the concern with avoiding unnecessary litigation burdens associated with inquiries into subjective good faith. Establishing that conduct was wrong is different from completing the qualified-immunity analysis.

Application and answer
Identify the actor, constitutional source, challenged conduct, and procedural posture. State the relevant rule from the source-backed guide, apply the material facts and strongest counterargument, then reach a limited conclusion about the requested relief. Distinguish the historical holding from unreviewed later decisions.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Presidential status conclusively resolves immunity regardless of function, remedy or type of proceeding.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Harlow’s qualified-immunity inquiry requires no consideration of the law at the time of the official’s conduct.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Clinton’s historical civil ruling itself answers every distinct criminal-immunity question in later assignments.

cards.title: Complete this principle: An immunity analysis must identify who is sued, for what conduct, in what proceeding and for which ____.
cards.answer:
remedy

Full explanation: An immunity analysis must identify who is sued, for what conduct, in what proceeding and for which remedy. Harlow concerns senior presidential aides and civil damages for official acts. Clinton v. Jones concerns civil litigation against a sitting President based on alleged unofficial conduct preceding the presidency. Neither can be used as a universal answer to every presidential criminal, civil or legislative-immunity problem.

modules.scope: Cumulative original study notes drawn from the existing module companions. No new assigned textbook content or official exam rubric is claimed.

sections.heading: Review method and limits
sections.body: This is a cumulative companion to existing source-linked module guides, not an additional assigned reading. Begin by identifying the parties, institutional roles, chronological sequence, claim, governing source and remedy. Organize an answer around the material issues rather than reciting every rule you remember. For each issue, state the relevant source-backed standard, apply the important facts, address the strongest counterargument and reach a limited conclusion. Keep historical holdings and unreviewed later developments separate. The topic summaries below are reused from the underlying original guides so that missing source material is not replaced by invented textbook content.

sections.heading: Federal Jurisdiction and Judicial Review
sections.body: Federal judicial power must fit an Article III category and a statutory jurisdictional grant. A claim’s federal character does not answer every jurisdictional question. Distinguish the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction from its appellate jurisdiction, and distinguish the constitutionally created Supreme Court from lower federal courts that Congress establishes. Identify the court and posture before discussing the merits.

sections.heading: Justiciability: Standing
sections.body: Analyze injury in fact, traceability, and redressability separately for each plaintiff, claim, and requested remedy. A concrete, personal injury must be actual or sufficiently imminent rather than an abstract desire for government compliance. Traceability asks whether the challenged conduct materially explains the injury; redressability asks whether the requested judicial relief would likely alleviate it. Uncontrolled third-party decisions can create problems for either inquiry.

sections.heading: Political Questions and Sovereign Immunity
sections.body: Start with the particular issue and Baker’s factors rather than declaring every politically important lawsuit nonjusticiable. Textual commitment to another branch and the absence of judicially manageable standards require explanation from the constitutional provision and requested decision. Baker allowed the equal-protection claim to proceed. United States v. Nixon concerned a concrete evidentiary dispute; Nixon v. United States concerned Senate impeachment procedures. Reversing the case names reverses the lesson.

sections.heading: Necessary and Proper Clause
sections.body: McCulloch separates a legitimate constitutional end from the means Congress selects to accomplish it. The Constitution need not list every instrument Congress may use in executing an enumerated power. The opinion treats incorporation of a national bank as an implementing measure rather than requiring a freestanding express bank clause. Explain the relation between the asserted end and chosen means; the Necessary and Proper Clause is not a substitute for identifying a constitutional objective.

sections.heading: Commerce Clause
sections.body: Lopez identifies channels of interstate commerce, instrumentalities and persons or things in commerce, and activities substantially affecting interstate commerce. Choose the relevant category before applying its test. The Gun-Free School Zones Act at issue addressed possession in a school zone without the interstate-commerce connection the government needed under the challenged theory. Do not assume that a local act is unreachable simply because it occurs within one state; explain why the asserted category does or does not cover it.

sections.heading: Taxing and Spending Clause
sections.body: A measure can involve more than one proposed source of congressional power. Do not assume that failure of one theory determines all others. Dole concerns conditions on federal funding rather than a direct national command to enact a particular drinking age. NFIB requires separating the commerce argument, constitutional tax construction and spending condition attached to Medicaid expansion. Identify the precise provision and theory before stating the result.

sections.heading: State Powers and Federalism
sections.body: New York addressed three mechanisms in a federal radioactive-waste scheme, not an undifferentiated rejection of federal environmental legislation. Congress could encourage state action through constitutionally permissible mechanisms, but could not simply compel the states to administer the federal regulatory choice. Identify who must act and what the challenged provision demands.

sections.heading: Limits on State Powers
sections.body: Separate discrimination against interstate commerce from incidental effects of an evenhanded local measure. Pike states the historical formulation for evenhanded regulation serving a legitimate local interest whose incidental burden is alleged to be clearly excessive relative to its putative local benefits. Hunt shows why facially neutral language does not end an inquiry into discriminatory effects. Identify the actual economic mechanism rather than choosing a test from the statute’s title.

sections.heading: Executive Express and Inherent Powers
sections.body: The steel-seizure dispute concerned whether the President could direct federal possession and operation of private mills to avert a strike during a wartime emergency. The majority’s starting point was that authority must come from an act of Congress or the Constitution. Neither the urgency of the policy problem nor the President’s description of the crisis supplied a free-standing lawmaking power.

sections.heading: Executive Appointment and Removal
sections.body: Whitman examines the statutory standard guiding EPA air-quality decisions and the objection that Congress had transferred legislative power without an adequate principle. Begin with the actual provision and what policy choices it leaves to the agency. Delegation, appointment, removal and review of an officer’s decision are different issues even if they arise in the same administrative setting.

sections.heading: Executive Pardon and Privilege
sections.body: This module combines different presidential powers. Schick concerns the conditions attached to a commutation; the earlier supplied United States v. Nixon notes concern a claim of executive privilege against a criminal-trial subpoena. Do not reason that a broad clemency power automatically answers an evidentiary privilege question, or that a limitation on privilege proves a particular commutation condition invalid.

sections.heading: Immunity and Impeachment
sections.body: An immunity analysis must identify who is sued, for what conduct, in what proceeding and for which remedy. Harlow concerns senior presidential aides and civil damages for official acts. Clinton v. Jones concerns civil litigation against a sitting President based on alleged unofficial conduct preceding the presidency. Neither can be used as a universal answer to every presidential criminal, civil or legislative-immunity problem.

sections.heading: Self-check before submitting
sections.body: Check that each conclusion follows from an actual rule and identified facts. Keep threshold issues, substantive authority, legal violations and remedies in separate analytical steps where the facts require them. Distinguish the status of a source, including supplemental editions and missing assigned opinions, from your confidence in an answer. Use case comparisons to explain boundaries rather than citing names without analysis. Revisit the module’s full notes and source references for qualifications that this compressed review does not reproduce. These are self-review materials, not an official grading rubric or a prediction of the examination’s content.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A President orders seizure of a private factory during an emergency without identifying a statute. How should the authority argument be analyzed?

Governing principle — Review method and limits
This is a cumulative companion to existing source-linked module guides, not an additional assigned reading. Begin by identifying the parties, institutional roles, chronological sequence, claim, governing source and remedy. Organize an answer around the material issues rather than reciting every rule you remember. For each issue, state the relevant source-backed standard, apply the important facts, address the strongest counterargument and reach a limited conclusion. Keep historical holdings and unreviewed later developments separate. The topic summaries below are reused from the underlying original guides so that missing source material is not replaced by invented textbook content.

Application and answer
Identify a statutory or constitutional source, Congress’s position and any asserted exclusive presidential power. Youngstown’s majority does not accept necessity alone as lawmaking authority. Distinguish Jackson’s separate concurrence and explain the appropriate category from the actual statutory facts.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: The word emergency eliminates the need to identify statutory or constitutional authority for executive action.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Calling a statute enforcement conclusively establishes its Fourteenth Amendment validity.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A threshold dismissal always establishes the substantive legality of the challenged governmental policy.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Congress calls a new state-law remedy Fourteenth Amendment enforcement. What should a constitutional analysis examine beyond that label?

Governing principle — Federal Jurisdiction and Judicial Review

Identify the court and posture before discussing the merits.

Application and answer
Identify the underlying constitutional right, state conduct, injury to be prevented or remedied, and fit of the statutory response. Apply the sourced enforcement framework, including Boerne’s congruence and proportionality distinction; Congress’s chosen label does not itself establish authority.

sections.heading: Constitutional source and procedural stage
sections.body: Identify the right, its source, the government action challenged, and the stage of the criminal process. Federal constitutional protections, state constitutions, statutes, procedural rules, and supervisory doctrines can supply different grounds. A rule applicable in a federal prosecution does not automatically have the same source or reach in a state prosecution. Keep incorporation through the Fourteenth Amendment separate from the historical meaning of a particular Bill of Rights guarantee.

sections.heading: Case brief — Gideon v. Wainwright
sections.body:
372 U.S. 335 (1963)

Facts: An indigent defendant requested counsel for a state felony trial. Florida denied appointment because the charge was not capital; he defended himself and was convicted.

Posture: Supreme Court review of the state conviction.

Issue: Did the state felony trial require appointed counsel for an indigent accused?

Holding: The Court recognized the fundamental right and overruled Betts v. Brady.

Reasoning: An adversarial criminal trial cannot reliably provide a fair contest where a person unable to afford counsel must face trained prosecution alone. The Sixth Amendment guarantee applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Rule: Indigent defendants have the recognized right to appointed counsel for the state felony-trial setting at issue.

Significance: Distinguish this trial right from Miranda counsel safeguards and do not extrapolate appointment to every government encounter.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Arrest
sections.body:
A taking into custody that subjects a person to the level of restraint associated with arrest. A lawful criminal arrest generally requires probable cause.

Identify the objective restraint and the legally relevant completion of the seizure, not simply an officer’s private intention. Distinguish an arrest from a consensual interaction and a brief investigative stop. Then separately ask whether the arrest had legal justification; an unlawful arrest is still an arrest for purposes of identifying the challenged conduct.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer orders a person to remain and applies handcuffs. Analyze the circumstances and degree of restraint before deciding whether this is an investigative stop or an arrest and what justification is required.

Pitfall: The handout’s shorthand about officer intention does not mean an uncommunicated thought alone arrests someone. Classification and lawfulness are separate questions.

sections.heading: Definition — Material witness
sections.body:
A person whose testimony is important to a criminal proceeding and whose attendance presents the relevant legal concern; detention requires the applicable legal authority and conditions.

The handout describes detention where testimony is needed and there is a danger of nonappearance. Identify the witness’s role, why the testimony matters, the attendance concern and the governing detention procedure. Keep witness detention separate from an arrest on probable cause that the witness committed an offense. Do not infer unlimited detention power merely from an investigator’s desire to interview someone.

Example: Hypothetical: police need testimony from a person not accused of an offense. Identify the asserted witness-related legal authority before analyzing detention as if it were an ordinary criminal arrest.

Pitfall: Being useful to an investigation does not itself establish every condition for detaining a material witness. Identify the actual proceeding and the specific legal mechanism.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Police question a person before formal prosecution, and the person later faces a felony trial without funds. Are all counsel questions governed by the same rule?

Governing principle — Constitutional source and procedural stage
Identify the right, its source, the government action challenged, and the stage of the criminal process. Federal constitutional protections, state constitutions, statutes, procedural rules, and supervisory doctrines can supply different grounds. A rule applicable in a federal prosecution does not automatically have the same source or reach in a state prosecution. Keep incorporation through the Fourteenth Amendment separate from the historical meaning of a particular Bill of Rights guarantee.

Application and answer
No. Distinguish custodial-interrogation safeguards from attachment and trial assistance-of-counsel questions. Gideon addresses appointed counsel in the state felony-trial setting; analyze the stage and source of each right.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every counsel issue has the same constitutional source regardless of custody and procedural stage.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A rule used in federal court automatically has identical authority and reach in every state proceeding.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Gideon’s felony-trial holding establishes appointed counsel for every interaction with government.

A litigant invokes a rule applicable in federal court and assumes the same source automatically governs state procedure. What must be checked?

The assignment should not be summarized as a right to a free attorney in every interaction with government. Ask which proceedings and consequences are involved before extending the rule.

Identify whether the rule is constitutional, incorporated, statutory, procedural or supervisory. The same result or label does not establish an identical source and reach in state proceedings.

sections.heading: Reliability of suggestive identification evidence
sections.body:
The Manson discussion treats reliability as central when applying the due-process identification doctrine. Relevant factors include viewing opportunity, attention, prior description, confrontation certainty and elapsed time, weighed against the procedure’s suggestive effect. Keep the threshold question about improper police-arranged suggestion separate from this reliability assessment.

sections.heading: Perry: identify the police-arrangement threshold
sections.body:
The casebook’s Perry discussion distinguishes an identification arising by happenstance from one arranged through improper police suggestion. Do not automatically apply a special due-process reliability screening merely because circumstances were suggestive. Identify police involvement before moving to the reliability factors.

Exam checklist: Identify how the confrontation arose and whether the police arranged the relevant suggestion.

sections.heading: Case brief — Kirby v. Illinois
sections.body:
406 U.S. 682 (1972)

Facts: The challenged identification was a showup conducted before indictment or other initiation of adversary judicial proceedings.

Posture: The supplied chapter discusses the Court’s refusal to extend the counsel rule to that pre-proceeding identification.

Issue: Had the Sixth Amendment assistance-of-counsel right attached at that point?

Holding: The Court refused to apply the identification counsel rule in that pre-proceeding setting.

Reasoning: Formal commencement marks the government’s commitment to prosecute and the point at which the Sixth Amendment prosecution-related guarantees attach. The Court distinguished the counsel inquiry from a due-process challenge to prejudicial identification procedures.

Rule: The Sixth Amendment counsel right attaches at or after initiation of adversary judicial criminal proceedings.

Significance: A failed Sixth Amendment argument does not eliminate a separate due-process challenge. Do not confuse Miranda safeguards with this attachment rule.

Source scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Case brief — Stack v. Boyle
sections.body:
342 U.S. 1 (1951)

Facts: Twelve Smith Act defendants received uniform $50,000 bail amounts. They offered individualized information, while the government relied on forfeitures by other defendants.

Posture: Review of unsuccessful efforts to reduce bail and obtain habeas relief.

Issue: Had bail been determined using methods appropriate to its permitted purpose?

Holding: The Court found the method improper and directed use of a renewed motion to reduce bail.

Reasoning: An amount above what is reasonably calculated to assure the particular defendant’s presence is excessive under the stated framework. The indictment and another person’s conduct did not replace an individualized assessment.

Rule: Bail must be set using standards relevant to assuring the individual defendant’s appearance.

Significance: Keep the historical federal bail framework and excessive-amount issue separate from an asserted unconditional constitutional right to release in every case.

Source scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Material witness
sections.body:
A person whose testimony is important to a criminal proceeding and whose attendance presents the relevant legal concern; detention requires the applicable legal authority and conditions.

The handout describes detention where testimony is needed and there is a danger of nonappearance. Identify the witness’s role, why the testimony matters, the attendance concern and the governing detention procedure. Keep witness detention separate from an arrest on probable cause that the witness committed an offense. Do not infer unlimited detention power merely from an investigator’s desire to interview someone.

Example: Hypothetical: police need testimony from a person not accused of an offense. Identify the asserted witness-related legal authority before analyzing detention as if it were an ordinary criminal arrest.

Pitfall: Being useful to an investigation does not itself establish every condition for detaining a material witness. Identify the actual proceeding and the specific legal mechanism.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
An identification occurs before formal prosecution. Does failure of a Sixth Amendment counsel claim dispose of a due-process challenge?

Governing principle — Identification theories
Separate a Sixth Amendment counsel challenge from a due-process reliability challenge. Ask when adversary judicial proceedings began and what type of identification procedure occurred. A physical lineup, a showup, and a photographic display do not necessarily have the same counsel analysis. Do not assume that any suggestive identification is governed only by one constitutional provision.

Application and answer
No. Kirby’s attachment inquiry is distinct from review of the identification procedure for due-process concerns. Analyze the governmental procedure and relevant reliability framework separately.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Failure of a Sixth Amendment identification claim automatically defeats every separate due-process theory.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A uniform bail amount needs no individualized assessment whenever defendants face similar charges.
Do not use this incorrect approach: An identification conducted before formal proceedings automatically satisfies the Sixth Amendment attachment requirement.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A court sets the same high bail for several defendants based only on the charge and another person’s forfeiture. What problem does Stack illustrate?

Governing principle — Due process and reliability
The supplemental identification chapter discusses police-arranged suggestiveness and reliability. Examine the witness’s opportunity to observe, attention, prior description, certainty in the relevant framework, and time elapsed. Describe the procedure and governmental involvement before applying the test. A finding that a process is suggestive does not by itself answer whether the resulting identification must be excluded. Nor does the absence of a particular counsel right automatically resolve a separate due-process argument.

Application and answer
The required individualized assessment cannot be replaced by those general facts. Analyze the permitted purpose, each defendant’s circumstances and whether the amount exceeds what is reasonably calculated under the governing framework.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Failure of a Sixth Amendment identification claim automatically defeats every separate due-process theory.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Introduction to Search and Seizure
references: Modern Criminal Procedure: Cases, Comments, Questions, 15th ed., chapters 6
modules.scope: Supplemental source: this casebook is not the assigned Criminal Procedure treatise, 7th edition. These notes support the listed assigned issues but do not certify completion of the assigned treatise pages. Review the assigned text when available.

sections.heading: Identify the protected interest
sections.body: Before asking whether police needed a warrant, determine whether governmental conduct was a search or seizure. Katz concerns interception of a private telephone conversation even without physical entry into the booth. Its rejection of a purely place-based or physical-entry approach does not convert every governmental observation into an invasion of a general constitutional right to privacy.

sections.heading: Keep privacy and property routes separate
sections.body: Jones identifies installation and use of a GPS device on a vehicle as an information-gathering physical intrusion on a protected effect. The property-based analysis remains available alongside the privacy approach associated with Katz. A conclusion that movements could be observed in public does not by itself dispose of an actual physical-intrusion theory. Identify precisely what was attached, entered, observed, or recorded.

sections.heading: From search to remedy
sections.body: A finding of a search begins rather than ends Fourth Amendment analysis. Identify the claimant’s own protected interest, the justification asserted, scope, and any warrant or exception. Then address exclusion separately. Do not say that Jones resolved every question about all location tracking or that Katz invalidates any recording. Mapp is assigned, but a general reference to exclusion does not substitute for a fully sourced brief of that opinion.

sections.heading: Katz and privacy-based search analysis
sections.body:
Fourth Amendment analysis asks whether government conduct intrudes on a protected privacy interest; technological observation and physical access require close attention to what was exposed and what remained private. The supplied discussion describes the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy approach and emphasizes protection of the home. This does not eliminate other recognized approaches to identifying a search.

Exam checklist: Identify government conduct, the interest invaded, exposure to others and the location or technology involved.

sections.heading: Case brief — Katz v. United States
sections.body:
389 U.S. 347 (1967)

Facts: FBI agents attached a listening device outside a public telephone booth and recorded Katz’s end of calls used in a wagering prosecution.

Posture: Review of a conviction upheld on the ground that agents had not physically entered the booth.

Issue: Could electronic interception constitute a search without physical entry?

Holding: The Court rejected the physical-entry limitation and found the surveillance constitutionally impermissible.

Reasoning: The conversation was something Katz sought to preserve as private despite the booth’s public accessibility. Visual exposure through glass did not mean his words were exposed for unrestricted listening.

Rule: Fourth Amendment protection is not confined to physical entry into a protected place.

Significance: Do not call every privacy interest a Fourth Amendment search; identify the actual governmental intrusion and the protected communication.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Case brief — United States v. Jones
sections.body:
565 U.S. 400 (2012)

Facts: Agents placed a GPS tracker on a vehicle and used it to monitor movements over several weeks.

Posture: Review following reversal of a drug conviction based on the tracking evidence.

Issue: Was installation and monitoring a search under the property-based theory?

Holding: Installation and use constituted a search.

Reasoning: Government physically occupied a protected effect to obtain information. Katz supplemented rather than eliminated the property-based protections of the Amendment.

Rule: An information-gathering physical intrusion on a protected person, house, paper, or effect can qualify as a search.

Significance: Keep property and privacy theories distinct. The search holding is not a universal resolution of every form of location surveillance.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Probable cause
sections.body:
A context-sensitive probability judgment based on sufficiently trustworthy facts, greater than mere suspicion but not proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Specify the object of the judgment: probable cause to arrest a particular person differs from probable cause to find particular evidence in a place. Identify facts known at the legally relevant time and the inferences they support under the totality of circumstances. The handout uses fair probability rather than a fixed numerical score. Do not use evidence learned only after the challenged act to supply its original justification.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have information linking an offense to a location but little connecting a particular occupant. Analyze place-search and person-arrest justifications separately.

Pitfall: The standard is not a trial verdict and not an unexplained hunch. Always specify probable cause for what, based on which facts, at what time.

sections.heading: Definition — Seizure
sections.body:
For property, meaningful interference with a possessory interest; for a person, the legally relevant restraint on liberty under the applicable seizure framework.

Identify which kind of seizure is alleged and the precise event that completed it. Separate taking property from searching for information about it. For people, the rules governing force, assertions of authority and submission require attention to the particular encounter. A stop and an arrest can both involve restraints while demanding different justifications.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer observes a bag, opens it, and keeps it. Distinguish observation, the information-gathering search and the interference with possession rather than treating all three as a single act.

Pitfall: Not every police interaction is a seizure. Equally, the fact that conduct is not a search does not establish that there was no seizure of property or a person.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Officers attach a tracker to a protected vehicle and argue its movements were public. What theory must be addressed besides privacy expectations?

Governing principle — Identify the protected interest
Before asking whether police needed a warrant, determine whether governmental conduct was a search or seizure. Katz concerns interception of a private telephone conversation even without physical entry into the booth. Its rejection of a purely place-based or physical-entry approach does not convert every governmental observation into an invasion of a general constitutional right to privacy.

Application and answer
Jones’s property-based information-gathering intrusion theory. Katz supplemented rather than eliminated that route. A conclusion about public observation alone does not resolve physical installation and use.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Public visibility of vehicle movements automatically defeats every information-gathering physical-intrusion theory.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Finding that a search occurred automatically establishes exclusion without considering justification or remedy.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Katz eliminated all property-based Fourth Amendment protections.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A court concludes that electronic interception was a search. Is suppression automatically established?

Governing principle — Keep privacy and property routes separate
Jones identifies installation and use of a GPS device on a vehicle as an information-gathering physical intrusion on a protected effect. The property-based analysis remains available alongside the privacy approach associated with Katz. A conclusion that movements could be observed in public does not by itself dispose of an actual physical-intrusion theory. Identify precisely what was attached, entered, observed, or recorded.

Application and answer

cards.title:
Explain and qualify this statement: 347 (1967)

Facts: FBI agents attached a listening device outside a public telephone booth and recorded Katz’s end of calls used in a wagering prosecution.
cards.answer:
389 U.S. 347 (1967)

Facts: FBI agents attached a listening device outside a public telephone booth and recorded Katz’s end of calls used in a wagering prosecution.

Posture: Review of a conviction upheld on the ground that agents had not physically entered the booth.

Issue: Could electronic interception constitute a search without physical entry?

Holding: The Court rejected the physical-entry limitation and found the surveillance constitutionally impermissible.

Reasoning: The conversation was something Katz sought to preserve as private despite the booth’s public accessibility. Visual exposure through glass did not mean his words were exposed for unrestricted listening.

Rule: Fourth Amendment protection is not confined to physical entry into a protected place.

Significance: Do not call every privacy interest a Fourth Amendment search; identify the actual governmental intrusion and the protected communication.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

references: Modern Criminal Procedure: Cases, Comments, Questions, 15th ed., chapters 6 and 7

sections.heading: Define what requires justification
sections.body: Identify whether the state conduct is a search, a seizure of property, or a seizure of a person. A warrant application must connect the facts to the place, person, or evidence targeted. Probable cause evaluates the factual basis in context rather than requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Keep an officer’s factual information separate from conclusions that simply repeat the statutory language.

sections.heading: Warrant validity and execution
sections.body: A warrant analysis should separate the issuing authority, factual basis, particularity, and how the warrant was executed. Even a valid authorization does not necessarily permit every later investigative act. Ask whether officers remained within the authorized location and scope and whether a new intrusion required an independent basis. A lawful initial presence is not a blanket license to manipulate or inspect everything encountered.

sections.heading: Assigned examples and limits
sections.body: Franks is identified in the supplied chapter’s discussion of challenges to an affidavit’s veracity; Hicks is assigned for a distinct additional-search problem. Do not collapse a challenge to the warrant’s factual foundation into a challenge to execution. For each issue, identify the alleged defect, its significance to the authorization, and the remedy. These notes are a roadmap from the supplemental chapters, not a claim that the assigned treatise sections or full case opinions have all been supplied.

sections.heading: Probable cause and the totality of circumstances
sections.body:
The Gates discussion uses a practical, contextual assessment of probabilities rather than a rigid checklist for informant information. Consider what the facts collectively establish about evidence or wrongdoing, including the basis and reliability of information. Probable cause is not certainty or the trial standard of proof.

Exam checklist: Consider the combined facts, information quality, corroboration and the practical probability being assessed.

sections.heading: Case brief — Arizona v. Hicks
sections.body:
480 U.S. 321 (1987)

Facts: During lawful entry responding to a fired weapon, an officer moved stereo components to expose serial numbers and then discovered that equipment was stolen.

Posture: Review of whether the additional manipulation was a permissible plain-view inspection.

Issue: Could reasonable suspicion support moving the equipment to inspect concealed serial numbers?

Holding: The movement was a separate search and was unreasonable under the asserted justification.

Reasoning: Looking at already exposed details differs from physically manipulating objects to reveal concealed information. The Court rejected a new intermediate category allowing this additional search solely because it was brief.

Rule: Lawful presence does not itself authorize a new search to expose information not already in view.

Significance: Analyze initial entry, observation, manipulation, and seizure as distinct acts. Do not use plain view as a label for information exposed only by another intrusion.

Source scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Arrest
sections.body:
A taking into custody that subjects a person to the level of restraint associated with arrest. A lawful criminal arrest generally requires probable cause.

Identify the objective restraint and the legally relevant completion of the seizure, not simply an officer’s private intention. Distinguish an arrest from a consensual interaction and a brief investigative stop. Then separately ask whether the arrest had legal justification; an unlawful arrest is still an arrest for purposes of identifying the challenged conduct.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer orders a person to remain and applies handcuffs. Analyze the circumstances and degree of restraint before deciding whether this is an investigative stop or an arrest and what justification is required.

Pitfall: The handout’s shorthand about officer intention does not mean an uncommunicated thought alone arrests someone. Classification and lawfulness are separate questions.

sections.heading: Definition — Plain view
sections.body:
A warrantless-seizure theory concerning an item observed from a legally justified position whose incriminating character has the required probable-cause basis.

Identify lawful observation, any separate access question, and why the item’s character was sufficiently apparent. Do not merge observation with a later act revealing hidden information. Hicks illustrates that moving equipment to expose a serial number is a separate search, even when the initial presence is lawful. Explain each intrusion in sequence rather than treating plain view as a general exploratory-search exception.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer sees a stereo but moves it to read a concealed number. Separate what was already exposed from what the additional manipulation revealed.

Pitfall: Plain view does not automatically authorize moving or opening an item to create the view. A bare suspicion of criminality is not the same as the required probable cause.

sections.heading: Definition — Probable cause
sections.body:
A context-sensitive probability judgment based on sufficiently trustworthy facts, greater than mere suspicion but not proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Specify the object of the judgment: probable cause to arrest a particular person differs from probable cause to find particular evidence in a place. Identify facts known at the legally relevant time and the inferences they support under the totality of circumstances. The handout uses fair probability rather than a fixed numerical score. Do not use evidence learned only after the challenged act to supply its original justification.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have information linking an offense to a location but little connecting a particular occupant. Analyze place-search and person-arrest justifications separately.

Pitfall: The standard is not a trial verdict and not an unexplained hunch. Always specify probable cause for what, based on which facts, at what time.

sections.heading: Definition — Search warrant
sections.body:
Judicial authorization to conduct a specified search and seize designated material under the governing legal requirements.

Identify the issuer, evidentiary showing, place to be searched, objects authorized and limits on execution. The uploaded handout notes that sworn information can be presented by affidavit or, in applicable procedures, oral testimony. Validity of the authorization is separate from whether officers executed it within its lawful scope. A warrant’s existence also differs from the separate remedial question whether evidence must be excluded if a defect is later found.

Example: Hypothetical: a warrant authorizes a search for a large item. Analyze whether the challenged location or container could hold it before assuming every space on the premises may be searched.

Pitfall: Judicial signature alone does not answer factual basis, particularity, execution, or the remedy for a defect. Address the particular issue raised.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
An officer lawfully enters a home and moves a stereo to expose a concealed serial number. Is lawful presence alone sufficient?

Governing principle — Define what requires justification
Identify whether the state conduct is a search, a seizure of property, or a seizure of a person. A warrant application must connect the facts to the place, person, or evidence targeted. Probable cause evaluates the factual basis in context rather than requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Keep an officer’s factual information separate from conclusions that simply repeat the statutory language.

Application and answer
No. Hicks treats the manipulation as a distinct search. Separate the lawful entry, exposed observations, additional intrusion and seizure, then evaluate the justification for each.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Lawful initial presence authorizes every later manipulation of concealed information without an independent basis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A challenge to an affidavit’s veracity is exactly the same issue as execution beyond a warrant’s scope.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A brief additional intrusion cannot be a search merely because an officer calls it cursory.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A warrant is supported on its face, but the defendant contests the affidavit’s veracity. Why is that different from an execution challenge?

Governing principle — Warrant validity and execution
A warrant analysis should separate the issuing authority, factual basis, particularity, and how the warrant was executed. Even a valid authorization does not necessarily permit every later investigative act. Ask whether officers remained within the authorized location and scope and whether a new intrusion required an independent basis. A lawful initial presence is not a blanket license to manipulate or inspect everything encountered.

Application and answer
The former attacks the factual basis for authorization; execution asks whether officers stayed within lawful scope when acting. Identify the alleged defect, its significance and the applicable remedial framework separately.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Lawful initial presence authorizes every later manipulation of concealed information without an independent basis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A challenge to an affidavit’s veracity is exactly the same issue as execution beyond a warrant’s scope.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A brief additional intrusion cannot be a search merely because an officer calls it cursory.

cards.title:
Complete this principle: 321 (1987)

Facts: During lawful entry ____ to a fired weapon, an officer moved stereo components to expose serial numbers and then discovered that equipment was stolen.
cards.answer:
responding

Full explanation: 480 U.S. 321 (1987)

Facts: During lawful entry responding to a fired weapon, an officer moved stereo components to expose serial numbers and then discovered that equipment was stolen.

Posture: Review of whether the additional manipulation was a permissible plain-view inspection.

Issue: Could reasonable suspicion support moving the equipment to inspect concealed serial numbers?

Holding: The movement was a separate search and was unreasonable under the asserted justification.

Reasoning: Looking at already exposed details differs from physically manipulating objects to reveal concealed information. The Court rejected a new intermediate category allowing this additional search solely because it was brief.

Rule: Lawful presence does not itself authorize a new search to expose information not already in view.

Significance: Analyze initial entry, observation, manipulation, and seizure as distinct acts. Do not use plain view as a label for information exposed only by another intrusion.

sections.heading: Encounter, stop, and arrest
sections.body: Identify the moment and method of restraint. A consensual conversation is not automatically a seizure, and a stop is not automatically an arrest. Explain the facts that change the category rather than attaching a label to the entire encounter. The outline’s Hodari D. and Bostick assignments concern important boundary questions, so a general Terry summary cannot substitute for those additional analyses.

sections.heading: Terry requires two justifications
sections.body: The investigative stop must have a sufficient particularized basis, and the protective frisk requires a separate safety rationale involving a reasonable belief that the person is armed and dangerous. Suspicion of criminal activity alone is not an automatic authorization for a weapons search. In Terry, repeated observation of men apparently checking a store supplied context; the officer did more than act on an unexplained feeling.

sections.heading: Scope and escalation
sections.body: A protective frisk is directed at weapons rather than a general search for evidence. Explain why the chosen manner and duration fit the safety concern, and identify any later fact justifying escalation. A useful answer divides the encounter into initial approach, restraint, frisk, discovery, and any further search. If one stage is invalid, trace its consequences without assuming that every later item is automatically admissible or automatically excluded.

sections.heading: Terry: the protective frisk is a separate inquiry
sections.body:
A protective frisk is a limited weapons search justified by a reasonable concern that the person is armed and dangerous, not an automatic evidence search following every investigative stop. Separate the justification for detaining someone from the justification and permissible scope of the frisk.

Exam checklist: Analyze the stop separately, then the safety facts and the limited weapons-search scope.

sections.heading: Case brief — Terry v. Ohio
sections.body:
392 U.S. 1 (1968)

Facts: An experienced officer observed repeated walks past a store and conversations suggesting a planned robbery. He approached the men, frisked Terry, and recovered a gun.

Posture: Review of denial of suppression in a concealed-weapon prosecution.

Issue: Could the limited stop and weapons frisk be reasonable without a full arrest supported by probable cause?

Holding: The limited intervention was upheld on the particular facts.

Reasoning: Reasonableness depended on specific observations and the safety concern that the suspected robbers were armed. The scope of the frisk was tied to finding weapons rather than an unlimited search for criminal evidence.

Rule: A justified investigative stop and a justified protective frisk require their respective particularized grounds.

Significance: Explain the stop and frisk separately. Mere suspicion of crime does not automatically authorize a weapons search.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Arrest
sections.body:
A taking into custody that subjects a person to the level of restraint associated with arrest. A lawful criminal arrest generally requires probable cause.

Identify the objective restraint and the legally relevant completion of the seizure, not simply an officer’s private intention. Distinguish an arrest from a consensual interaction and a brief investigative stop. Then separately ask whether the arrest had legal justification; an unlawful arrest is still an arrest for purposes of identifying the challenged conduct.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer orders a person to remain and applies handcuffs. Analyze the circumstances and degree of restraint before deciding whether this is an investigative stop or an arrest and what justification is required.

Pitfall: The handout’s shorthand about officer intention does not mean an uncommunicated thought alone arrests someone. Classification and lawfulness are separate questions.

sections.heading: Definition — Mere encounter
sections.body:
A consensual police-citizen interaction that the person may decline or terminate without being compelled to cooperate.

Assess the total circumstances objectively. Separate an officer’s request for information from conduct communicating compulsory compliance. Do not classify an encounter solely by the officer’s unexpressed intent. If an initially consensual interaction becomes a stop or arrest, identify when the change occurred and what justified the new restraint. The handout’s emphasis on ability to decline helps distinguish cooperation from compelled participation.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer asks a pedestrian a question without restraining movement. Identify any additional facts indicating coercion before treating the request itself as a seizure.

Pitfall: The categories can change during one encounter. Voluntary cooperation at the beginning does not authorize every later detention or search.

sections.heading: Definition — Probable cause
sections.body:
A context-sensitive probability judgment based on sufficiently trustworthy facts, greater than mere suspicion but not proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Specify the object of the judgment: probable cause to arrest a particular person differs from probable cause to find particular evidence in a place. Identify facts known at the legally relevant time and the inferences they support under the totality of circumstances. The handout uses fair probability rather than a fixed numerical score. Do not use evidence learned only after the challenged act to supply its original justification.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have information linking an offense to a location but little connecting a particular occupant. Analyze place-search and person-arrest justifications separately.

Pitfall: The standard is not a trial verdict and not an unexplained hunch. Always specify probable cause for what, based on which facts, at what time.

sections.heading: Definition — Reasonable suspicion
sections.body:
A particularized and objective basis for suspicion supported by specific articulable facts and rational inferences, assessed in context.

State what is suspected and why. The facts supporting an investigative stop do not automatically establish that a person is armed and dangerous for frisk purposes. The handout’s fair-possibility shorthand is not a numerical formula. Distinguish a justified inference from an unexplained impression and evaluate the facts available before the restraint or search being challenged.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer describes suspicious conduct but supplies no reason to believe a weapon is present. Evaluate the stop justification and the separate frisk justification.

Pitfall: Do not use the same conclusory sentence to establish a stop, an arrest and a weapons search. The required suspicion and permissible intrusion vary with the action.

sections.heading: Definition — Seizure
sections.body:
For property, meaningful interference with a possessory interest; for a person, the legally relevant restraint on liberty under the applicable seizure framework.

Identify which kind of seizure is alleged and the precise event that completed it. Separate taking property from searching for information about it. For people, the rules governing force, assertions of authority and submission require attention to the particular encounter. A stop and an arrest can both involve restraints while demanding different justifications.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer observes a bag, opens it, and keeps it. Distinguish observation, the information-gathering search and the interference with possession rather than treating all three as a single act.

Pitfall: Not every police interaction is a seizure. Equally, the fact that conduct is not a search does not establish that there was no seizure of property or a person.

sections.heading: Definition — Stop and frisk
sections.body:
A limited investigative stop and a separately justified protective weapons frisk under the Terry framework.

The stop requires the relevant reasonable suspicion of criminal activity. The frisk requires the additional reasonable armed-and-dangerous safety basis and remains limited to its protective purpose. Work through approach, restraint, frisk, discovery and any escalation as separate stages. Facts that arise after a weapon is found cannot simply be projected backward to justify the initial frisk.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer reasonably stops a suspect but searches pockets for ordinary evidence without a safety basis. Analyze why a justified stop does not itself establish a justified frisk.

Pitfall: A frisk is not an automatic incident of every stop and is not a general evidentiary search. Explain both justification and scope.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
An officer has grounds for an investigative stop and automatically frisks the person for evidence. What separate inquiries are missing?

Governing principle — Encounter, stop, and arrest
Identify the moment and method of restraint. A consensual conversation is not automatically a seizure, and a stop is not automatically an arrest. Explain the facts that change the category rather than attaching a label to the entire encounter. The outline’s Hodari D. and Bostick assignments concern important boundary questions, so a general Terry summary cannot substitute for those additional analyses.

Application and answer
The frisk needs its own armed-and-dangerous safety basis and limited weapons-related scope. Grounds to investigate crime are not an automatic authorization for a general evidence search.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A justified stop automatically authorizes a general evidentiary search without a separate safety basis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Facts discovered after a frisk can simply be projected backward to justify its original commencement.
Do not use this incorrect approach: One label for an entire encounter replaces separate analysis of approach, restraint, frisk and escalation.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
During a street encounter, when should an answer assess whether the interaction became a seizure?

Governing principle — Terry requires two justifications
The investigative stop must have a sufficient particularized basis, and the protective frisk requires a separate safety rationale involving a reasonable belief that the person is armed and dangerous. Suspicion of criminal activity alone is not an automatic authorization for a weapons search. In Terry, repeated observation of men apparently checking a store supplied context; the officer did more than act on an unexplained feeling.

Application and answer
At the specific point and by the specific restraint alleged. Divide the approach, restraint, frisk, discovery and escalation; explain supporting facts rather than assigning one label to the whole encounter.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A justified stop automatically authorizes a general evidentiary search without a separate safety basis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Facts discovered after a frisk can simply be projected backward to justify its original commencement.
Do not use this incorrect approach: One label for an entire encounter replaces separate analysis of approach, restraint, frisk and escalation.

sections.heading: Chimel rationale
sections.body: A search incident to a lawful arrest is justified by officer safety and preservation of accessible evidence. Identify the arrestee’s person and the area within immediate control rather than treating arrest as authorization to search every nearby room or container. The scope must remain tied to the reasons for the exception.

Explain each route independently; a secured arrestee can defeat the first without logically deciding the second.

sections.heading: Independent exceptions
