The assigned Opperman reading requires separate inventory analysis rather than a label borrowed from Gant.

sections.heading: Vehicle search incident to arrest under Gant
sections.body:
A recent occupant’s arrest does not by itself authorize a routine search of the passenger compartment. The casebook discusses both access-related concerns and a vehicle-specific basis when evidence relevant to the arrest offense may reasonably be found there. Identify which rationale is actually supported; do not equate every traffic arrest with an evidence search.

Exam checklist: Check the arrestee’s access at search time and whether offense-related evidence may reasonably be in the vehicle.

sections.heading: Case brief — Arizona v. Gant
sections.body:
556 U.S. 332 (2009)

Facts: After a suspended-license arrest, Gant was handcuffed and secured in a patrol car. Officers searched his vehicle and found cocaine in a jacket.

Posture: Review of the Arizona decision rejecting the asserted incident-to-arrest search.

Issue: Did the arrest automatically authorize the vehicle search?

Holding: The search was not justified by the asserted incident-to-arrest rationale.

Reasoning: Gant could not reach the car when searched, and the arrest offense did not supply a reasonable basis to expect relevant evidence in the car. The Court rejected an automatic search rule detached from those justifications.

Rule: A vehicle search incident to arrest requires the specified accessibility condition or the distinct reasonable-belief route for offense-of-arrest evidence.

Significance: Analyze both routes separately and do not silently substitute an inventory, consent, or general vehicle exception.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Arrest
sections.body:
A taking into custody that subjects a person to the level of restraint associated with arrest. A lawful criminal arrest generally requires probable cause.

Identify the objective restraint and the legally relevant completion of the seizure, not simply an officer’s private intention. Distinguish an arrest from a consensual interaction and a brief investigative stop. Then separately ask whether the arrest had legal justification; an unlawful arrest is still an arrest for purposes of identifying the challenged conduct.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer orders a person to remain and applies handcuffs. Analyze the circumstances and degree of restraint before deciding whether this is an investigative stop or an arrest and what justification is required.

Pitfall: The handout’s shorthand about officer intention does not mean an uncommunicated thought alone arrests someone. Classification and lawfulness are separate questions.

sections.heading: Definition — Automobile exception
sections.body:
A vehicle-evidence search doctrine permitting a warrantless search when the required probable cause supports finding evidence or contraband in the place searched.

Define the object of the search and explain why the facts establish probable cause. The permitted area depends on where that object could be located. The handout explains that the vehicle need not literally be moving when probable cause arises and that delay does not by itself require a different result. Do not confuse this theory with searching incident to an occupant’s arrest.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have probable cause to believe a particular vehicle contains a weapon. Explain which spaces could contain that weapon and distinguish that justification from a separate inventory policy.

Pitfall: A vehicle’s presence alone is not probable cause. A traffic arrest alone is not the same justification as probable cause to find evidence in the vehicle.

sections.heading: Definition — Exigent circumstances
sections.body:
Emergency circumstances that can justify acting without a warrant within the limits of the particular emergency.

Describe the actual urgency and explain why obtaining a warrant was incompatible with addressing it. Identify the government interest, supporting facts, action taken, scope and duration. A lawful initial emergency response is not an unlimited authorization for a later evidence search. Distinguish this justification from consent, a protective sweep, an inventory, or a vehicle search, even when more than one theory is asserted.

Example: Hypothetical: officers enter to address an immediate danger and later continue searching after it ends. Analyze the initial entry and later investigative activity separately.

Pitfall: Calling something an emergency does not establish it. Tie the scope and timing of police action to the facts supporting the exception rather than listing the exception’s name.

sections.heading: Definition — Inventory search
sections.body:
A search associated with lawful custody of property for recognized caretaking purposes and carried out under the applicable standardized policy.

Start with the lawfulness of the custody or impoundment. Identify the inventory policy, its permitted scope, and how officers followed it. The handout emphasizes protecting property and guarding against missing-property claims. Distinguish those purposes from a general evidence investigation. The absence of a probable-cause requirement for the asserted inventory theory does not mean the inventory is free of legal constraints.

Example: Hypothetical: officers impound a vehicle and make an inventory. Explain the authority for impoundment and the governing procedures instead of treating a list of items as proof of a valid inventory.

Pitfall: Saying inventory after a search is not a substitute for a valid policy and its lawful application. Keep a vehicle-evidence search and an inventory analytically separate.

sections.heading: Definition — Plain view
sections.body:
A warrantless-seizure theory concerning an item observed from a legally justified position whose incriminating character has the required probable-cause basis.

Identify lawful observation, any separate access question, and why the item’s character was sufficiently apparent. Do not merge observation with a later act revealing hidden information. Hicks illustrates that moving equipment to expose a serial number is a separate search, even when the initial presence is lawful. Explain each intrusion in sequence rather than treating plain view as a general exploratory-search exception.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer sees a stereo but moves it to read a concealed number. Separate what was already exposed from what the additional manipulation revealed.

Pitfall: Plain view does not automatically authorize moving or opening an item to create the view. A bare suspicion of criminality is not the same as the required probable cause.

sections.heading: Definition — Probable cause
sections.body:
A context-sensitive probability judgment based on sufficiently trustworthy facts, greater than mere suspicion but not proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Specify the object of the judgment: probable cause to arrest a particular person differs from probable cause to find particular evidence in a place. Identify facts known at the legally relevant time and the inferences they support under the totality of circumstances. The handout uses fair probability rather than a fixed numerical score. Do not use evidence learned only after the challenged act to supply its original justification.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have information linking an offense to a location but little connecting a particular occupant. Analyze place-search and person-arrest justifications separately.

Pitfall: The standard is not a trial verdict and not an unexplained hunch. Always specify probable cause for what, based on which facts, at what time.

sections.heading: Definition — Protective sweep
sections.body:
A limited safety inspection of spaces where a dangerous person could be found, subject to the legal conditions for the particular sweep.

The handout’s brief description should be read with Buie’s distinctions. In its in-home-arrest setting, immediately adjoining spaces from which an attack could be launched receive a different analysis from a broader sweep, which needs the specified articulable danger-based facts. The inspection is cursory, person-focused and limited in duration. Do not convert lawful presence or an arrest label into permission to search the entire premises for evidence.

Example: Hypothetical: following an in-home arrest, officers inspect an area farther from the arrest scene. Identify the safety facts and explain why the location could conceal a dangerous person.

Pitfall: The handout’s broad reference to entry or an outside arrest is not a universal rule covering every setting. Check the governing authority and its factual prerequisites.

sections.heading: Definition — Search incident to arrest
sections.body:
A search tied to a lawful arrest and its recognized safety or evidence-preservation justifications, limited by the governing rule for the place and circumstances.

Analyze the arrestee and accessible area under the Chimel rationale. For a vehicle, Gant distinguishes the specified accessibility condition from the separate reasonable-belief route for evidence of the arrest offense. Identify conditions at the time of search. A secured arrestee’s inability to reach the vehicle can defeat one rationale without automatically resolving every independent exception.

Example: Hypothetical: a handcuffed driver is secured away from a car after a suspended-license arrest. Explain accessibility and evidence-of-that-offense separately before reaching a conclusion.

Pitfall: The right to arrest is not an unlimited right to search every nearby location. Do not substitute inventory or probable-cause vehicle reasoning without establishing that distinct basis.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
After a suspended-license arrest, a handcuffed occupant is locked in a patrol car. Does the arrest automatically authorize searching a jacket in the vehicle?

Governing principle — Chimel rationale
A search incident to a lawful arrest is justified by officer safety and preservation of accessible evidence. Identify the arrestee’s person and the area within immediate control rather than treating arrest as authorization to search every nearby room or container. The scope must remain tied to the reasons for the exception.

Application and answer
No. Apply Gant’s accessibility route and its distinct reasonable-belief route for offense-of-arrest evidence. A secured occupant and the nature of that offense matter to both analyses.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Any arrest of a recent occupant automatically authorizes searching the entire vehicle under Gant.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Calling an evidence search an inventory supplies a valid policy and lawful custody by itself.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A secured arrestee is necessarily within reaching distance of the passenger compartment at the time of search.

sections.body:

A separate vehicle-specific route asks whether it is reasonable to believe evidence of the offense of arrest might be found in the vehicle. Explain each route independently; a secured arrestee can defeat the first without logically deciding the second.

Application and answer
Each exception has its own trigger, purpose and scope. Establish an actual independent justification from the facts rather than treating the names of exceptions as interchangeable.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Any arrest of a recent occupant automatically authorizes searching the entire vehicle under Gant.

Do not use this incorrect approach: A secured arrestee is necessarily within reaching distance of the passenger compartment at the time of search.

sections.heading: Case brief — Georgia v. Randolph
sections.body:
547 U.S. 103 (2006)

Facts: A physically present resident refused permission to search the shared home. Officers obtained consent from his wife, entered, and used the observations to obtain a warrant.

Posture: Review of exclusion based on the initial disputed-consent entry.

Issue: Did the other resident’s consent alone justify entry over the present resident’s express objection?

Holding: The Court upheld the rejection of the asserted consent justification on these facts.

Reasoning: Shared social expectations did not give one co-tenant’s invitation superiority over a present co-tenant’s objection. A separate safety justification would require its own analysis rather than reliance on the disputed invitation.

Rule: In the decision’s specified present-and-objecting setting, another co-occupant’s consent did not itself justify the entry.

Significance: Identify presence, objection, timing, scope, and the asserted exception. Do not state a rule for every absent-occupant or emergency situation from this brief alone.

Source scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Consent search
sections.body:
A warrantless search resting on permission that is voluntarily given under the totality of the circumstances and valid for the asserted scope.

Analyze voluntariness, the consenting person’s authority, and the scope of permission as separate elements. Identify the words used, surrounding pressures, and the particular place or item searched. Where occupants disagree, the applicable co-occupant rules require their own analysis. Consent does not erase every problem arising from an earlier unlawful detention.

Example: Hypothetical: a person permits inspection of a bag but disputes a later search elsewhere. Determine what the permission reasonably covered instead of declaring the entire investigation consensual.

Pitfall: Permission to one search is not permission to any search. A polite request does not alone establish voluntariness, and a person’s lack of ownership does not alone resolve authority.

sections.heading: Definition — Voluntariness
sections.body:
A context-dependent inquiry into whether consent or a statement resulted from a legally impermissible coercive setting or conduct; the governing doctrine depends on the right and event.

For consent searches, assess the total circumstances instead of treating a yes response as conclusive. For a confession, analyze the applicable due-process and interrogation safeguards separately. The handout’s references to threats, coercion and deception are issue signals, not a rule that every deception has an identical legal result. State which doctrine governs and how the actual pressure affected the choice.

Example: Hypothetical: a search follows permission given during a contested detention. Analyze the detention, voluntary consent and any resulting causal-remedy problem separately.

Pitfall: Do not collapse voluntariness, knowledge, waiver and the effects of earlier illegality into a single conclusion. A Miranda issue and a consent-search issue are not the same test.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A physically present co-occupant expressly refuses consent while another agrees. What does Randolph require you to distinguish?

Governing principle — Consent as a distinct theory
A consent argument requires examining whether consent was voluntary, whether the person had authority relevant to the search, and what scope was actually permitted. These are separate questions. Do not assume that a polite request establishes consent or that agreeing to one location or purpose authorizes an unlimited investigation. The actual words, surrounding pressures, and conduct matter.

Application and answer
Analyze the specified presence and objection situation, authority, timing, scope and any independent safety justification. The other occupant’s invitation alone did not prevail on the facts of Randolph.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: One occupant’s consent always overrides a present co-occupant’s express refusal in every setting.
Do not use this incorrect approach: An undercover officer’s concealment of identity alone establishes every element of entrapment.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Permission for one limited search automatically authorizes all later searches wherever officers choose.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Exclusionary Rule
references: Modern Criminal Procedure: Cases, Comments, Questions, 15th ed., chapters 6 and 12
modules.scope: Supplemental source: this casebook is not the assigned Criminal Procedure treatise, 7th edition. These notes support the listed assigned issues but do not certify completion of the assigned treatise pages. Review the assigned text when available.

sections.heading: Separate violation and exclusion
sections.body: Begin by identifying the specific constitutional violation and whose rights were affected. Then determine whether the challenged evidence was obtained through it. Exclusion is a remedy with its own scope and exceptions; neither the existence of a violation nor an officer’s assertion of good intentions alone resolves admissibility.

sections.heading: Trace the evidence
sections.body: Draw a timeline for statements, physical objects, witness information, and later police actions. For derivative evidence, explain the causal relationship to the initial illegality and test the actually applicable doctrine: an independent lawful source differs from attenuation of an existing causal link. Do not assume that any intervening event automatically cures the original violation. Identify the facts that matter under the assigned case rather than listing exception names.

sections.heading: Leon’s distinct inquiry
sections.body: Leon examines objectively reasonable reliance on a judicially issued warrant later found unsupported by probable cause. The analysis asks whether exclusion would serve the deterrence rationale in the circumstances and recognizes limits on reasonable reliance. It does not say that an officer’s subjective good intentions validate an unconstitutional search. Keep the warrant’s legal defect separate from the remedy and explain why reliance was or was not objectively reasonable. The outline’s additional Wong Sun, Brown, Elstad, and Strieff readings remain separate assignments.

sections.heading: Derivative evidence and an independent source
sections.body:
The Wong Sun discussion illustrates that exclusion can reach evidence derived from unlawful conduct, not just the immediate physical item seized. It also distinguishes knowledge obtained independently of the unlawful activity. Trace the causal chain and identify the particular doctrine that allegedly permits use of later evidence rather than assuming all later discoveries are automatically admissible or automatically excluded.

Exam checklist: Identify the illegality, evidence chain and whether the claimed independent source truly avoids that illegality.

sections.heading: Leon and objectively reasonable reliance
sections.body:
The good-faith discussion focuses on objective reliance and the exclusionary rule’s deterrent purpose. A magistrate’s error does not necessarily require suppressing evidence when officers reasonably obtain and execute a warrant. This is not a blanket exception for every warrant or for the officer’s subjective claim of good intentions; the surrounding circumstances and limits still matter.

Exam checklist: Identify the warrant process, the claimed error, officers’ objective conduct and the exception’s limits.

sections.heading: Definition — Arrest
sections.body:
A taking into custody that subjects a person to the level of restraint associated with arrest. A lawful criminal arrest generally requires probable cause.

Identify the objective restraint and the legally relevant completion of the seizure, not simply an officer’s private intention. Distinguish an arrest from a consensual interaction and a brief investigative stop. Then separately ask whether the arrest had legal justification; an unlawful arrest is still an arrest for purposes of identifying the challenged conduct.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer orders a person to remain and applies handcuffs. Analyze the circumstances and degree of restraint before deciding whether this is an investigative stop or an arrest and what justification is required.

Pitfall: The handout’s shorthand about officer intention does not mean an uncommunicated thought alone arrests someone. Classification and lawfulness are separate questions.

sections.heading: Definition — Automobile exception
sections.body:
A vehicle-evidence search doctrine permitting a warrantless search when the required probable cause supports finding evidence or contraband in the place searched.

Define the object of the search and explain why the facts establish probable cause. The permitted area depends on where that object could be located. The handout explains that the vehicle need not literally be moving when probable cause arises and that delay does not by itself require a different result. Do not confuse this theory with searching incident to an occupant’s arrest.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have probable cause to believe a particular vehicle contains a weapon. Explain which spaces could contain that weapon and distinguish that justification from a separate inventory policy.

Pitfall: A vehicle’s presence alone is not probable cause. A traffic arrest alone is not the same justification as probable cause to find evidence in the vehicle.

sections.heading: Definition — Consent search
sections.body:
A warrantless search resting on permission that is voluntarily given under the totality of the circumstances and valid for the asserted scope.

Analyze voluntariness, the consenting person’s authority, and the scope of permission as separate elements. Identify the words used, surrounding pressures, and the particular place or item searched. Where occupants disagree, the applicable co-occupant rules require their own analysis. Consent does not erase every problem arising from an earlier unlawful detention.

Example: Hypothetical: a person permits inspection of a bag but disputes a later search elsewhere. Determine what the permission reasonably covered instead of declaring the entire investigation consensual.

Pitfall: Permission to one search is not permission to any search. A polite request does not alone establish voluntariness, and a person’s lack of ownership does not alone resolve authority.

sections.heading: Definition — Custodial interrogation
sections.body:
Interrogation occurring while the person is in custody for purposes of the Miranda framework. Custody and interrogation are distinct requirements.

The handout combines an arrest-like custody description with questioning. Keep the two inquiries separate: determine the restraint and circumstances relevant to custody, then ask whether express questioning or its functional equivalent occurred. Innis includes conduct officers should know is reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, beyond conduct ordinarily attendant to custody. A statement may be volunteered without being a product of interrogation.

Example: Hypothetical: officers transport a restrained suspect without asking questions. Custody does not by itself establish interrogation; examine any remarks or actions alleged to be its functional equivalent.

Pitfall: The fact that someone cannot leave does not by itself establish every Miranda requirement. Conversely, avoiding a question mark does not necessarily avoid interrogation.

sections.heading: Definition — Mere encounter
sections.body:
A consensual police-citizen interaction that the person may decline or terminate without being compelled to cooperate.

Assess the total circumstances objectively. Separate an officer’s request for information from conduct communicating compulsory compliance. Do not classify an encounter solely by the officer’s unexpressed intent. If an initially consensual interaction becomes a stop or arrest, identify when the change occurred and what justified the new restraint. The handout’s emphasis on ability to decline helps distinguish cooperation from compelled participation.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer asks a pedestrian a question without restraining movement. Identify any additional facts indicating coercion before treating the request itself as a seizure.

Pitfall: The categories can change during one encounter. Voluntary cooperation at the beginning does not authorize every later detention or search.

sections.heading: Definition — Exigent circumstances
sections.body:
Emergency circumstances that can justify acting without a warrant within the limits of the particular emergency.

Describe the actual urgency and explain why obtaining a warrant was incompatible with addressing it. Identify the government interest, supporting facts, action taken, scope and duration. A lawful initial emergency response is not an unlimited authorization for a later evidence search. Distinguish this justification from consent, a protective sweep, an inventory, or a vehicle search, even when more than one theory is asserted.

Example: Hypothetical: officers enter to address an immediate danger and later continue searching after it ends. Analyze the initial entry and later investigative activity separately.

Pitfall: Calling something an emergency does not establish it. Tie the scope and timing of police action to the facts supporting the exception rather than listing the exception’s name.

sections.heading: Definition — Independent source doctrine
sections.body:
A basis for admitting evidence actually obtained through a lawful source genuinely independent of the challenged illegality.

Trace the actual acquisition of the evidence. In the supplied exclusionary-rule chapter, an untainted later warrant can present a different issue from merely relying on information gained through an unlawful entry. Explain which facts supported the lawful source and whether the investigation or decision depended on the earlier illegality. Keep actual independence separate from a hypothetical assertion about what police would have found.

Example: Hypothetical: police make an unlawful entry and later obtain a warrant. Identify what supported the warrant and why the later acquisition was or was not genuinely independent.

Pitfall: A later warrant is not automatically independent merely because it exists. Identify the source of its information and the causal role of the original illegality.

sections.heading: Definition — Inevitable discovery rule
sections.body:
A remedial doctrine allowing evidence obtained unlawfully when the government makes the required showing that lawful discovery was inevitable.

The uploaded handout specifies proof by a preponderance of the evidence. Explain the lawful route, actual investigative circumstances, and why discovery would have occurred rather than merely could have occurred. Unlike an actual independent source, this inquiry evaluates a counterfactual lawful path. State the facts that make that path inevitable under the governing doctrine rather than filling the gap with speculation.

Example: Hypothetical: the government claims a lawful search already underway would have located the same item. Examine the actual search area, timing and established steps supporting that claim.

Pitfall: Possibility is not inevitability. The doctrine concerns admissibility and does not retroactively make the unlawful investigative act lawful.

sections.heading: Definition — Inventory search
sections.body:
A search associated with lawful custody of property for recognized caretaking purposes and carried out under the applicable standardized policy.

Start with the lawfulness of the custody or impoundment. Identify the inventory policy, its permitted scope, and how officers followed it. The handout emphasizes protecting property and guarding against missing-property claims. Distinguish those purposes from a general evidence investigation. The absence of a probable-cause requirement for the asserted inventory theory does not mean the inventory is free of legal constraints.

Example: Hypothetical: officers impound a vehicle and make an inventory. Explain the authority for impoundment and the governing procedures instead of treating a list of items as proof of a valid inventory.

Pitfall: Saying inventory after a search is not a substitute for a valid policy and its lawful application. Keep a vehicle-evidence search and an inventory analytically separate.

sections.heading: Definition — Material witness
sections.body:
A person whose testimony is important to a criminal proceeding and whose attendance presents the relevant legal concern; detention requires the applicable legal authority and conditions.

The handout describes detention where testimony is needed and there is a danger of nonappearance. Identify the witness’s role, why the testimony matters, the attendance concern and the governing detention procedure. Keep witness detention separate from an arrest on probable cause that the witness committed an offense. Do not infer unlimited detention power merely from an investigator’s desire to interview someone.

Example: Hypothetical: police need testimony from a person not accused of an offense. Identify the asserted witness-related legal authority before analyzing detention as if it were an ordinary criminal arrest.

Pitfall: Being useful to an investigation does not itself establish every condition for detaining a material witness. Identify the actual proceeding and the specific legal mechanism.

sections.heading: Definition — Plain view
sections.body:
A warrantless-seizure theory concerning an item observed from a legally justified position whose incriminating character has the required probable-cause basis.

Identify lawful observation, any separate access question, and why the item’s character was sufficiently apparent. Do not merge observation with a later act revealing hidden information. Hicks illustrates that moving equipment to expose a serial number is a separate search, even when the initial presence is lawful. Explain each intrusion in sequence rather than treating plain view as a general exploratory-search exception.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer sees a stereo but moves it to read a concealed number. Separate what was already exposed from what the additional manipulation revealed.

Pitfall: Plain view does not automatically authorize moving or opening an item to create the view. A bare suspicion of criminality is not the same as the required probable cause.

sections.heading: Definition — Probable cause
sections.body:
A context-sensitive probability judgment based on sufficiently trustworthy facts, greater than mere suspicion but not proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Specify the object of the judgment: probable cause to arrest a particular person differs from probable cause to find particular evidence in a place. Identify facts known at the legally relevant time and the inferences they support under the totality of circumstances. The handout uses fair probability rather than a fixed numerical score. Do not use evidence learned only after the challenged act to supply its original justification.

Example: Hypothetical: officers have information linking an offense to a location but little connecting a particular occupant. Analyze place-search and person-arrest justifications separately.

Pitfall: The standard is not a trial verdict and not an unexplained hunch. Always specify probable cause for what, based on which facts, at what time.

sections.heading: Definition — Protective sweep
sections.body:
A limited safety inspection of spaces where a dangerous person could be found, subject to the legal conditions for the particular sweep.

The handout’s brief description should be read with Buie’s distinctions. In its in-home-arrest setting, immediately adjoining spaces from which an attack could be launched receive a different analysis from a broader sweep, which needs the specified articulable danger-based facts. The inspection is cursory, person-focused and limited in duration. Do not convert lawful presence or an arrest label into permission to search the entire premises for evidence.

Example: Hypothetical: following an in-home arrest, officers inspect an area farther from the arrest scene. Identify the safety facts and explain why the location could conceal a dangerous person.

Pitfall: The handout’s broad reference to entry or an outside arrest is not a universal rule covering every setting. Check the governing authority and its factual prerequisites.

sections.heading: Definition — Reasonable suspicion
sections.body:
A particularized and objective basis for suspicion supported by specific articulable facts and rational inferences, assessed in context.

State what is suspected and why. The facts supporting an investigative stop do not automatically establish that a person is armed and dangerous for frisk purposes. The handout’s fair-possibility shorthand is not a numerical formula. Distinguish a justified inference from an unexplained impression and evaluate the facts available before the restraint or search being challenged.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer describes suspicious conduct but supplies no reason to believe a weapon is present. Evaluate the stop justification and the separate frisk justification.

Pitfall: Do not use the same conclusory sentence to establish a stop, an arrest and a weapons search. The required suspicion and permissible intrusion vary with the action.

sections.heading: Definition — Search incident to arrest
sections.body:
A search tied to a lawful arrest and its recognized safety or evidence-preservation justifications, limited by the governing rule for the place and circumstances.

Analyze the arrestee and accessible area under the Chimel rationale. For a vehicle, Gant distinguishes the specified accessibility condition from the separate reasonable-belief route for evidence of the arrest offense. Identify conditions at the time of search. A secured arrestee’s inability to reach the vehicle can defeat one rationale without automatically resolving every independent exception.

Example: Hypothetical: a handcuffed driver is secured away from a car after a suspended-license arrest. Explain accessibility and evidence-of-that-offense separately before reaching a conclusion.

Pitfall: The right to arrest is not an unlimited right to search every nearby location. Do not substitute inventory or probable-cause vehicle reasoning without establishing that distinct basis.

sections.heading: Definition — Search warrant
sections.body:
Judicial authorization to conduct a specified search and seize designated material under the governing legal requirements.

Identify the issuer, evidentiary showing, place to be searched, objects authorized and limits on execution. The uploaded handout notes that sworn information can be presented by affidavit or, in applicable procedures, oral testimony. Validity of the authorization is separate from whether officers executed it within its lawful scope. A warrant’s existence also differs from the separate remedial question whether evidence must be excluded if a defect is later found.

Example: Hypothetical: a warrant authorizes a search for a large item. Analyze whether the challenged location or container could hold it before assuming every space on the premises may be searched.

Pitfall: Judicial signature alone does not answer factual basis, particularity, execution, or the remedy for a defect. Address the particular issue raised.

sections.heading: Definition — Seizure
sections.body:
For property, meaningful interference with a possessory interest; for a person, the legally relevant restraint on liberty under the applicable seizure framework.

Identify which kind of seizure is alleged and the precise event that completed it. Separate taking property from searching for information about it. For people, the rules governing force, assertions of authority and submission require attention to the particular encounter. A stop and an arrest can both involve restraints while demanding different justifications.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer observes a bag, opens it, and keeps it. Distinguish observation, the information-gathering search and the interference with possession rather than treating all three as a single act.

Pitfall: Not every police interaction is a seizure. Equally, the fact that conduct is not a search does not establish that there was no seizure of property or a person.

sections.heading: Definition — Stop and frisk
sections.body:
A limited investigative stop and a separately justified protective weapons frisk under the Terry framework.

The stop requires the relevant reasonable suspicion of criminal activity. The frisk requires the additional reasonable armed-and-dangerous safety basis and remains limited to its protective purpose. Work through approach, restraint, frisk, discovery and any escalation as separate stages. Facts that arise after a weapon is found cannot simply be projected backward to justify the initial frisk.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer reasonably stops a suspect but searches pockets for ordinary evidence without a safety basis. Analyze why a justified stop does not itself establish a justified frisk.

Pitfall: A frisk is not an automatic incident of every stop and is not a general evidentiary search. Explain both justification and scope.

sections.heading: Definition — Voluntariness
sections.body:
A context-dependent inquiry into whether consent or a statement resulted from a legally impermissible coercive setting or conduct; the governing doctrine depends on the right and event.

For consent searches, assess the total circumstances instead of treating a yes response as conclusive. For a confession, analyze the applicable due-process and interrogation safeguards separately. The handout’s references to threats, coercion and deception are issue signals, not a rule that every deception has an identical legal result. State which doctrine governs and how the actual pressure affected the choice.

Example: Hypothetical: a search follows permission given during a contested detention. Analyze the detention, voluntary consent and any resulting causal-remedy problem separately.

Pitfall: Do not collapse voluntariness, knowledge, waiver and the effects of earlier illegality into a single conclusion. A Miranda issue and a consent-search issue are not the same test.

sections.heading: Definition — Waiver
sections.body:
Relinquishment of a legal right under the knowledge, voluntariness and other requirements applicable to that particular right.

Identify the right, who held it, the event said to relinquish it, and the governing standard. In the Miranda setting, warnings, understanding, a sufficient waiver, invocation and later renewed questioning each require analysis. Some doctrines permit an implied waiver, but an inference still needs support. Consent-search voluntariness should not automatically be recast as the identical formal waiver requirement used for every other constitutional right.

Example: Hypothetical: an arrested suspect signs a form after warnings. Explain why the signature is evidence to evaluate rather than a conclusive answer to knowledge, voluntariness, prior invocation or the lawfulness of renewed questioning.

Pitfall: The word waiver does not supply one universal test. A later answer or signed form cannot erase the need to analyze the right and sequence of events.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
An unconstitutional investigation is followed by a later lawful investigative step. Is all later evidence automatically admissible?

Governing principle — Separate violation and exclusion
Begin by identifying the specific constitutional violation and whose rights were affected. Then determine whether the challenged evidence was obtained through it. Exclusion is a remedy with its own scope and exceptions; neither the existence of a violation nor an officer’s assertion of good intentions alone resolves admissibility.

Application and answer
No. Trace the evidence’s acquisition and examine the applicable independent-source, attenuation or other doctrine. A later event does not itself establish the legal conditions for an exception.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: An unlawful investigative act becomes lawful retroactively whenever resulting evidence is admitted.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A later warrant is automatically independent even when it relies on information from the unlawful entry.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A showing that lawful discovery was merely possible is identical to establishing inevitability.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
An officer says they honestly believed a warrant was valid. Does that statement alone establish Leon?

Governing principle — Trace the evidence
Draw a timeline for statements, physical objects, witness information, and later police actions. For derivative evidence, explain the causal relationship to the initial illegality and test the actually applicable doctrine: an independent lawful source differs from attenuation of an existing causal link. Do not assume that any intervening event automatically cures the original violation. Identify the facts that matter under the assigned case rather than listing exception names.

Application and answer
No. The inquiry concerns objectively reasonable reliance and its limits, not merely subjective good intentions. Separate the warrant defect from the deterrence-based exclusion analysis.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: An unlawful investigative act becomes lawful retroactively whenever resulting evidence is admitted.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A later warrant is automatically independent even when it relies on information from the unlawful entry.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A showing that lawful discovery was merely possible is identical to establishing inevitability.

cards.answer:
A taking into custody that subjects a person to the level of restraint associated with arrest. A lawful criminal arrest generally requires probable cause.

Identify the objective restraint and the legally relevant completion of the seizure, not simply an officer’s private intention. Distinguish an arrest from a consensual interaction and a brief investigative stop. Then separately ask whether the arrest had legal justification; an unlawful arrest is still an arrest for purposes of identifying the challenged conduct.

Example: Hypothetical: an officer orders a person to remain and applies handcuffs. Analyze the circumstances and degree of restraint before deciding whether this is an investigative stop or an arrest and what justification is required.

Pitfall: The handout’s shorthand about officer intention does not mean an uncommunicated thought alone arrests someone. Classification and lawfulness are separate questions.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Limitations on Prosecutors
references: Modern Criminal Procedure: Cases, Comments, Questions, 15th ed., chapters 21
modules.scope: Supplemental source: this casebook is not the assigned Criminal Procedure treatise, 7th edition. These notes support the listed assigned issues but do not certify completion of the assigned treatise pages. Review the assigned text when available.

sections.heading: Three linked questions
sections.body: Identify evidence favorable to the defense, suppression or nondisclosure attributable to the prosecution, and materiality. Favorability can include impeachment as well as directly exculpatory information. The significance of an item depends on the charges, defense theory, witnesses, and record as a whole. Do not equate any discovery violation with the same constitutional remedy.

sections.heading: Bagley and witness incentives
sections.body: The supplied chapter uses Bagley to develop the Brady obligation. Bagley involved undisclosed arrangements providing payment incentives to important government witnesses despite a defense request concerning inducements. That setting illustrates how information affecting credibility can matter even if it does not independently establish innocence. Ask what the undisclosed material could have done to the fact-finder’s assessment of the government’s case.

sections.heading: Materiality and separate preservation questions
sections.body: The reasonable-probability formulation concerns confidence in the outcome, not a requirement that the defendant prove with certainty that acquittal would have occurred. Evaluate the combined significance of the suppressed evidence rather than isolating each item artificially. Distinguish a failure to disclose existing evidence from loss or destruction of material, which the outline addresses through Trombetta. These are supplemental notes on the topic; the assigned treatise pages and all preservation decisions are not certified complete.

sections.heading: Brady disclosure and materiality
sections.body:
The Bagley discussion builds on Brady’s concern with prosecution suppression of favorable, material evidence. Favorable evidence can include material useful for impeaching a government witness, not just directly exculpatory facts. Identify what was withheld, its favorable use and the applicable materiality analysis; a discovery-rule question and a due-process disclosure question are not always identical.

Exam checklist: Identify prosecution suppression, favorable use and materiality to guilt or punishment.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Prosecutors fail to disclose a payment arrangement with an important witness. Can impeachment information count as favorable evidence?

Governing principle — Three linked questions
Identify evidence favorable to the defense, suppression or nondisclosure attributable to the prosecution, and materiality. Favorability can include impeachment as well as directly exculpatory information. The significance of an item depends on the charges, defense theory, witnesses, and record as a whole. Do not equate any discovery violation with the same constitutional remedy.

Application and answer
Yes. Bagley illustrates that witness incentives can affect credibility and fall within the favorable-evidence analysis. Then analyze suppression and materiality in the context of the whole case.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Witness impeachment material cannot qualify as favorable evidence because it is not direct proof of innocence.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every nondisclosure requires automatic reversal without any significance or materiality inquiry.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Failure to disclose existing evidence and destruction of material always use one identical legal analysis.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Does every nondisclosure require automatic reversal without considering its significance?

Governing principle — Bagley and witness incentives
The supplied chapter uses Bagley to develop the Brady obligation. Bagley involved undisclosed arrangements providing payment incentives to important government witnesses despite a defense request concerning inducements. That setting illustrates how information affecting credibility can matter even if it does not independently establish innocence. Ask what the undisclosed material could have done to the fact-finder’s assessment of the government’s case.

Application and answer
No. Identify the applicable legal disclosure rule and materiality or prejudice framework. The constitutional inquiry is not identical to every discovery-rule violation, and lost evidence raises separate preservation questions.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Witness impeachment material cannot qualify as favorable evidence because it is not direct proof of innocence.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every nondisclosure requires automatic reversal without any significance or materiality inquiry.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Failure to disclose existing evidence and destruction of material always use one identical legal analysis.

references: Modern Criminal Procedure: Cases, Comments, Questions, 15th ed., chapters 9

sections.heading: Identify the trigger
sections.body: The Miranda framework concerns custodial interrogation, not every conversation between a suspect and an officer. Analyze custody and interrogation separately and identify the time each condition began. Distinguish the underlying privilege against compelled self-incrimination from the procedural warnings used to protect it. A statement can raise a voluntariness question even where a particular warning issue is absent.

sections.heading: Warnings, waiver, and invocation
sections.body: Record which warnings were given, whether a legally sufficient waiver occurred, and whether the person later invoked silence or counsel. The fact that warnings were read does not automatically establish every element of waiver. Separate initial waiver from the rules governing renewed questioning after invocation. A later answer does not erase the need to analyze how police obtained permission to proceed.

sections.heading: Interrogation beyond direct questions
sections.body: Innis includes express questions and their functional equivalent: police words or actions, apart from those normally attendant to custody, that officers should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response. The focus is not solely on an officer’s stated intention. Innis itself found the short conversation about a missing gun insufficient on the record to constitute interrogation. Apply the test to the known circumstances rather than declaring any overheard police conversation an interrogation.

sections.heading: The privilege and custodial safeguards
sections.body:
The text describes protections against compelled self-incrimination and the particular concern posed by custodial interrogation. Distinguish the underlying constitutional privilege from the warning-and-waiver framework designed to protect it. A statement’s voluntariness and compliance with Miranda can require separate analysis.

Exam checklist: Identify compulsion, custody/interrogation where relevant, warnings, waiver and the doctrine governing admissibility.

sections.heading: Case brief — Miranda v. Arizona
sections.body:
384 U.S. 436 (1966)

Facts: Police questioned Miranda in custody and obtained a written confession without advising him of the right to counsel during questioning. A printed assertion of rights knowledge appeared on the statement.

Posture: Review of convictions affirmed by the Arizona court.

Issue: Were the interrogation statements admissible without the required safeguards and waiver?

Holding: The conviction was reversed; the statements were inadmissible under the stated framework.

Reasoning: Custodial interrogation threatened the privilege against compelled self-incrimination. Required warnings and a knowing, intelligent waiver could not be replaced by a boilerplate assertion in a signed confession.

Rule: The custodial-interrogation framework requires the recognized warnings or effective equivalent safeguards and an adequate waiver before use of resulting statements.

Significance: Analyze custody, interrogation, warnings, waiver, and invocation distinctly; do not infer waiver from a signature alone.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Case brief — Rhode Island v. Innis
sections.body:
446 U.S. 291 (1980)

Facts: After Innis requested counsel, officers transporting him discussed a missing shotgun and the risk to children. Innis interrupted and offered to show them the gun.

Posture: Review of the state court’s conclusion that the discussion was interrogation.

Issue: Was the conversation the functional equivalent of questioning under Miranda?

Holding: The Court found no interrogation on the circumstances presented.

Reasoning: The test includes conduct officers should know is reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, beyond routine custody conduct. The short discussion and what officers knew did not satisfy that test on this record.

Rule: Interrogation includes express questions and their functional equivalent under the reasonably-likely-to-elicit formulation.

Significance: Do not classify every police conversation within hearing as interrogation or limit the analysis solely to an officer’s asserted intent.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Definition — Custodial interrogation
sections.body:
Interrogation occurring while the person is in custody for purposes of the Miranda framework. Custody and interrogation are distinct requirements.

The handout combines an arrest-like custody description with questioning. Keep the two inquiries separate: determine the restraint and circumstances relevant to custody, then ask whether express questioning or its functional equivalent occurred. Innis includes conduct officers should know is reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, beyond conduct ordinarily attendant to custody. A statement may be volunteered without being a product of interrogation.

Example: Hypothetical: officers transport a restrained suspect without asking questions. Custody does not by itself establish interrogation; examine any remarks or actions alleged to be its functional equivalent.

Pitfall: The fact that someone cannot leave does not by itself establish every Miranda requirement. Conversely, avoiding a question mark does not necessarily avoid interrogation.

sections.heading: Definition — Voluntariness
sections.body:
A context-dependent inquiry into whether consent or a statement resulted from a legally impermissible coercive setting or conduct; the governing doctrine depends on the right and event.

For consent searches, assess the total circumstances instead of treating a yes response as conclusive. For a confession, analyze the applicable due-process and interrogation safeguards separately. The handout’s references to threats, coercion and deception are issue signals, not a rule that every deception has an identical legal result. State which doctrine governs and how the actual pressure affected the choice.

Example: Hypothetical: a search follows permission given during a contested detention. Analyze the detention, voluntary consent and any resulting causal-remedy problem separately.

Pitfall: Do not collapse voluntariness, knowledge, waiver and the effects of earlier illegality into a single conclusion. A Miranda issue and a consent-search issue are not the same test.

sections.heading: Definition — Waiver
sections.body:
Relinquishment of a legal right under the knowledge, voluntariness and other requirements applicable to that particular right.

Identify the right, who held it, the event said to relinquish it, and the governing standard. In the Miranda setting, warnings, understanding, a sufficient waiver, invocation and later renewed questioning each require analysis. Some doctrines permit an implied waiver, but an inference still needs support. Consent-search voluntariness should not automatically be recast as the identical formal waiver requirement used for every other constitutional right.

Example: Hypothetical: an arrested suspect signs a form after warnings. Explain why the signature is evidence to evaluate rather than a conclusive answer to knowledge, voluntariness, prior invocation or the lawfulness of renewed questioning.

Pitfall: The word waiver does not supply one universal test. A later answer or signed form cannot erase the need to analyze the right and sequence of events.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Officers read warnings, obtain a signature and begin questioning. Does the signature conclusively prove an adequate waiver?

Governing principle — Identify the trigger
The Miranda framework concerns custodial interrogation, not every conversation between a suspect and an officer. Analyze custody and interrogation separately and identify the time each condition began. Distinguish the underlying privilege against compelled self-incrimination from the procedural warnings used to protect it. A statement can raise a voluntariness question even where a particular warning issue is absent.

Application and answer
No. Examine the required knowledge, understanding and voluntariness under the applicable rule, along with custody, interrogation and invocation. Miranda rejects replacing the safeguards with a boilerplate assertion.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A signature alone conclusively establishes a sufficient waiver regardless of understanding or coercion.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Avoiding a direct question categorically prevents conduct from being interrogation under Innis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Custody alone establishes every element of custodial interrogation without analyzing police conduct.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Officers avoid direct questions but speak near a suspect. Does that automatically prevent Miranda interrogation?

Governing principle — Warnings, waiver, and invocation
Record which warnings were given, whether a legally sufficient waiver occurred, and whether the person later invoked silence or counsel. The fact that warnings were read does not automatically establish every element of waiver. Separate initial waiver from the rules governing renewed questioning after invocation. A later answer does not erase the need to analyze how police obtained permission to proceed.

Application and answer
No. Innis includes the functional equivalent: relevant conduct officers should know is reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response. Apply that standard to what officers knew and did; not every overheard conversation qualifies.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A signature alone conclusively establishes a sufficient waiver regardless of understanding or coercion.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Avoiding a direct question categorically prevents conduct from being interrogation under Innis.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Custody alone establishes every element of custodial interrogation without analyzing police conduct.

sections.body: List custody, warnings, questions, waiver, invocation, any break, renewed initiation, and later statements. sections.heading: Fifth and Sixth Amendment separation
sections.body: The Miranda counsel safeguard addresses custodial interrogation; the Sixth Amendment assistance-of-counsel right concerns adversary criminal proceedings and its own framework. An undercover interaction can therefore require analysis different from a standard warned interview. Identify the constitutional source before analyzing an informant’s conduct. The supplied chapter supports this distinction, but these notes do not assert a fully sourced brief or current-law update for every decision named in the outline.

sections.heading: Interrogation under Innis
sections.body:
Miranda interrogation includes express questioning and its functional equivalent: police words or actions, beyond ordinary incidents of custody, that officers should recognize as reasonably likely to produce an incriminating response. Evaluate the circumstances from the suspect-oriented protection described in the opinion rather than relying only on an officer’s stated intent.

Exam checklist: First establish custody; then express questioning or its functional equivalent and any applicable exception.

sections.heading: Warnings and waiver
sections.body:
The reproduced Miranda discussion identifies silence, potential use of statements, access to counsel and appointed counsel when appropriate as core warning subjects. The prosecution must establish the relevant warnings and waiver before relying on covered interrogation evidence. Do not infer a valid waiver solely from the existence of a printed waiver clause.

Exam checklist: Identify required warnings, understanding, voluntary choice and the specific waiver evidence.

sections.heading: Definition — Custodial interrogation
sections.body:
Interrogation occurring while the person is in custody for purposes of the Miranda framework. Custody and interrogation are distinct requirements.

The handout combines an arrest-like custody description with questioning. Keep the two inquiries separate: determine the restraint and circumstances relevant to custody, then ask whether express questioning or its functional equivalent occurred. Innis includes conduct officers should know is reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, beyond conduct ordinarily attendant to custody. A statement may be volunteered without being a product of interrogation.

Example: Hypothetical: officers transport a restrained suspect without asking questions. Custody does not by itself establish interrogation; examine any remarks or actions alleged to be its functional equivalent.

Pitfall: The fact that someone cannot leave does not by itself establish every Miranda requirement. Conversely, avoiding a question mark does not necessarily avoid interrogation.

sections.heading: Definition — Voluntariness
sections.body:
A context-dependent inquiry into whether consent or a statement resulted from a legally impermissible coercive setting or conduct; the governing doctrine depends on the right and event.

For consent searches, assess the total circumstances instead of treating a yes response as conclusive. For a confession, analyze the applicable due-process and interrogation safeguards separately. The handout’s references to threats, coercion and deception are issue signals, not a rule that every deception has an identical legal result. State which doctrine governs and how the actual pressure affected the choice.

Example: Hypothetical: a search follows permission given during a contested detention. Analyze the detention, voluntary consent and any resulting causal-remedy problem separately.

Pitfall: Do not collapse voluntariness, knowledge, waiver and the effects of earlier illegality into a single conclusion. A Miranda issue and a consent-search issue are not the same test.

sections.heading: Definition — Waiver
sections.body:
Relinquishment of a legal right under the knowledge, voluntariness and other requirements applicable to that particular right.

Identify the right, who held it, the event said to relinquish it, and the governing standard. In the Miranda setting, warnings, understanding, a sufficient waiver, invocation and later renewed questioning each require analysis. Some doctrines permit an implied waiver, but an inference still needs support. Consent-search voluntariness should not automatically be recast as the identical formal waiver requirement used for every other constitutional right.

Example: Hypothetical: an arrested suspect signs a form after warnings. Explain why the signature is evidence to evaluate rather than a conclusive answer to knowledge, voluntariness, prior invocation or the lawfulness of renewed questioning.

Pitfall: The word waiver does not supply one universal test. A later answer or signed form cannot erase the need to analyze the right and sequence of events.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A suspect invokes counsel and later answers a renewed police question. Why is the later answer not the end of the analysis?

Governing principle — Build a chronology

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A later answer conclusively erases any need to analyze prior invocation or initiation of renewed questioning.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Miranda counsel safeguards and Sixth Amendment counsel rights have identical procedural triggers.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Double Jeopardy, Speedy Trial and Guilty Pleas
references: Modern Criminal Procedure: Cases, Comments, Questions, 15th ed., chapters 20, 22 and 26
modules.scope: Supplemental source: this casebook is not the assigned Criminal Procedure treatise, 7th edition. These notes support the listed assigned issues but do not certify completion of the assigned treatise pages. Review the assigned text when available.

sections.heading: Speedy trial balancing
sections.body: Barker evaluates length of delay, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice together. Delay is not assessed by a single constitutional number applicable to all cases. Identify which periods count and why the prosecution or defense caused them. A defendant’s failure to demand trial is relevant but not an automatic waiver of the constitutional protection.

sections.heading: Pleas and informed choice
sections.body: A guilty plea changes the litigation posture and requires its own validity inquiry. Identify the defendant’s understanding of the charge and consequences relevant to the governing rule, voluntariness, counsel, and the record supporting acceptance. Do not treat an attractive bargain as conclusive proof that the plea was valid or that no earlier claim can matter. State which challenge survives the plea under the applicable assignment.

sections.heading: Jeopardy and the second proceeding
sections.body: Before asking whether a new prosecution is prohibited, identify when jeopardy attached, how the first proceeding ended, who requested termination, and whether the same offense or a distinct issue is involved. A mistrial, acquittal, dismissal, and conviction have different consequences. The outline’s Perez, Kennedy, Lee, and Johnson assignments require these distinctions. Avoid the shorthand that any second courtroom appearance is unconstitutional.

sections.heading: Barker speedy-trial balancing
sections.body:
The Barker discussion uses a contextual balance rather than a fixed constitutional stopwatch. Its factors are delay length, reason for delay, assertion of the right and prejudice. Delay length can trigger the fuller inquiry, while different reasons for delay receive different weight. Statutory deadlines are a separate issue.

Exam checklist: Assess length, reasons, assertion and prejudice together; distinguish constitutional and statutory rules.

sections.heading: Attachment of jeopardy
sections.body:
The supplied discussion states the usual attachment points: a jury is empaneled and sworn in a jury trial, while the first witness is sworn in a bench trial. Attachment starts the analysis rather than deciding every mistrial or reprosecution question. Determine the procedural event before considering the doctrine governing a later prosecution.

Exam checklist: Identify trial type and attachment; then analyze termination, mistrial or later-prosecution issues separately.

sections.heading: A valid guilty plea and waived trial rights
sections.body:
A guilty plea gives up important trial protections, including jury trial, confrontation and the privilege against self-incrimination. The discussion therefore requires a voluntary choice and knowing, intelligent waivers with sufficient awareness of relevant circumstances and likely consequences. Do not reduce the inquiry to whether the defendant merely said guilty.

Exam checklist: Identify voluntariness, understanding and the particular trial rights relinquished.

sections.heading: Case brief — Barker v. Wingo
sections.body:
407 U.S. 514 (1972)

Facts: Barker’s trial was repeatedly continued while the prosecution pursued a codefendant whose testimony it wanted. Barker did not object to many continuances.

Posture: Constitutional speedy-trial challenge after conviction.

Issue: How should lengthy delay be evaluated?

Holding: The Court adopted balancing and found no speedy-trial violation on this record.

Reasoning: Length, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice interact. The record indicated Barker did not truly want an earlier trial and did not establish the prejudice needed in the overall assessment.

Rule: The constitutional test balances the four identified factors rather than applying one fixed deadline.

Significance: Do not treat silence as automatic waiver or long delay as automatically conclusive; explain the weight of each factor.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A defendant experiences lengthy delay but makes no early demand for trial. Is the constitutional claim automatically waived?

Governing principle — Speedy trial balancing
Barker evaluates length of delay, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice together. Delay is not assessed by a single constitutional number applicable to all cases. Identify which periods count and why the prosecution or defense caused them. A defendant’s failure to demand trial is relevant but not an automatic waiver of the constitutional protection.

Application and answer
No. Barker balances length, reasons, assertion and prejudice together. Failure to assert is relevant, not a universal automatic waiver; explain the particular periods and effects.

sections.heading: Jury entitlement and waiver
sections.body: The right to a jury depends on the nature of the offense and the governing seriousness threshold, not merely the label criminal. Keep the existence of the right separate from whether it was validly waived and what participation the judge and prosecution must have under the applicable rule. The assigned Baldwin and Patton readings address these distinct issues.

sections.heading: What facts change authorized punishment
sections.body: The supplemental sentencing chapter presents the distinction between facts used to select a sentence within an authorized range and facts that increase the legal maximum. Apprendi assigns qualifying maximum-increasing facts to a jury under the reasonable-doubt standard, subject to the prior-conviction exception stated in that decision. Identify the maximum authorized by the verdict before evaluating the additional fact-finding; a legislature’s label alone does not answer the constitutional question.

sections.heading: Do not combine every sentencing issue
sections.body: Discretion over sentencing information, constitutional limits on capital punishment, and jury allocation of aggravating facts are different subjects. The outline assigns Williams, Furman, and Apprendi for those reasons. State the procedural rule and the particular restriction actually implicated. These notes preserve the assigned historical decision’s framing and are not a claim that every later sentencing case or current statutory scheme has been reviewed.

sections.heading: Serious versus petty offenses and the jury right
sections.body:
The chapter explains that an offense authorizing more than six months of imprisonment is not petty for the jury-trial inquiry. A maximum of six months or less is presumptively petty, but sufficiently serious additional statutory penalties can matter. Use the authorized penalties, not merely the sentence eventually imposed.

Exam checklist: Identify maximum authorized incarceration and any sufficiently severe additional statutory penalties.

sections.heading: Apprendi and sentence-increasing facts
sections.body:
The reproduced Apprendi rule generally reserves to the jury, using proof beyond a reasonable doubt, facts that increase punishment beyond the prescribed statutory maximum, apart from the stated prior-conviction exception. Identify the legally relevant ceiling and the fact increasing it; do not equate this inquiry with every fact a judge considers in sentencing.

Exam checklist: Identify the statutory maximum, the fact increasing it, who found the fact and the proof standard.

sections.heading: Case brief — Apprendi v. New Jersey
sections.body:
530 U.S. 466 (2000)

Facts: A firearm offense carried a ten-year maximum. After finding a bias-related purpose by a preponderance, a judge imposed a twelve-year sentence under an enhancement.

Posture: Constitutional challenge to the enhanced sentence after a guilty plea.

Issue: Could the judge’s finding authorize punishment above the maximum otherwise supported by the offense?

Holding: The Court rejected that allocation and standard of proof for the maximum-increasing fact.

Reasoning: Constitutional jury and proof protections concern the facts authorizing punishment, not merely whether the legislature calls them elements or sentencing factors. The decision stated a prior-conviction exception.

Rule: Other than the stated prior-conviction exception, a fact increasing the maximum must be submitted to a jury and proved beyond a reasonable doubt.

Significance: Find the maximum authorized before the disputed finding. Keep the assigned historical formulation separate from later sentencing developments not reviewed here.

Source scope: Review draft from the supplied casebook’s reproduction or discussion of this decision. This is supplemental to the assigned seventh-edition treatise and does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A judge finds an additional fact and imposes punishment above the maximum otherwise authorized. What starting comparison does Apprendi require?

Governing principle — Jury entitlement and waiver
The right to a jury depends on the nature of the offense and the governing seriousness threshold, not merely the label criminal. Keep the existence of the right separate from whether it was validly waived and what participation the judge and prosecution must have under the applicable rule. The assigned Baldwin and Patton readings address these distinct issues.

Application and answer
Compare the maximum authorized before the disputed finding with the enhanced punishment. Analyze jury allocation and proof beyond a reasonable doubt under the decision’s rule and stated prior-conviction exception.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A legislature’s sentencing-factor label conclusively decides whether a fact must go to a jury.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A finding increasing the legal maximum is always identical to selecting a sentence within an authorized range.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Apprendi requires no comparison between the original authorized maximum and the enhanced punishment.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Does a statutory label calling a maximum-increasing fact a sentencing factor by itself answer the jury question?

Governing principle — What facts change authorized punishment
The supplemental sentencing chapter presents the distinction between facts used to select a sentence within an authorized range and facts that increase the legal maximum. Apprendi assigns qualifying maximum-increasing facts to a jury under the reasonable-doubt standard, subject to the prior-conviction exception stated in that decision. Identify the maximum authorized by the verdict before evaluating the additional fact-finding; a legislature’s label alone does not answer the constitutional question.

Application and answer
No. The constitutional analysis concerns the effect of the fact on authorized punishment, not merely the legislative label. Distinguish that question from selection within an already authorized range.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A legislature’s sentencing-factor label conclusively decides whether a fact must go to a jury.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A finding increasing the legal maximum is always identical to selecting a sentence within an authorized range.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Apprendi requires no comparison between the original authorized maximum and the enhanced punishment.

sections.heading: Case brief — Faretta v. California
sections.body:
422 U.S. 806 (1975)

Facts: Faretta asked to represent himself before trial. The judge tested his legal knowledge and required representation by appointed counsel despite his stated choice.

Posture: Review of the resulting conviction.

Issue: Could a competent defendant make an informed choice to conduct the trial defense personally?

Holding: The Court recognized the right of self-representation in the trial setting.

Reasoning: The Sixth Amendment gives defense rights to the accused personally. Legal skill and an informed choice to surrender counsel are distinct; unwanted counsel cannot simply replace the defendant’s considered decision.

Rule: A legally sufficient knowing and intelligent choice can support trial self-representation despite lack of a lawyer’s technical ability.

Significance: Keep trial self-representation separate from appellate representation and later competency or procedural limitations not resolved by this brief.

Source scope: Primary decision reproduced in the supplied Modern Criminal Procedure casebook, 15th ed. The assigned source is a different seventh-edition treatise; this does not certify completion of its pages.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A defendant wishes to conduct the trial defense personally but lacks a lawyer’s technical knowledge. What distinction does Faretta draw?

Governing principle — Identify the review vehicle
Direct appeal, discretionary review, and collateral relief are not interchangeable. Identify the judgment challenged, the reviewing court, the source of review authority, and any preservation or finality issue. A claim that an error occurred at trial is different from a showing that this particular review vehicle authorizes relief for it. The supplemental chapter notes the distinction between creation of an appeal and constitutional requirements governing an appeal once available.

Application and answer
Technical legal skill differs from a legally sufficient informed choice to surrender counsel. Analyze the trial self-representation right and awareness of disadvantages without automatically demanding professional legal expertise.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A defendant must demonstrate professional legal skill before any informed self-representation choice can be recognized.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Faretta’s trial holding automatically decides every separate appellate-representation question.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A collateral-review court may ignore the review vehicle’s prerequisites whenever a trial error is alleged.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A defendant alleges trial error in a collateral-review petition. May the court ignore the review vehicle’s requirements?

Governing principle — Self-representation
