sections.heading: Review method and limits
sections.body: This is a cumulative companion to existing source-linked module guides, not an additional assigned reading. Begin by identifying the parties, institutional roles, chronological sequence, claim, governing source and remedy. Organize an answer around the material issues rather than reciting every rule you remember. For each issue, state the relevant source-backed standard, apply the important facts, address the strongest counterargument and reach a limited conclusion. Keep historical holdings and unreviewed later developments separate. The topic summaries below are reused from the underlying original guides so that missing source material is not replaced by invented textbook content.

sections.heading: Introduction to Search and Seizure
sections.body: Before asking whether police needed a warrant, determine whether governmental conduct was a search or seizure. Katz concerns interception of a private telephone conversation even without physical entry into the booth. Its rejection of a purely place-based or physical-entry approach does not convert every governmental observation into an invasion of a general constitutional right to privacy.

sections.heading: Warrant Requirement
sections.body: Identify whether the state conduct is a search, a seizure of property, or a seizure of a person. A warrant application must connect the facts to the place, person, or evidence targeted. Probable cause evaluates the factual basis in context rather than requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Keep an officer’s factual information separate from conclusions that simply repeat the statutory language.

sections.heading: Stop and Frisk
sections.body: Identify the moment and method of restraint. A consensual conversation is not automatically a seizure, and a stop is not automatically an arrest. Explain the facts that change the category rather than attaching a label to the entire encounter. The outline’s Hodari D. and Bostick assignments concern important boundary questions, so a general Terry summary cannot substitute for those additional analyses.

sections.heading: Warrantless Vehicle, Premises and Container Searches
sections.body: A search incident to a lawful arrest is justified by officer safety and preservation of accessible evidence. Identify the arrestee’s person and the area within immediate control rather than treating arrest as authorization to search every nearby room or container. The scope must remain tied to the reasons for the exception.

sections.heading: Consent Searches and Entrapment
sections.body: A consent argument requires examining whether consent was voluntary, whether the person had authority relevant to the search, and what scope was actually permitted. These are separate questions. Do not assume that a polite request establishes consent or that agreeing to one location or purpose authorizes an unlimited investigation. The actual words, surrounding pressures, and conduct matter.

sections.heading: Exclusionary Rule
sections.body: Begin by identifying the specific constitutional violation and whose rights were affected. Then determine whether the challenged evidence was obtained through it. Exclusion is a remedy with its own scope and exceptions; neither the existence of a violation nor an officer’s assertion of good intentions alone resolves admissibility.

sections.heading: Limitations on Prosecutors
sections.body: Identify evidence favorable to the defense, suppression or nondisclosure attributable to the prosecution, and materiality. Favorability can include impeachment as well as directly exculpatory information. The significance of an item depends on the charges, defense theory, witnesses, and record as a whole. Do not equate any discovery violation with the same constitutional remedy.

sections.heading: Fifth Amendment Privilege
sections.body: The Miranda framework concerns custodial interrogation, not every conversation between a suspect and an officer. Analyze custody and interrogation separately and identify the time each condition began. Distinguish the underlying privilege against compelled self-incrimination from the procedural warnings used to protect it. A statement can raise a voluntariness question even where a particular warning issue is absent.

sections.heading: Miranda
sections.body: List custody, warnings, questions, waiver, invocation, any break, renewed initiation, and later statements. Different rules can turn on which event happened first and who restarted the discussion. Do not treat a new signature on a warning form as a complete answer to a prior invocation problem.

sections.heading: Double Jeopardy, Speedy Trial and Guilty Pleas
sections.body: Barker evaluates length of delay, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice together. Delay is not assessed by a single constitutional number applicable to all cases. Identify which periods count and why the prosecution or defense caused them. A defendant’s failure to demand trial is relevant but not an automatic waiver of the constitutional protection.

sections.heading: Trial Rights and Sentencing
sections.body: The right to a jury depends on the nature of the offense and the governing seriousness threshold, not merely the label criminal. Keep the existence of the right separate from whether it was validly waived and what participation the judge and prosecution must have under the applicable rule. The assigned Baldwin and Patton readings address these distinct issues.

sections.heading: Appellate Review
sections.body: Direct appeal, discretionary review, and collateral relief are not interchangeable. Identify the judgment challenged, the reviewing court, the source of review authority, and any preservation or finality issue. A claim that an error occurred at trial is different from a showing that this particular review vehicle authorizes relief for it. The supplemental chapter notes the distinction between creation of an appeal and constitutional requirements governing an appeal once available.

sections.heading: Self-check before submitting

An officer justifies a frisk solely by the grounds for an investigative stop, then calls the discovered item admissible because the stop was lawful. What steps are missing?

Governing principle — Review method and limits

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Non-Corporate Entities
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 1.7–1.12, 1.14–1.15
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law.

sections.heading: Formation and identifying the enterprise
sections.body: A general partnership is identified by a co-owned business for profit, not merely by the label on a document. An express agreement helps establish the relationship, but conduct may show an implied arrangement. Separate the evidence of profit participation from the ability to participate in important management decisions. An agreement that profit shares compensate a loan or services can have a different legal effect from an ownership arrangement. A joint venture generally concerns a narrower project or shorter duration, but its essential co-ownership and control questions resemble partnership questions.

sections.heading: Liability and organization are separate inquiries
sections.body: A limited partnership uses a statutory formation process and separates general-partner and limited-partner positions. Identify the governing statute before applying the fifth edition’s historical discussion of limited-partner participation in management. An LLC combines an entity liability shield with an operating agreement and statutory defaults. Determine whether members manage directly or have appointed managers; the word member alone does not establish authority to transact. An entity shield does not answer whether a person is liable for that person’s own conduct or separate contractual undertaking.

sections.heading: Contract, tax, and less familiar forms
sections.body: The LLC operating agreement supplies negotiated rules on governance, transfers, duration, and exits, subject to nonwaivable statutory limits. Read the statute and agreement together rather than assuming corporate defaults apply. The book contrasts pass-through treatment with entity-level taxation and possible owner-level tax on distributions; its historical tax eligibility numbers should not be reused as current advice. Joint stock companies can offer centralized management and transferable interests without the corporate liability shield. In a business trust, trustees hold legal title and manage assets for beneficial owners under the declaration of trust.

sections.heading: Exam method and comparison
sections.body: Build a separate row for formation, management, owner exposure, transferability, duration, and tax treatment for each candidate form. On a lender-control problem, identify which provisions merely protect repayment and which give the lender meaningful participation as an owner. Do not equate economic dependence, a profit-based return, or a veto by itself with partnership. In an LLC problem, quote the operating-agreement term that displaces a default and identify any mandatory rule preventing displacement. The point is to explain the legal consequences of the facts, not select a label based only on the parties’ preferred terminology.

sections.heading: Recognizing a general partnership
sections.body:
A partnership can arise from how people conduct a profit-making business together, even without a formal partnership agreement or filing. Analyze co-ownership through both economic participation and the power to share in significant management decisions. Profit sharing is evidence, not a complete substitute for the co-ownership inquiry. Keep entity treatment for particular legal purposes separate from the partners’ own liability.

Exam checklist: Identify two or more persons; a business for profit; co-ownership; profit participation and meaningful management power.

sections.heading: Limited partnerships and statutory formation
sections.body:
A limited partnership is a statutory business form, unlike a general partnership that may arise informally. The traditional structure separates general partners, who manage and face general-partner liability, from limited partners whose liability protection depends on the governing statute. Check the formation filing and applicable statutory version before treating an investor as protected.

Exam checklist: Check the governing limited-partnership statute, required certificate, partner classes and statutory liability provisions.

sections.heading: LLC ownership and operating agreements
sections.body:
An LLC is a statutory entity with members rather than corporate shareholders. Its operating agreement organizes the owners’ economic and management relationship. Limited liability and flexible governance are important features, but distribution rights, management rights and tax treatment are distinct questions. Do not infer that a share of profits necessarily gives a member an immediate right to demand a distribution.

Exam checklist: Identify members, applicable statute, operating agreement, management arrangement and distribution terms.

sections.heading: Case brief — Martin v. Peyton
sections.body:
158 N.E. 77 (N.Y. 1927)

Facts: Creditors providing financial support to a brokerage firm received profit-related returns and contractual protections. Another creditor sought to treat them as partners.

Posture: Appeal from a judgment rejecting actual-partnership liability.

Issue: Did the financing arrangement make the lenders co-owners of a business for profit?

Holding: The court affirmed that the lenders were not actual partners under the agreement.

Reasoning: The arrangement had to be assessed as a whole. Profit participation could compensate a loan, and protective terms did not necessarily transfer the ownership role. A disclaimer of partnership was relevant but not conclusive.

Rule: The relationship’s substance controls; a share of profits is important evidence but not invariably determinative of partnership.

Significance: Identify meaningful co-ownership and management powers, not just profit-based compensation or a no-partnership label.

Source scope: Decision reproduced in the supplied Macey, Moll & Hamilton casebook, 14th ed.; the syllabus assigns the 15th edition. Use the case citation, not an assumed edition-to-edition page match.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Hypothetical: A lender receives a profit-based return and a veto over unusually risky borrowing. Does that alone establish a partnership?

Governing principle — Formation and identifying the enterprise
A general partnership is identified by a co-owned business for profit, not merely by the label on a document. An express agreement helps establish the relationship, but conduct may show an implied arrangement. Separate the evidence of profit participation from the ability to participate in important management decisions. An agreement that profit shares compensate a loan or services can have a different legal effect from an ownership arrangement. A joint venture generally concerns a narrower project or shorter duration, but its essential co-ownership and control questions resemble partnership questions.

Application and answer
No. Evaluate the whole arrangement for co-ownership and meaningful management participation. Profit-based loan compensation and protective restrictions are evidence to evaluate, not automatic ownership.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Any profit-based return necessarily makes a lender an owner regardless of the complete arrangement.
Do not use this incorrect approach: LLC membership alone supplies authority to make every possible contract for the entity.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A limited-liability form eliminates every owner’s liability for personal conduct or separate undertakings.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
An LLC member says that membership automatically authorizes any contract. What documents and legal questions must you examine?

Governing principle — Liability and organization are separate inquiries
A limited partnership uses a statutory formation process and separates general-partner and limited-partner positions. Identify the governing statute before applying the fifth edition’s historical discussion of limited-partner participation in management. An LLC combines an entity liability shield with an operating agreement and statutory defaults. Determine whether members manage directly or have appointed managers; the word member alone does not establish authority to transact. An entity shield does not answer whether a person is liable for that person’s own conduct or separate contractual undertaking.

Application and answer
Identify member-managed or manager-managed governance, the operating agreement, statutory defaults and mandatory limits, and the actual or apparent authority for this transaction. Membership alone does not answer every authority question.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Any profit-based return necessarily makes a lender an owner regardless of the complete arrangement.
Do not use this incorrect approach: LLC membership alone supplies authority to make every possible contract for the entity.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A limited-liability form eliminates every owner’s liability for personal conduct or separate undertakings.

sections.heading: Different classification questions
sections.body: Governmental or municipal corporations must be distinguished from private business corporations. A publicly held company is not necessarily a public governmental body: publicly held ordinarily concerns dispersed ownership and market trading of shares. Closely held describes ownership and the absence of a ready public market, not simply a business’s small size. A substantial enterprise can remain closely held. These classifications answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Nonprofit organization and economic activity
sections.body: Nonprofit corporate status concerns the organization’s purposes and restrictions on distributing benefits; it does not establish that the entity never receives revenue, owns valuable property, or pays employees. Identify the statutory category and permitted beneficiaries. Keep incorporation under nonprofit law separate from tax exemption. A conclusion about one does not automatically establish the other. Start with the actual organizational statute and governing documents rather than the everyday meaning of charity.

sections.heading: Concentrated control and professional entities
sections.body: A corporation may have one shareholder, be family controlled, or be owned wholly or partly by a parent company. Sole ownership does not automatically erase the entity. Minority-investor risks arise where a controller can shape compensation, distributions, and exit opportunities. Professional corporations and professional LLCs add licensing constraints: the organizational form cannot authorize unlicensed practice. Distinguish a professional’s own service-related responsibility from exposure based solely on being an investor in the firm.

sections.heading: Analysis checklist
sections.body: Ask who created the entity, what statutory purpose it serves, who holds ownership rights, whether a trading market exists, and whether occupational licensing limits ownership or management. For a parent-subsidiary problem, preserve the distinction between ownership control and the additional facts needed to disregard separate entities. For a nonprofit, do not infer tax exemption from the charter label. Use the classification to identify the applicable legal rules rather than treating classification itself as the answer to every liability question.

sections.heading: Government corporations versus public companies
sections.body:
A government or public corporation performs a public function under public creation and control. That category is different from a publicly held business corporation whose shares trade among investors. Identify the kind of entity before applying private corporate-law assumptions; some government-created entities operate under a separate statutory framework.

Exam checklist: Distinguish government creation/control from public trading of business shares.

sections.heading: Nonprofit corporate categories
sections.body:
Nonprofit corporations can pursue charitable, mutual-benefit or religious purposes under special statutes. The supplied text discusses a model framework distinguishing these categories and their regulation. Identify the organization’s purpose and governing nonprofit statute rather than treating every nonprofit like an ordinary business corporation.

Exam checklist: Identify charitable/public benefit, mutual benefit or religious purposes; then locate the governing nonprofit statute.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A company has thousands of shareholders and publicly traded shares. Is it therefore a governmental corporation?

Governing principle — Different classification questions
Governmental or municipal corporations must be distinguished from private business corporations. A publicly held company is not necessarily a public governmental body: publicly held ordinarily concerns dispersed ownership and market trading of shares. Closely held describes ownership and the absence of a ready public market, not simply a business’s small size. A substantial enterprise can remain closely held. These classifications answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Application and answer
No. Public trading describes ownership and market characteristics; governmental status concerns its creation, purpose, and governing public law. Analyze the classifications separately.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A publicly traded company is necessarily a governmental corporation.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A nonprofit label automatically establishes tax exemption and prohibits all earned revenue.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Ownership by one person automatically erases corporate entity separateness.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A nonprofit earns substantial revenue. Does that fact alone prove that its nonprofit status is invalid or that it owes no tax?

Governing principle — Nonprofit organization and economic activity
Nonprofit corporate status concerns the organization’s purposes and restrictions on distributing benefits; it does not establish that the entity never receives revenue, owns valuable property, or pays employees. Identify the statutory category and permitted beneficiaries. Keep incorporation under nonprofit law separate from tax exemption. A conclusion about one does not automatically establish the other. Start with the actual organizational statute and governing documents rather than the everyday meaning of charity.

Application and answer
Neither follows. Review the organizational statute, purposes and distribution restrictions. Tax exemption is a separate inquiry and cannot be inferred from revenue or the nonprofit label alone.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Agency
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 1.24, 8.1, 8.5, 8.10, 8.12
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law.

sections.heading: Actual authority
sections.body: A corporation can act only through human agents. Actual authority concerns the principal’s communications to the agent and the powers reasonably included in the assignment. Read the charter, bylaws, board resolutions, delegated responsibilities, and established course of dealing. Express authorization for a task can include incidental acts needed to accomplish it. Distinguish the existence of authority from whether the agent complied with internal instructions; a departure can matter differently to the agent and the third party.

sections.heading: Apparent authority and transaction type
sections.body: Apparent authority concerns the principal’s manifestations to a third party and the resulting reasonable understanding of the agent’s authority. An agent cannot establish it merely by asserting that authority exists. A president or CEO may have authority to carry out ordinary business through express delegation, implied responsibilities, or the corporation’s acquiescence. The title does not automatically authorize extraordinary transactions. Explain why the transaction is ordinary or exceptional in the business’s context.

sections.heading: Ratification and evidence
sections.body: Ratification addresses an originally unauthorized act that the principal later adopts with the legally required knowledge and intent. It is an alternative to proving authority existed at the time of contracting. Acceptance of benefits may matter, but identify what the corporation knew and what conduct communicated adoption. For a major conveyance, mortgage, or long-term commitment, the book recommends obtaining formal evidence such as a certified board resolution rather than relying only on an officer’s assurance.

sections.heading: Exam structure
sections.body: Identify the alleged principal, agent, third party, transaction, and relevant time. Analyze actual authority first, apparent authority separately, then ratification or estoppel if supported. For apparent authority, identify the principal’s particular manifestation and why reliance on it was reasonable. An internal restriction unknown to the third party is not necessarily dispositive. Conclude separately about the corporation’s obligation and any claim concerning the agent’s unauthorized conduct.

sections.heading: Actual and apparent authority
sections.body:
Actual authority concerns what the agent reasonably understands the principal authorized, based on the principal’s manifestations to the agent. Apparent authority instead examines manifestations attributable to the principal that reach a third party. An agent cannot establish apparent authority merely by asserting that it exists. Identify whose communication supports the claimed authority.

Exam checklist: Actual: principal to agent. Apparent: principal to third party. Identify the act and the relevant manifestation.

sections.heading: Ratification of unauthorized corporate acts
sections.body:
A corporation may later adopt an agent’s unauthorized but lawful act when it has capacity to perform that act and the ratifying decision-maker could originally have authorized it. Ratification may be express or inferred from knowledgeable acceptance of benefits or other conduct treating the transaction as binding. Silence alone should not be treated as automatic ratification without the surrounding facts.

Exam checklist: Identify original authority, corporate capacity, the ratifier’s power, knowledge of facts, and express or implied adoption.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A CEO signs an extraordinary asset transaction after merely telling the buyer that the board authorized it. Is apparent authority established?

Governing principle — Actual authority
A corporation can act only through human agents. Actual authority concerns the principal’s communications to the agent and the powers reasonably included in the assignment. Read the charter, bylaws, board resolutions, delegated responsibilities, and established course of dealing. Express authorization for a task can include incidental acts needed to accomplish it. Distinguish the existence of authority from whether the agent complied with internal instructions; a departure can matter differently to the agent and the third party.

Application and answer
Not by the agent’s assertion alone. Identify a manifestation by the corporation and reasonable third-party reliance, examine actual delegation, and distinguish ordinary operations from an extraordinary transaction.

Common mistakes to avoid

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Introduction to Corporations
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 1.10, 2.1–2.9, 7.1–7.2, 9.1
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law.

sections.heading: Entity and investors
sections.body: Corporate personality means that the corporation holds its own assets and contractual rights and bears its own obligations. A shareholder owns an equity interest rather than a fraction of each corporate asset. Keep limited liability analytically separate from that entity status: the corporation can owe a debt without its shareholders automatically owing the debt. Ownership changes ordinarily do not require the corporation to transfer every asset or renegotiate every obligation.

sections.heading: Governance structure
sections.body: The conventional arrangement gives shareholders the power to elect directors and vote on specified fundamental matters; the board directs or oversees corporate affairs; officers conduct delegated operations. A shareholder majority is not automatically authorized to make every management decision directly. Conversely, the board’s broad management role is not a license to ignore shareholder votes required by statute or governing documents. State which institution has initial authority and what approvals the specific transaction requires.

sections.heading: Historical development and enabling law
sections.body: The assigned history explains the transition from special governmental grants toward general incorporation statutes and greater organizational flexibility. The practical drafting consequence is to distinguish mandatory rules from defaults that may be changed in the charter or bylaws. Do not use the history to assume that every present statute is identical. The entity’s state of incorporation supplies the starting framework for its internal governance.

sections.heading: Worked analysis method
sections.body: When an owner orders an officer to sign an agreement, identify whether the owner is acting as shareholder, director, officer, or a specially authorized agent. Then determine whether that capacity supplies the power asserted. A person may occupy several roles, but the legal consequences of each role differ. For a tax question, distinguish the entity’s state-law form from its tax classification and flag the historical scope of the assigned edition.

sections.heading: The corporate governance structure
sections.body:
The traditional structure separates shareholders, directors and officers. Shareholders select directors; the board manages or supervises corporate affairs and appoints officers; officers execute the business’s policies. Certain fundamental transactions require shareholder approval under governing statutes. Ownership therefore does not make each shareholder an independent manager or agent of the corporation.

Exam checklist: Separate ownership, board supervision, officer execution and statutorily reserved shareholder decisions.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A shareholder owns every share and claims personal ownership of each corporate asset. What distinction is missing?

Governing principle — Entity and investors
Corporate personality means that the corporation holds its own assets and contractual rights and bears its own obligations. A shareholder owns an equity interest rather than a fraction of each corporate asset. Keep limited liability analytically separate from that entity status: the corporation can owe a debt without its shareholders automatically owing the debt. Ownership changes ordinarily do not require the corporation to transfer every asset or renegotiate every obligation.

Application and answer
The corporation owns its assets; the shareholder owns an equity interest. Sole ownership does not automatically erase entity separateness or determine liability for corporate obligations.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A sole shareholder personally owns each corporate asset rather than an equity interest.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A shareholder majority automatically has every management power in a shareholder capacity.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Statutory shareholder approvals can always be ignored because directors have a general management role.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A majority shareholder instructs an officer to make a management decision. Which roles must the answer distinguish?

Governing principle — Governance structure
The conventional arrangement gives shareholders the power to elect directors and vote on specified fundamental matters; the board directs or oversees corporate affairs; officers conduct delegated operations. A shareholder majority is not automatically authorized to make every management decision directly. Conversely, the board’s broad management role is not a license to ignore shareholder votes required by statute or governing documents. State which institution has initial authority and what approvals the specific transaction requires.

Application and answer
Shareholder voting powers, collective board authority, and the officer’s delegated agency authority. A person can hold several roles, but each asserted act needs authority in the relevant capacity.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A sole shareholder personally owns each corporate asset rather than an equity interest.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A shareholder majority automatically has every management power in a shareholder capacity.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Statutory shareholder approvals can always be ignored because directors have a general management role.

sections.body:

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A local business chooses an out-of-state corporate domicile solely because it is popular. What costs should the advice address?

Governing principle — Choosing a legal form
Selection is a comparison of legal and practical consequences, not a universal preference for incorporation. Identify who will invest, who will manage, how much personal exposure participants accept, the expected duration of the venture, and how an owner can leave. Financing and transfer needs may favor an entity with stable centralized governance. Tax treatment, administrative expense, and the parties’ appetite for negotiated arrangements also matter. A form suitable at inception may require later conversion as the business changes.

Application and answer
Compare governing law and desired flexibility with foreign qualification, duplicate fees or taxes, recurring administration, counsel familiarity, and the actual locations of operations. Popularity alone is insufficient.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Popularity of a domicile conclusively establishes the best state of incorporation for every local business.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Out-of-state incorporation automatically removes qualification duties in every operating state.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A recommendation naming an entity form needs no connection to control, liability, financing or exit objectives.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Incorporation and Premature Commencement
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 3.3–3.11, 5.1–5.12, 6.1–6.7
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law.

sections.heading: Formation chronology
sections.body: Separate planning and promotion from filing and organizational action after filing. The book’s sequence includes financing arrangements, name reservation, selecting a registered office and agent, preparing and filing articles, paying fees, and conducting organizational meetings. Directors then organize governance through officers, bylaws, and authorized share issuances. Determine the point at which the governing statute recognizes corporate existence before analyzing who could act for it.

sections.heading: Promoter contracts
sections.body: A promoter’s agreement made before incorporation raises separate questions about the promoter’s liability and the later corporation’s liability. A nonexistent principal cannot itself have authorized a contract when it was signed. Review the contract’s language about the parties, intended obligor, and any condition that incorporation occur. The later corporation may adopt the arrangement, but adoption does not necessarily release the promoter. Identify an actual agreement substituting the corporation and discharging the prior obligor before concluding that a novation occurred.

sections.heading: Charter, bylaws, and statutory defaults
sections.body: Some provisions may be varied only in the articles; others may be placed in bylaws. Broad lawful-purpose clauses can allow operational flexibility, while an intentionally narrow purpose provision can constrain management. Determine whether a disputed term is permitted, properly located, and consistent with mandatory law. A charter is not merely a private deal among original founders because later investors also take interests under it.

sections.heading: Defects and equitable doctrines
sections.body: When filing or organization is defective, distinguish statutory liability provisions from de facto corporation and corporation-by-estoppel reasoning. De facto analysis concerns an attempted formation and operation under a valid authorizing law. Estoppel examines a party’s conduct in treating the enterprise as corporate and the context of the claim. Do not assume either doctrine survives unchanged under every modern statute. Build a timeline linking the defect, the contract or injury, the parties’ knowledge, and the later corrective act.

sections.heading: The future corporation is not yet a principal
sections.body:
Before formation there is no existing corporation for a promoter to represent as its agent. Incorporation alone does not automatically make the new corporation liable for the promoter’s earlier contracts. Analyze the separate legal basis on which the corporation later becomes bound rather than treating formation itself as adoption.

Exam checklist: Ask whether the corporation existed, who signed, and what later conduct or statute supplies corporate liability.

sections.heading: Adoption does not automatically release the promoter
sections.body:
Corporate adoption and a promoter’s release are separate questions. When a promoter personally contracted for a proposed corporation, the corporation’s later adoption ordinarily does not itself extinguish that liability. A novation or comparable agreement with the other contracting party is needed to substitute the corporation and release the promoter.

Exam checklist: Separate corporate adoption from promoter release; identify assent to a novation.

sections.heading: De facto corporation analysis
sections.body:
The traditional de facto doctrine can protect an imperfectly formed business under specified conditions, including an available incorporation statute, a good-faith formation effort, apparent compliance and use of corporate powers. The doctrine and its survival depend on the relevant statute and jurisdiction. It is not a universal cure for ignoring formation requirements.

Exam checklist: Check applicable law; good-faith formation effort; colorable compliance; exercise of corporate powers.

sections.heading: Corporation by estoppel is transaction-specific
sections.body:
Estoppel may prevent a party from denying corporate existence in a particular dealing even when general de facto status is unavailable. It does not necessarily create a corporation for every purpose. Focus on the transaction, the parties’ dealings and the jurisdiction’s doctrine rather than labeling the entity fully valid.

Exam checklist: Identify the specific transaction, the party denying corporate status and the applicable estoppel rule.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A promoter signs before incorporation. The later corporation adopts the contract. Has the promoter necessarily been released?

Governing principle — Formation chronology
Separate planning and promotion from filing and organizational action after filing. The book’s sequence includes financing arrangements, name reservation, selecting a registered office and agent, preparing and filing articles, paying fees, and conducting organizational meetings. Directors then organize governance through officers, bylaws, and authorized share issuances. Determine the point at which the governing statute recognizes corporate existence before analyzing who could act for it.

Application and answer
No. Analyze promoter liability, corporate adoption, and a separate novation or agreement releasing the earlier obligor. Corporate adoption alone need not establish the required discharge.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Later corporate adoption necessarily discharges the promoter without any release or novation inquiry.
Do not use this incorrect approach: An informal agreement always satisfies a statutory requirement that a term appear in the articles.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every formation defect automatically receives the same equitable treatment in every modern statute.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Organizers informally agree to a governance variation that the statute permits only in the articles. Is an oral agreement enough?

Governing principle — Promoter contracts
A promoter’s agreement made before incorporation raises separate questions about the promoter’s liability and the later corporation’s liability. A nonexistent principal cannot itself have authorized a contract when it was signed. Review the contract’s language about the parties, intended obligor, and any condition that incorporation occur. The later corporation may adopt the arrangement, but adoption does not necessarily release the promoter. Identify an actual agreement substituting the corporation and discharging the prior obligor before concluding that a novation occurred.

Application and answer
Not on that premise. Identify the mandatory document requirement, whether it was satisfied, and the effect of the defect. Distinguish charter provisions, bylaws and informal understandings.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Later corporate adoption necessarily discharges the promoter without any release or novation inquiry.
Do not use this incorrect approach: An informal agreement always satisfies a statutory requirement that a term appear in the articles.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every formation defect automatically receives the same equitable treatment in every modern statute.

references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. § 4.4, §§ 7.1–7.6; Macey, Moll & Hamilton, supplied 14th ed., ch. 6
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law. The casebook supplied is the fourteenth edition; the outline names the fifteenth.

sections.heading: Starting presumption
sections.body: Separate corporate existence is the starting point. A corporation’s debt is its own, and incorporation for limited liability is itself legitimate. A parent’s ownership of all shares or an individual’s complete control does not automatically make the controller liable. Identify the specific creditor, the unpaid obligation, the person or related entity sought to be charged, and the legal reason for crossing the entity boundary.

sections.heading: Operational separateness
sections.body: Relevant facts include separate accounts, accurate records, corporate decision-making, treatment of receipts, payment of personal expenses, and transfers among related companies. Explain how each fact shows genuine separateness or its misuse. The book treats intermingled affairs and disregard of formalities as important, but do not reduce a multi-factor inquiry to a single missed meeting. The governing jurisdiction and type of entity affect the weight of formalities.

sections.heading: Domination, capitalization, and injury
sections.body: Domination is commonly paired with an additional requirement involving fraud, illegality, or serious unfairness. Connect the alleged misuse to the creditor’s loss. Undercapitalization is a factor, especially where foreseeable tort risks arise, but insufficient assets after an ordinary business failure do not by themselves prove abuse at formation. Distinguish voluntary contract creditors’ knowledge of the entity from injured persons who had no opportunity to bargain for protection.

sections.heading: Case comparison and exam method
sections.body: Bartle refused to impose a subsidiary’s contract debts on its parent where separate indicia were maintained and the findings showed no fraud, deception, or injurious asset depletion. Use that result as a comparison, not a universal immunity for parent companies. Contrast facts showing deliberate diversion of assets or misleading treatment of the entities. Identify the governing test before applying ownership, control, records, capitalization, misuse, and the resulting inequity.

sections.heading: Commingling and disregard of separateness
sections.body:
Veil-piercing analysis examines whether controlling owners actually respected the corporation as a separate business. Intermingled assets and affairs, diverted receipts and serious failures to observe formalities can support a challenge, depending on governing law and context. The issue is not simply that one shareholder controls the company.

Exam checklist: Identify intermingling, misuse of corporate property, ignored boundaries and creditor consequences.

sections.heading: Capital adequacy is a factor, not an automatic test
sections.body:
Capitalization may matter when evaluating whether the corporate form improperly shifts business risks to creditors, especially in tort and closely held settings. The text cautions against treating undercapitalization as a mechanical, standalone ground in every case. Analyze the business’s risks and other circumstances under the governing standard.

Exam checklist: Compare capital with business risks; identify other separateness factors and the relevant jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Case brief — Bartle v. Home Owners Co-op.
sections.body:
127 N.E.2d 832 (N.Y. 1955)

Facts: A cooperative created a wholly owned construction subsidiary. After cost overruns and bankruptcy, the trustee sought to impose the subsidiary’s contract debts on the parent.

Posture: Appeal from refusal to pierce the subsidiary’s veil.

Issue: Did ownership and control justify charging the parent with these debts?

Holding: The refusal to pierce was affirmed.

Reasoning: Findings established maintained separate corporate indicia, no creditor deception, no fraud, and no injurious asset depletion. Forming an entity to obtain limited liability was itself legitimate.

Rule: Ownership and control alone do not necessarily supply the misuse or inequity required to disregard an entity.

Significance: Compare the claimant’s facts to actual abuse. Do not turn this result into immunity for every parent-subsidiary arrangement.

Source scope: Decision reproduced in the supplied Macey, Moll & Hamilton casebook, 14th ed.; the syllabus assigns the 15th edition. Use the case citation, not an assumed edition-to-edition page match.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A subsidiary fails while its parent owns all shares. Is ownership alone enough to make the parent pay its contract debts?

Governing principle — Starting presumption
Separate corporate existence is the starting point. A corporation’s debt is its own, and incorporation for limited liability is itself legitimate. A parent’s ownership of all shares or an individual’s complete control does not automatically make the controller liable. Identify the specific creditor, the unpaid obligation, the person or related entity sought to be charged, and the legal reason for crossing the entity boundary.

Application and answer
No. Start with separateness, identify the governing piercing test, and examine misuse, records, intermingling, capitalization, deception and the link to injury. Bartle illustrates the importance of additional facts.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Complete ownership and control alone necessarily make a parent liable for every subsidiary debt.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Insolvency after ordinary business losses alone conclusively proves capitalization abuse sufficient to pierce.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Incorporating for limited liability is itself an unlawful misuse of the corporate form.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A corporation cannot satisfy a judgment. Why does that not by itself prove inadequate capitalization justifying piercing?

Governing principle — Operational separateness
Relevant facts include separate accounts, accurate records, corporate decision-making, treatment of receipts, payment of personal expenses, and transfers among related companies. Explain how each fact shows genuine separateness or its misuse. The book treats intermingled affairs and disregard of formalities as important, but do not reduce a multi-factor inquiry to a single missed meeting. The governing jurisdiction and type of entity affect the weight of formalities.

Application and answer
Failure after ordinary business losses differs from capitalization inadequate for foreseeable risks under the applicable test. Analyze timing, business risks, other misuse factors, and the jurisdiction’s requirements rather than treating insolvency as conclusive.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Complete ownership and control alone necessarily make a parent liable for every subsidiary debt.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Insolvency after ordinary business losses alone conclusively proves capitalization abuse sufficient to pierce.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Incorporating for limited liability is itself an unlawful misuse of the corporate form.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Closely Held Corporations and Shares
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 16.1–16.12 and ch. 18
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law.

sections.heading: How investors obtain shares
sections.body: Distinguish an original subscription, a sale of treasury shares, and a transfer from an existing shareholder. An issuance brings newly created shares into investor ownership; a secondary transfer substitutes an owner of already outstanding shares. Authorized, issued, and outstanding describe different quantities. A share is the ownership interest, while a certificate is evidence of it. Do not infer that replacing or losing the certificate creates or extinguishes the underlying interest.

sections.heading: Price and consideration
sections.body: A subscription must establish an enforceable undertaking to take and pay for specified shares. Unpaid subscription liability ordinarily runs to the corporation, with creditor remedies depending on the applicable procedural and statutory framework. Par value is not market value. Where a statute retains par value, identify its particular legal consequences rather than assuming it measures economic worth. For no-par shares, directors may have pricing flexibility, but the form and valuation of consideration remain separate issues.

sections.heading: Payment and valuation

sections.heading: Shares versus share certificates

sections.heading: Authorized, issued and outstanding shares
sections.body:
Authorization establishes the shares the charter permits. Issuance creates share interests in owners. Outstanding shares remain in shareholders’ hands; shares reacquired by the corporation may be treasury shares rather than outstanding shares. Keep these categories separate when calculating ownership or evaluating an issuance.

Exam checklist: Determine authorization, issuance, current holders, reacquisition and retirement.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
An investor buys shares from an existing holder. Is that necessarily an original issuance bringing new capital to the corporation?

Governing principle — How investors obtain shares
Distinguish an original subscription, a sale of treasury shares, and a transfer from an existing shareholder. An issuance brings newly created shares into investor ownership; a secondary transfer substitutes an owner of already outstanding shares. Authorized, issued, and outstanding describe different quantities. A share is the ownership interest, while a certificate is evidence of it. Do not infer that replacing or losing the certificate creates or extinguishes the underlying interest.

Application and answer
No. A secondary transfer changes ownership of outstanding shares. Distinguish it from an original subscription and a corporate disposition of treasury shares.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Buying shares from an existing owner is necessarily an original issuance that brings capital to the corporation.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Par value conclusively measures current market value and decides every consideration question.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A share certificate and the underlying ownership interest are legally identical for every purpose.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
Shares have a stated par value. Does that establish their market value or resolve whether services are valid payment?

Governing principle — Price and consideration
A subscription must establish an enforceable undertaking to take and pay for specified shares. Unpaid subscription liability ordinarily runs to the corporation, with creditor remedies depending on the applicable procedural and statutory framework. Par value is not market value. Where a statute retains par value, identify its particular legal consequences rather than assuming it measures economic worth. For no-par shares, directors may have pricing flexibility, but the form and valuation of consideration remain separate issues.

Application and answer
No. Par value, market value, eligibility of the consideration and valuation are separate issues. Apply the governing statute and examine the board’s valuation under the relevant standard.

Do not use this incorrect approach: Buying shares from an existing owner is necessarily an original issuance that brings capital to the corporation.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Par value conclusively measures current market value and decides every consideration question.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A share certificate and the underlying ownership interest are legally identical for every purpose.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Preemptive Rights and Dilution
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. § 16.14
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law.

sections.heading: Purpose of preemptive rights
sections.body: Preemptive rights give qualifying existing owners an opportunity to subscribe proportionately to certain new issuances. Their purpose is to protect against dilution of economic participation and voting influence. Distinguish the existence of that opportunity from a guarantee that the corporation will never issue new shares. An investor who declines a valid proportional offer can still experience a reduced percentage holding.

sections.heading: Finding the source and scope
sections.body: The book describes different statutory and charter approaches, including denying a default right or recognizing a right only when affirmatively granted. Begin with the governing statute and charter. Identify the covered class, type of issuance, eligible holders, and any exception. Do not infer a universal preemptive right solely because the investor acquired shares first.

sections.heading: Proportionate analysis
sections.body: Calculate existing shares and voting power before the issuance, identify the total proposed new issue, and determine the eligible holder’s proportional allocation under the operative provision. Then test whether the offer honored notice, price, and timing requirements. Keep dilution of voting percentage distinct from whether an issuance transferred economic value by selling below an appropriate price.

sections.heading: Fiduciary issues remain
sections.body: Compliance with a preemptive-right clause does not necessarily resolve whether directors used issuance authority for an improper purpose or unfairly favored insiders. Conversely, the absence of a contractual preemptive right does not eliminate all fiduciary constraints. State the particular legal basis for the challenge rather than treating preemption as the only possible objection. Address the requested remedy and the effect on both the corporation and existing holders.

sections.heading: Preemptive rights and dilution
sections.body:
A preemptive right can give an existing shareholder an opportunity to buy a proportionate part of a new issuance. Modern availability depends on the governing statute and charter; it should not be assumed. Analyze the right separately from fiduciary limits on abusive issuance or dilution.

Exam checklist: Check statutory default, charter provisions, scope of the proposed issuance and any distinct fiduciary issue.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A minority investor claims a universal right to buy a proportional share of every new issue. What must be established first?

Governing principle — Purpose of preemptive rights
Preemptive rights give qualifying existing owners an opportunity to subscribe proportionately to certain new issuances. Their purpose is to protect against dilution of economic participation and voting influence. Distinguish the existence of that opportunity from a guarantee that the corporation will never issue new shares. An investor who declines a valid proportional offer can still experience a reduced percentage holding.

Application and answer
Find the governing statutory and charter source, eligible class and covered issuance, including any exceptions. The assigned discussion describes different approaches; no universal entitlement should be assumed.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every existing owner has an unqualified preemptive right for every issuance in every state.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A preemptive opportunity guarantees that no owner will ever experience dilution after declining an offer.
Do not use this incorrect approach: The absence of a preemptive right eliminates every independent fiduciary challenge to an issuance.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A shareholder declines a valid proportional offer and later complains of a lower voting percentage. What distinction matters?

Governing principle — Finding the source and scope
The book describes different statutory and charter approaches, including denying a default right or recognizing a right only when affirmatively granted. Begin with the governing statute and charter. Identify the covered class, type of issuance, eligible holders, and any exception. Do not infer a universal preemptive right solely because the investor acquired shares first.

Application and answer
A preemptive opportunity is different from a guarantee against all dilution. Also analyze any independent fiduciary challenge to pricing or purpose rather than assuming the proportional offer resolves every issue.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every existing owner has an unqualified preemptive right for every issuance in every state.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A preemptive opportunity guarantees that no owner will ever experience dilution after declining an offer.
Do not use this incorrect approach: The absence of a preemptive right eliminates every independent fiduciary challenge to an issuance.

sections.heading: Quorum and voting requirements
sections.body:

sections.heading: Cumulative voting and minority representation
sections.body:
Cumulative voting permits a shareholder to multiply shares by seats being filled and concentrate or distribute those votes. Its function is to facilitate minority board representation compared with straight voting. First establish that cumulative voting is available; then calculate the voting pool and allocation.

Exam checklist: Verify availability; compute shares multiplied by seats; decide allocation among candidates.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Directors separately send informal approvals. Does a majority of messages necessarily equal valid board action?

Governing principle — Who exercises management power
The board has a collective governance role, while officers implement delegated operations. A majority shareholder is not automatically the corporation’s manager in a shareholder capacity. Distinguish selecting directors from controlling each board decision. A person who is simultaneously a shareholder, director, and officer must act through the powers and procedures associated with the relevant role.

No. Check the statute and governing documents, meeting rules, and any authorized written-consent procedure. The book’s discussed no-meeting route requires the relevant unanimity; separate messages are not automatically a lawful meeting.

Do not use this incorrect approach: Quorum alone cures a failure to give legally required notice to a director.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Controlling ownership eliminates the distinction between shareholder voting and board management powers.

sections.heading: Why close corporations create special risks
sections.body: In a closely held firm, ownership may be tied to employment, compensation, management participation, and an expected stream of distributions. Without a ready trading market, a minority owner cannot necessarily escape unfavorable treatment by selling. The same conduct that appears to be an ordinary management choice in a public company can therefore affect an owner’s entire investment arrangement.

sections.heading: Deadlock
sections.body: Identify whether the blockage concerns shareholder votes, board votes, or both, and what business action cannot occur. Equal ownership does not establish that every decision is deadlocked; examine actual voting rules and the disputed action. Determine what tie-breaking, buyout, voting, or succession arrangements the parties adopted. A dissolution request requires the applicable statutory ground, not merely interpersonal hostility.

sections.heading: Oppression and legitimate expectations
sections.body: A claim may concern termination of employment, denial of distributions, excessive compensation to controllers, exclusion from agreed management, or selective access to liquidity. State the jurisdiction’s theory rather than declaring that every disappointed expectation creates liability. Explain the investment-related expectation, the basis for treating it as legitimate, and any competing business justification. Separate harm to the corporation from an owner’s distinct individual injury.

sections.heading: Remedies and planning
sections.body: Compare dissolution, a buyout, enforcement of an agreement, and other relief available under the governing statute and case law. Valuation and who must buy can be as important as establishing wrongdoing. Donahue illustrates a particular jurisdiction’s concern with equal access to a corporate share purchase in a close corporation; it is not an all-jurisdiction rule governing every redemption. Planning provisions should specify valuation, triggering events, funding, and the mechanics of exit rather than relying on an informal promise to be fair.

sections.heading: Deadlock and dissolution
sections.body:
Deadlock can provide a statutory basis for judicial dissolution, but the required circumstances are jurisdiction-specific. The model provisions discussed in the text connect management deadlock with inability to resolve it and resulting injury or business impairment, and separately address prolonged shareholder failure to elect directors. Dissolution is a remedy analysis, not an automatic response to disagreement.

Exam checklist: Identify the statutory ground, decision-making impasse, inability to resolve it and relevant harm or duration.

sections.heading: Oppression in a closely held corporation
sections.body:
Close-company disputes can involve more than voting stalemate. Statutes and equitable doctrines may address fraud, illegality, mismanagement or oppression of minority owners. Because triggers and remedies differ by state, identify the particular protected interest and statutory test rather than assuming a single national reasonable-expectations formula.

Exam checklist: Identify control, alleged oppressive conduct, applicable statutory test and available remedy.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
Two equal owners disagree. What facts distinguish actual deadlock from ordinary disagreement?

Governing principle — Why close corporations create special risks
In a closely held firm, ownership may be tied to employment, compensation, management participation, and an expected stream of distributions. Without a ready trading market, a minority owner cannot necessarily escape unfavorable treatment by selling. The same conduct that appears to be an ordinary management choice in a public company can therefore affect an owner’s entire investment arrangement.

Application and answer
Identify the decision, voting body, applicable thresholds and actual inability to act, plus tie-breaking or exit arrangements. Equal ownership and hostility alone do not establish every statutory dissolution ground.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Equal ownership and interpersonal hostility conclusively establish every statutory dissolution ground.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A minority owner’s investment-related expectations can never matter once shares were issued.
Do not use this incorrect approach: All close-corporation exits and buyouts necessarily use one universal valuation and remedy rule.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
A controller ends a minority owner’s employment and distributions. Why does the investment arrangement matter?

Governing principle — Deadlock
Identify whether the blockage concerns shareholder votes, board votes, or both, and what business action cannot occur. Equal ownership does not establish that every decision is deadlocked; examine actual voting rules and the disputed action. Determine what tie-breaking, buyout, voting, or succession arrangements the parties adopted. A dissolution request requires the applicable statutory ground, not merely interpersonal hostility.

Application and answer
In a close corporation, employment, management and distributions may be central to legitimate investment expectations and liquidity. Analyze the governing oppression or fiduciary theory, business justification, individual versus corporate injury, and available remedies.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Equal ownership and interpersonal hostility conclusively establish every statutory dissolution ground.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A minority owner’s investment-related expectations can never matter once shares were issued.
Do not use this incorrect approach: All close-corporation exits and buyouts necessarily use one universal valuation and remedy rule.

modules.title: Complete module study guide — Duty of Care and Business Judgment Rule
references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 10.1–10.8; Macey, Moll & Hamilton, supplied 14th ed., ch. 10
modules.scope: The supplied fifth edition matches the outline. These notes cover the identified topics, not every proposition in every assigned section. Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law. The casebook is a supplemental fourteenth-edition text.

sections.heading: Conduct standard versus judicial review
sections.body: The duty of care addresses what directors should do; the business judgment rule addresses when a court will defer to a decision. A bad result does not by itself establish a breach, and a favorable result does not prove an adequate process. Identify an actual decision, the information available, the time taken, and whether disinterested directors exercised judgment in good faith. Distinguish a decision from a failure to pay attention at all.

sections.heading: Information and attention
sections.body: The assigned discussion treats regular attendance and attention to corporate affairs as real responsibilities. Analyze how directors obtained information, questioned assumptions, used advisors, and responded to warning signs. Reliance is not a synonym for blind acceptance. Evaluate the reason for relying, the subject matter, and what directors knew or should have investigated under the applicable standard.

sections.heading: Comparing the case illustrations
sections.body: Shlensky involved objections to the Cubs’ refusal to install lights and play night baseball. The case illustrates why a court does not substitute business policy merely because an investor predicts a more profitable alternative. Smith v. Van Gorkom instead examined whether the merger decision was informed and concluded the process was deficient. Keep disagreement over business strategy separate from a claim that the board failed to inform itself before approving a major transaction.

sections.heading: Exam sequence
sections.body: Identify the alleged failure and responsible directors, state the governing care and review standards, assess process using concrete facts, and analyze causation and remedy separately. Check whether a charter provision or statute limits monetary liability and whether its exceptions apply; do not assume it extinguishes every duty or every type of relief. Explain why the facts support deference or rebut it rather than using the business judgment rule as a conclusion without analysis.

sections.heading: Business judgment rule versus duty of care
sections.body:
The duty of care states a conduct obligation; the business judgment rule concerns judicial review of business decisions. Courts generally resist substituting hindsight for a board’s protected judgment, while rationality, good faith and the decision process remain relevant. A bad business outcome alone is not the same thing as an actionable care violation.

Exam checklist: Separate the directors’ conduct standard from the standard of judicial review; examine process and disqualifying facts.

sections.heading: Care is evaluated in context
sections.body:
The text describes an ordinarily prudent director in a comparable position and circumstances, rather than an abstract promise of business success. Consider the corporation’s situation, the director’s role and the attention reasonably required. A conduct breach and damages liability are separate inquiries, including causation and any applicable protection.

Exam checklist: Identify role, circumstances, expected care and attention, causation and governing liability rules.

sections.heading: Case brief — Shlensky v. Wrigley
sections.body:
237 N.E.2d 776 (Ill. App. Ct. 1968)

Facts: A minority shareholder sought damages and installation of lights for night games at Wrigley Field, alleging that refusing night games harmed the Cubs financially.

Posture: Appeal from dismissal of an amended derivative complaint.

Issue: Did the pleaded objections to the directors’ refusal to install lights state a claim warranting judicial interference?

Holding: The dismissal was affirmed.

Reasoning: The alleged disagreement over business policy did not show the fraud, illegality or conflict-related basis for intervention discussed by the court; merely declining to follow other teams was insufficient.

Rule: Business-policy disagreement and a disappointing outcome do not alone establish a basis for judicial substitution of business judgment.

Significance: Separate business disagreement from pleaded facts that defeat deference. This is a supplied-edition case illustration, not a complete account of current director-liability law.

Source scope: Supplied fourteenth edition differs from assigned fifteenth edition; case text and citation were checked in the supplied file.

sections.heading: Case brief — Smith v. Van Gorkom
sections.body:
488 A.2d 858 (Del. 1985)

Facts: Trans Union directors approved a cash-out merger. Shareholders challenged whether the board had adequately informed itself before approving the transaction.

Posture: Appeal from Chancery judgment for the directors.

Issue: Was the merger approval the product of an informed business judgment?

Holding: The judgment for directors was reversed; the Court found the decision uninformed.

Reasoning: The decision-making process, rather than merely the perceived attractiveness of the deal, was central. The record did not support the finding that the board had acted on an adequate informed basis.

Rule: Business judgment deference does not dispense with the governing duty to become adequately informed before deciding.

Significance: Compare the process challenge with Shlensky’s policy disagreement. Keep historical liability rules separate from any later exculpation analysis.

Source scope: Decision reproduced in the supplied Macey, Moll & Hamilton casebook, 14th ed.; the syllabus assigns the 15th edition. Use the case citation, not an assumed edition-to-edition page match.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A board chooses an unpopular strategy after an informed, disinterested process, and the business loses money. Is loss alone a care breach?

Governing principle — Conduct standard versus judicial review
The duty of care addresses what directors should do; the business judgment rule addresses when a court will defer to a decision. A bad result does not by itself establish a breach, and a favorable result does not prove an adequate process. Identify an actual decision, the information available, the time taken, and whether disinterested directors exercised judgment in good faith. Distinguish a decision from a failure to pay attention at all.

Application and answer
No. Separate the conduct standard from business judgment review and evaluate process, good faith and the applicable legal test. A disappointing outcome is not itself proof of deficient decision-making.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A loss alone proves a care breach even when directors used an informed disinterested process.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Business judgment deference removes every need to assess information and deliberation.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A strategy disagreement and an uninformed-process challenge present the same issue in every case.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:
How does a rushed, uninformed merger-approval allegation differ from the disagreement over night baseball in Shlensky?

Governing principle — Information and attention
The assigned discussion treats regular attendance and attention to corporate affairs as real responsibilities. Analyze how directors obtained information, questioned assumptions, used advisors, and responded to warning signs. Reliance is not a synonym for blind acceptance. Evaluate the reason for relying, the subject matter, and what directors knew or should have investigated under the applicable standard.

Application and answer
The former challenges the decision-making process, as illustrated by Van Gorkom; the latter challenged a business-policy choice. Explain the information and deliberation actually used instead of treating every objection as mere strategy disagreement.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: A loss alone proves a care breach even when directors used an informed disinterested process.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Business judgment deference removes every need to assess information and deliberation.
Do not use this incorrect approach: A strategy disagreement and an uninformed-process challenge present the same issue in every case.

references: Cox & Hazen, Business Organizations Law, 5th ed. §§ 10.9–10.15, 11.8–11.10; Macey, Moll & Hamilton, supplied 14th ed., ch. 11A–E

Historical statutory and tax discussions are not a statement of current law. Supplied casebook is the fourteenth edition, not the fifteenth assigned.

sections.heading: Identify the conflict precisely
sections.body: A loyalty problem concerns the fiduciary’s personal interest or competing obligation, not simply an unsuccessful transaction. Identify the corporation, fiduciary, other party, financial interest, and decision influenced by that interest. Distinguish a transaction with the corporation, compensation, use of corporate property or information, and taking an opportunity that may belong to the corporation. Each category can involve different procedures and remedies.

sections.heading: Disclosure, approval, and fairness

sections.heading: Corporate opportunities
sections.body:
A fiduciary may not exploit a position or confidential corporate knowledge to divert an opportunity belonging to the firm for personal benefit. The difficult inquiry is whether the opportunity is sufficiently connected to the corporation and what the relevant jurisdiction requires. Separate the opportunity question from whether the fiduciary disclosed it or obtained valid rejection/approval.

Exam checklist: Identify fiduciary role, connection to corporate business, use of position or information and applicable opportunity test.

sections.heading: Case brief — Marciano v. Nakash
sections.body:
535 A.2d 400 (Del. 1987)

Facts: Fifty-fifty owners disputed loans made to a deadlocked corporation by entities associated with one ownership faction. The loans had not obtained majority board or shareholder approval.

Posture: Appeal from validation of loan claims in the corporation’s liquidation.

Issue: Were the interested loans automatically voidable, or could full fairness support enforcement?

Holding: The court affirmed the finding that the loans were valid and enforceable because the fairness determination was supported.

Reasoning: The opinion rejected treating the absence of majority approval as automatic invalidity on these facts and examined the interested transactions for full fairness.

Rule: The supplied case illustrates substantive fairness review of an interested transaction rather than automatic invalidity based solely on the interest.

Significance: Spot the conflict, then identify the applicable statutory and substantive review framework. Do not treat a 1987 case as an unqualified statement of later statutory law.

Source scope: Supplied fourteenth edition differs from assigned fifteenth edition; case text and citation were checked in the supplied file.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 1
sections.body:
A director benefits from a transaction approved by other directors. What facts must be examined before saying the conflict is cured?

Governing principle — Identify the conflict precisely
A loyalty problem concerns the fiduciary’s personal interest or competing obligation, not simply an unsuccessful transaction. Identify the corporation, fiduciary, other party, financial interest, and decision influenced by that interest. Distinguish a transaction with the corporation, compensation, use of corporate property or information, and taking an opportunity that may belong to the corporation. Each category can involve different procedures and remedies.

Application and answer
Identify material disclosure, disinterestedness and independence, voting requirements, the governing statutory route, substantive fairness and effects on review or burden. Approval alone is not a universal cure.

Common mistakes to avoid
Do not use this incorrect approach: Any board approval automatically cures a conflict without examining disclosure or disinterestedness.
Do not use this incorrect approach: Every opportunity encountered by an officer necessarily belongs to the corporation.
Do not use this incorrect approach: All harm to corporate assets automatically gives every shareholder a separate personal claim.

sections.heading: Worked practice example 2
sections.body:

Governing principle — Disclosure, approval, and fairness
